No more permanent coalitions: What the midterm results reveal

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that senate Democratic leader Charles E.
  • ANALYSIS -- “Life moves pretty fast,” that famed 20th-century philosopher Ferris Bueller once remarked.
  • In 2024, Democrats were consigned to the political wilderness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer poses in his office on Nov. 9 for a group photo with incoming members of his caucus: from left, Ohio's Sherrod Brown, Texas' James Talarico, Iowa's Josh Turek, Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed, North Carolina's Roy Cooper, Illinois' Juliana Stratton, New Hampshire's Chris Pappas, South Carolina's Annie Andrews, Minnesota's Peggy Flanagan, Maine's Troy Jackson and Kansas' Adam Hamilton. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

ANALYSIS -- “Life moves pretty fast,” that famed 20th-century philosopher Ferris Bueller once remarked. “If you don't stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.”.

In 2024, Democrats were consigned to the political wilderness. Republicans had captured the White House, flipped the Senate and held the House. President Donald Trump had completely altered the party coalitions as he led the ascendant GOP to victory.

Recent findings suggest that now, just two years later, Democrats are on the rise. A historic midterm tsunami has swept them into such commanding Senate and House majorities that some are questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again. And if Texas is blue, how does the GOP have any chance in the Electoral College again?

A massive takeaway from the midterm results should be that there’s very little permanence in our politics.

What may have looked like a new GOP coalition was really more of a Trump coalition, and it crumbled in the face of economic frustrations, affordability concerns and the president’s unpopular policies.

With Trump’s negative job approval rating weighing them down, Republican candidates suffered losses among virtually all demographic groups – including by wide margins among constituencies thought to make up the GOP’s core.

In a recent development, trump or the Republicans finished ahead among male voters by 4 points in 2018, 8 points in 2020, 14 points in 2022 and 12 points in 2024, according to the exit polls. Men went for Democratic candidates by 4 points (51 percent to 47 percent) this cycle. Meanwhile, Republicans lost even more ground among women. While Kamala Harris finished ahead of Trump by 8 points in 2024, that margin grew to 21 points for Democratic candidates this year.

Sources indicate that trump closed the gap among Hispanic voters to just 5 points behind Harris two years ago. This year, Hispanic voters nationwide supported Democratic candidates by 32 points (65 percent to 33 percent). Even white voters shifted significantly. They backed Trump or  Republican candidates by 10 points in 2018, 17 points in 2020, 18 points in 2022 and 15 points in 2024. And yet Democrats edged out Republicans by a point (50 percent to 49 percent) on Nov. 3.

In a recent development, voters without a college degree were supposed to be a key cog in Republicans’ latest populist coalition. But they went from +13 (56 percent to 43 percent) for Trump in 2024 to backing Republican candidates by just 1 point this year. Meanwhile, the gap among voters with a college degree went from 14 points for Harris in 2024 to 30 points for Democrats this cycle.

Recent findings suggest that republicans had closed the gap among young voters aged 18 to 29 from 35 points in 2018 to just 11 points in 2024. But younger voters supported Democratic candidates this year by 50 points (74 percent to 24 percent). Not to mention Democrats flipped voters aged 45 to 64 for the first time in nearly two decades.

In a recent development, white evangelicals appear to be one of the only groups that didn’t shift toward Democrats. They supported GOP candidates 82 percent to 17 percent. But they only made up 17 percent of the electorate, according to the exit polls, which is down from a very consistent 25 percent for more than a decade. So there was still a problem with that group of voters, but it was more about turnout than persuasion.

While there was an unmistakable leftward shift this year, the results should not be considered a permanent party realignment any more than 2024 was. While Democrats did extremely well in Texas this year, they still haven’t won the Lone Star State in a presidential race in 50 years. So maybe it’s wise for everyone to take a deep breath.

It has been revealed that if you take this year’s election results and match them with the Senate seats on the ballot in 2028, there doesn’t appear to be a viable path for Republicans back to the majority. But there wasn’t a particularly viable Democratic path to the Senate majority at this point two years ago. And if the Alaska election goes their way, they will end up winning Senate races in seven states that were initially rated Solid Republican.

In a recent development, if one party starts to get too comfortable, voters have a way of bringing politicians back down to earth. If Democrats come to Congress and push too far to the left or become too defined by their most extreme members, they will squander the opportunity they earned this year.

The dramatic demographic swings should be evidence that many voters are not beholden to either party and are open to switching allegiances, particularly in a time of economic uncertainty.

Recent findings suggest that at the same time, if Republicans don’t go through some time of reflection and instead triple down on the policies that led to the blue wave, they risk cementing some of the shifts that started this cycle. It just won’t be thick cement.

Airline Flew Passengers To The Wrong City, Blamed The Weather, Then Admitted The Truth Three Years Later

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (764 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An airline flew passengers to the wrong city, welcomed them to the city they were supposed to reach, then blamed bad weather for the detour.
  • Speaking at the World Public Relations Forum in Abuja on November 17, 2026, United Nigeria Airlines Executive Chairman Obiora Okonkwo acknowledged that his company made an operational failure worse by issuing an inaccurate explanation.
  • According to PUNCH, Okonkwo said a dispatcher entered the wrong destination in the flight documentation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An airline flew passengers to the wrong city, welcomed them to the city they were supposed to reach, then blamed bad weather for the detour. Now the chairman of United Nigeria Airlines is revisiting that embarrassing episode as a lesson in why companies should tell the truth. I agree with that lesson, though I have a few questions about the flight itself….

Speaking at the World Public Relations Forum in Abuja on November 17, 2026, United Nigeria Airlines Executive Chairman Obiora Okonkwo acknowledged that his company made an operational failure worse by issuing an inaccurate explanation.

According to PUNCH, Okonkwo said a dispatcher entered the wrong destination in the flight documentation. The pilots flew to that destination, while the cabin crew apparently believed they had reached the city printed on the passenger tickets.

The airline then blamed the weather. The flight occurred in November 2023. This week’s news is the chairman discussing the false explanation and the damage it caused.

It has been revealed that on November 26, 2023, United Nigeria Airlines flight 0504 was supposed to carry passengers from Lagos (LOS) to Abuja (ABV), the Nigerian capital. Instead, it landed in Asaba (ABB), 197 nautical miles away.

That would have been confusing enough, but passengers reported that the cabin crew welcomed them to Abuja after landing. Imagine looking out the window and realizing that the airport does not quite match the announcement….

According to reporting at the time, passengers noted the pilot subsequently explained that he had received the wrong flight initiative. The aircraft eventually continued to Abuja. But the airline’s public explanation was different. It attributed the stop in Asaba to “poor destination weather” and said an incorrect cabin announcement had caused the confusion.

Nigeria’s aviation minister, Festus Keyamo, challenged the explanation in November 2023. He remarked there was no bad weather in Abuja and described the incident as an administrative problem. Keyamo also said a review of air traffic control communications revealed that the pilot intended to fly to Asaba.

Industry observers note that I suppose that is some consolation: the issue was not that the pilots somehow mistook one airport for another while trying to land in Abuja. According to the accounts from the minister and now the airline chairman, the cockpit was operating toward the correct destination acceding to the flight strategy, just the wrong destination the carrier was supposed to fly to.

But that does not make the situation reassuring. It raises a different question: how did the discrepancy survive the preparations for departure?

According to recent reports, okonkwo’s remarks this week focused on communication. As The Guardian (Nigeria) reports, he acknowledged that the airline’s communications team blamed bad weather despite the documentation error. He offered this broader lesson:.

“Whenever the truth is told, it builds trust, it builds confidence, and it also shows respect for stakeholders.”.

I can be understanding when an airline makes a mistake and explains what happened. That understanding depends on the nature of the mistake, of course, but acknowledging a failure is an vital first step (ahem).

In a recent development, an inaccurate weather explanation accomplishes the opposite. Once passengers discover that the explanation does not hold up, why should they trust the next one or trust the airline at all?

I do not know who approved the original statement or what information that person had, but I am reminded that the truth will find you out.

The problem with treating this primarily as a communications lesson is that the underlying event deserves at least as much scrutiny.

It has been revealed that A dispatcher can enter an incorrect destination, but an airline operation should have checks that catch a discrepancy between where passengers have booked and where the aircraft is being sent. I appreciate the chairman’s candor now. Still, an honest explanation needs to include how the airline addressed the operational failure, along with why it gave passengers an inaccurate account. I guess we should be thankful for what we have….

Recent findings suggest that united Nigeria Airlines flew an Abuja-bound planeload of passengers to Asaba in 2023, then blamed bad weather. Its chairman now acknowledges three years later that the explanation made an embarrassing incident worse.

In a recent development, there is something almost comical about being welcomed to a city you have not reached. But I doubt I would have found it particularly funny had I been onboard. Communication is key and the truth is essential. In all things in life.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, on Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television shows, and more.
  • Recent findings suggest that the celestial saga that is Frank Herbert’s Dune was practically made for cinema.
  • On December 18, 2026, Denis Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Three arrives, overcoming the hurdles that had tripped up its predecessors and capping off the decade-in-the-making trilogy in an explosive finale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, on Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television shows, and more. This time, we take a look at Dune: Part Three.

Recent findings suggest that the celestial saga that is Frank Herbert’s Dune was practically made for cinema. And yet, for so long, adapting the breathtakingly expansive space opera seemed like something of a curse. David Lynch called his turn at the franchise “a huge, gigantic sadness” in his life, and for Alejandro Jodorowsky, his psychedelically expensive vision for Dune never escaped development hell.

On December 18, 2026, Denis Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Three arrives, overcoming the hurdles that had tripped up its predecessors and capping off the decade-in-the-making trilogy in an explosive finale. Key to the creation of the trilogy’s universe was keeping it as grounded as possible in ours, with otherworldly planets raised from the volcanic shores of Iceland’s beaches and the banded dunes of the United Arab Emirates’ Liwa Desert. By this point, fans of the first two installments are well-acquainted with settings like the desert planet of Arrakis, but Villeneuve's latest offering delves deeper than ever into their intricate textures. Condé Nast Traveler spoke with production designer Patrice Vermette, location manager Duncan Broadfoot, and director of photography Linus Sandgren to learn how this much-anticipated conclusion was crafted.

Dune: Part Three opens with Fremen forces landing on Enfeil, a wetland planet that stuns the soldiers—used to desert and drought—with its rain. After the battle concludes, the Fremen forces run to the black sand shores of the planet and wade into the sea. This sequence was filmed in Iceland, specifically at Ingólfshöfði Beach, a nearly 250-foot-tall cape and nature reserve. “Denis [Villeneuve] always envisioned a black surface going on for forever, a super flat surface with those low clouds and a band of light, just the sun piercing through the horizon," remarked Vermette, “Because of the black sand, we thought, obviously, Iceland. We also looked to see if it was possible to shoot in the Canary Islands.” At the end of the day, Iceland won the booking, leading the team to spearhead an unprecedented film shoot. “When we scouted Iceland, there were multiple options,” said Broadfoot, “but this particular beach that we ended up on is part of a nature reserve, and actually during the summer, you can book puffin tours, but it's never been shot on before, so that was also an appealing aspect.”.

Recent findings suggest that twenty different locations across the UAE's Liwa Desert were stitched together to comprise Arrakis. Across all three films, the Liwa Desert has been used as a stand-in for the desert planet at the center of it all. “There's a reward to travel to the Liwa Desert, which is close to the border of Saudi Arabia, and the dunes there are like the kind you've seen in Lawrence of Arabia,” said Sandgren, “it's magical just to be there; they're beautiful and contain copper sand and beige sand, and the mix of the two creates these incredible patterns of ripples from the wind each night, and every morning, you see newly introduced patterns.” While Sandgren arrived at the desert for the first time to film for Part Three, for Broadfoot and Vermette, returning to the region was like a homecoming for the crew. “Denis [Villenueve] and Patrice [Vermette] are always very keen to find something new that we haven't filmed on before, so that was always the challenge," said Broadfoot, “specifically for Part Three, we had to go deeper and further into the desert than we had done in Part Two.” Filming in the ever-shifting landscape with temperatures peaking at a boiling 120 degrees Fahrenheit posed significant challenges to the shoot, especially as the crew based themselves even deeper into the desert, but getting comfortable was almost counter to the brief. “We love making movies because we thrive on challenges, you know?," said Vermette, "If it was easy, I don't think we'd want to make them.”.

According to recent reports, while nearly all of the Arrakis scenes were shot in the Liwa Desert, select sequences were set in Al Ain, the UAE's “Garden City.” Though scenes shot in Al Ain didn't take up as much screen time as those shot in the desert, they span a considerable range as the area served as the setting for Alia Atreides's personal Golgotha—the site where Paul's sadistic younger sister crucifies traitors to the regime—as well as where Chani plays with her young children. “It's an incredible area that is still very unknown,” mentioned Vermette. “We shot on a mountain called Jebel Hafeet, the only real mountain in the area,” said Broadfoot, “we scouted the entire mountain and found a plateau up high, which gave you this sort of scale and rocky, craggy environment that's very different than the desert which we were filming in. It was a blank canvas for Patrice [Vermette] to take over and create his beautiful set.”.

It has been revealed that to enhance all the footage that was shot on location, several landscapes from Part Three were recreated using a combination of practical and digital effects across four facilities in Budapest: NFI Studios, HungExpo Budapest Congress and Exhibition Centre, Korda Studios, and Waberer. Much of the battle scene on Enfeil was shot in Budapest. “Most of it was in the back lot of Waberer,” noted Vermette, “the amazingly technical thing achieved by Denis [Villeneuve] and Linus [Sandgren] was that they erected a 65-foot-tall by 470-something-foot-long LED screen wall, which was the biggest wall of that sort ever built." The sheer scale of the shoot even required the crew to break out cranes to navigate the airspace around production to move props and equipment around.

Atreides home planet Caladan has made an appearance in all three films of the trilogy. The visual opposite of Arrakis, Caladan was shot on the northwestern Kråkenes region of Norway. The agrestic shoreline is hugged by verdant cliffs and the frosty Norwegian Sea. Caladan's cameos in Part Three come as brief flashes, but Vermette also winks to the filming location in an Easter egg on Arrakis. “In the movie, in the interior courts of Alia's meditation room, there's a tree,” indicates Vermette, “I had the idea of putting a pine tree, a Norwegian pine tree there, because it's the roots of their family; it's something that anchors their family. The only pine tree in all of Arrakis is right there.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The EuroAirport Skyview Lounge in Basel (BSL) remains the only lounge option in the airport, but a nice one with a respectable selection of food and drinks and is now managed by Aspire.

I’m not sure what to even call this lounge, because the airport still calls it by its original name, the EuroAirport Skyview Lounge, as does Google and Priority Pass, but the signage has changed and the lounge is now managed by Aspire. Looking at the sign, it looks like there are four “Sky Lounges” in one, though at least for me there was only two….

One key difference is that the ground level of the lounge is now as a separate café open to all passengers: but you pay for everything from coffee to cake to other drinks (and tragically, the lounge got rid of its beautiful old school Belle Époque espresso machine and now has a push-button one).

Then upstairs there is a gate that you must scan your boarding pass with in order to enter the lounge itself, which includes a large atrium-like lounge area, buffet, restrooms, and a nice terrace for planespotting (or smoking).

There’s one more level up: the bar, but that appears to be permanently closed. Instead, there is a self-service bar in the buffet area.

You can check out my original review to see the old signage, but it still gives you a good idea of what to expect concerning seating and other amenities in this lounge.

My original comprehensive review from 2023 is below.

Prior to our flight to London, my family spent an hour in the EuroAirport Skyview Lounge in Basel. This is a very solid Priority Pass Lounge.

Industry observers note that access is granted for Priority Pass members and some premium cabin travelers. It was closed for an extended time (much longer than most lounges) during the pandemic, but thankfully is open again.

We arrived about an hour before our British Airways flight and enjoyed some lunch in the lounge.

As you enter, the ground floor has a seating area with a full bar (including a great manual coffee machine, though it is almost always closed, as it was during our visit) with an outdoor feel including palm tress and a pond with a bridge over it.

Upstairs the floor-to-ceiling windows forming a semi-circle give the lounge a very modern feel.

Food is set out according to the following schedule:.

Our stay was from 3:00 pm to 4:00 pm and staff were beginning to set up dinner as we departed. But we just ate salad and soup.

Drinks are self-service, including alcoholic beverages, soft drinks, and coffee.

The kids were amused by the phone rooms and worked quietly there during our stay….

Finally, the lounge has a nice outdoor terrace (intended for smokers, but a great place for fresh air or to planespot).

I am quite thankful for this lounge at my “home” airport in Europe and for the ability to bring my entire family in Priority Pass (via AMEX, Chase, Capital One, or Citi).

My original review, published on January 27, 2020, is below.

How is sole lounge at at Basel-Mulhouse-Freiburg Airport (BSL/MLH/EAP)? [yes, the airport has three codes].

According to recent reports, the EuroAirport Skyview Lounge serves as the business class lounges for a handful of airlines as well as a Priority Pass lounge. It opens daily at 5:00AM. Sunday thru Friday it closes at 8:30PM. On Saturday it closes at 7:30PM. It is just prior to passport control in the airport’s only terminal.

Sources indicate that as the only lounge you might expect crowds, poor service, and limited amenities. On the contrary, however, this is one of my favorite Priority Pass lounges.

Recent findings suggest that first, I love this lounge because it is full of natural light and greenery. You’ll find trees–mostly palm trees–throughout the lounge. And the lounge is called “Skyview” for a reason–the roof is glass, filling the lounge with beautiful natural light on sunny days.

Typically, I’m in this lounges before the sun rises, but a couple times I have visited on a hot afternoon. Yes, you do get a bit of greenhouse feel inside…but it’s so much nicer than a dingy, fluorescent-lit lounge.

The lounge spans two floors (with the slowest elevator in the world). The ground floor is smaller and sometimes roped off.

Industry observers note that I wouldn’t call the food in the lounge excellent, but it’s also not bad at all. The eggs are from a box in the morning and fruit is limited, but there’s also fresh baked goods, yogurt, and cold cuts. In the afternoon you can make yourself a very nice salad with a cup of soup.

All drinks are complimentary and self-serve.

On the ground floor, there is a “piazza bar” with a nice coffee machine…I’m sure it makes great espresso. Small problem: I’ve never seen it turned on. Maybe it’s turned on later in the day, but never in the morning. Such a shame. That said, the coffee machines are not bad. Beer, wine, soft drinks, and water are available on both levels as well.

Note there’s a top floor bar that appears permanently closed. I snuck up there once and it’s quite nice, but I’ve never seen it open and there’s always a sign indicating that it is closed.

It has been revealed that restrooms are small, but clean. No showers.

An outdoor smoking terrace not only offers a place to smoke, but a great place to watch airplanes land and takeoff.

A rack of newspapers is available on the ground floor.

According to recent reports, two desktop computers are available for internet browsing and printing. By the way, the lounge has plenty of plugs and you generally won’t need an adapter to plug in your device. No USB plugs, though.

This is one of my “home” airports and thus a lounge I visit often. Over the years, it has really grown on me. I appreciate how it is rarely crowded and especially the natural light. With the growth of budget carriers at Basel, it is also a nice place to wait before a flight on EasyJet or WizzAir.

Beginner’s luck: Freshmen leave it to chance at House office lottery

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (924 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, rep.-elect Mark Teixeira reacts after drawing the worst chip during Tuesday’s lottery for newly elected members of Congress.
  • As far as birthdays go, Rep.-elect Shannon Taylor was having a pretty good one.
  • Crowded into a room in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday morning with the rest of her freshman class, the Virginia Democrat walked up to a table with a wooden box and reached in.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, rep.-elect Mark Teixeira reacts after drawing the worst chip during Tuesday’s lottery for newly elected members of Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

As far as birthdays go, Rep.-elect Shannon Taylor was having a pretty good one.

Crowded into a room in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday morning with the rest of her freshman class, the Virginia Democrat walked up to a table with a wooden box and reached in.

“This is so nervewracking,” she said, before pulling out a chip with a “1” printed on it.

According to recent reports, her prize was a coveted one — first choice of office space. Every two years, incoming members of the House play a game of chance to see who can land the best real estate and who will be relegated to less desirable corners of the Capitol complex.

In a recent development, the room broke out in raucous applause and a standing ovation. Her latest colleagues started singing “Happy Birthday.”.

Sources indicate that not everyone was so lucky. Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira, R-Texas, pulled number 105 — the very last one. The former MLB player raised his arms in a mock celebration.

“Lets all hope for the luck of the Taylors,” said Rep.-elect Brent Taylor, R-Tenn., only to emerge with number 81.

The newly-elected members got their turn in a random order, walking up one by one to a table where deputy executive director of House Office Buildings Kornell Rancy kept watch over the box of chips.

In a recent development, rep.-elect John Cowan, R-Ga., was the first to pick a number. The first neurosurgeon to be elected to Congress, Cowan wore his white doctor’s coat as he pulled number 11 out of the box.

“I wanted to do something where I’m just representing health care providers around the country,” Cowan said.

As returning members lay claim to more desirable offices made available by those who resign, retire or lose elections, the space they’ve abandoned is left for the newcomers, who are on the Hill this week for orientation. Many of them will end up in the Longworth Building, where suites can be awkward or cramped.

In a recent development, not all offices are created equal, and the calculus has changed over the years. The previously undesirable Cannon Building just underwent a budget-busting renovation that lasted more than a decade, with a spacious courtyard opening earlier this year. But the coveted Rayburn Building still retains its prestige, despite repeated and dire warnings from the Architect of the Capitol about its crumbling infrastructure.

“You’re welcome,” said Rep.-elect Amish Shah, D-Ariz., after pulling a disappointing number 94.

Prior to the lottery, Rep.-elect Trever Nehls, R-Texas, was hoping for the best but had a backup strategy in case his number said otherwise.

“If I don’t pick number one, I’m going to offer one of these cigars as a trade to whoever gets it,” he stated, pointing to three of them sticking out of his jacket pocket. He’s preparing to take over the seat at the moment held by his twin brother Troy, who shares a fondness for stogies.

Recent findings suggest that the office space lottery dates back to 1908, when members of the 60th Congress received their first office assignments after the completion of what would be named the Cannon Building. A House page drew names and numbers from a box, and members selected their offices from a chart, according to House Office Buildings executive director of facility operations Joe Yates, who kicked things off Tuesday with a history lesson.

The lottery now is a little more modern, with members poring over virtual office layouts and doing walkthroughs of spaces on laptops.

“If somebody had to get 105, I’m glad it was me because I am here to serve, and I’m serving my freshman class by picking the worst office,” Teixeira remarked. “This is low on my priority list.”.

Some members confirmed their lucky draws themselves, while others let Yates break the news.

“Come visit me,” noted Rep.-elect Chris Gober, R-Texas, after pulling number 2 from the box.

After the lottery itself, members huddled with their staff to strategize about the next steps — how to leverage their numbers and select the best suites left on the list, while also exploring layouts, paint colors and carpeting.

It has been revealed that “First and foremost, a good layout, so we can do good work, and people can be comfortable in doing the work, and then a convenient location. Very utilitarian,” mentioned Rep.-elect Scott Wiener, D-Calif., of his priorities.

“We’ll get a decent Longworth office,” remarked Wiener, who drew pick 43. “Cannon would have been ideal, but I’m happy with any office.”.

In a recent development, rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, D-Colo., was hoping to replicate the good luck of some of his colleagues. “I’m going to do the Shannon Taylor and Sam Forstag. It’s eyes closed, behind the back,” he noted of his moves, reaching into the box. But it wasn’t enough, and Rutinel pulled number 69.

According to recent reports, “These are not red numbers, these are not blue numbers. These are the remaining numbers, and there ain’t that many,” said Rep.-elect Johnny Garcia, D-Texas, who was among the last few people to pick. He emerged with number 75.

And when Rep.-elect Joe Strada, R-Fla., the last of the incoming members to draw, walked up to the table, the whole room cheered.

“Wouldn’t it be crazy if I picked number 1?” he joked, pulling out the last chip in the box.

Setting Sail With Kids? These Are the Best Cruise Lines for Families

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The best cruise lines for families with kids and teens are likely more diverse than you realize.
  • Sources indicate that I’ve sailed on more than 80 cruises, sometimes with my kids, often surrounded by everyone else’s.
  • A cruise line that devotes a day to all things LEGO and offers a special baby laundry service gets top marks in my list of the best cruises for kids and teens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best cruise lines for families with kids and teens are likely more diverse than you realize. Many are the substantial-ship brands you see in ads, tricked out with waterslides, dazzling shows, and an abundance of onboard restaurants to satisfy picky toddlers and ravenous teens alike. Yet other family-friendly cruise lines let mom and dad get the taste of luxury they crave or provide the entire crew with adventure and active pursuits around the globe.

Sources indicate that I’ve sailed on more than 80 cruises, sometimes with my kids, often surrounded by everyone else’s. I can tell you that the best family cruises won’t make bedtime any easier, but they will do their best to make sure no one in your crew ever feels the need to cry, “I’m so bored!”.

A cruise line that devotes a day to all things LEGO and offers a special baby laundry service gets top marks in my list of the best cruises for kids and teens. MSC Cruises is a European significant-ship cruise line that’s making waves in the US with its family-friendly mega-ships.

Recent findings suggest that five kids clubs for babies, preschoolers, kids, tweens, and teens target activities to different age groups. MSC is constantly developing fresh family programs, including family discos, original game shows, drone races for teens, MasterChef at Sea cooking challenges, and obstacle course competitions.

It has been revealed that world Class ships feature the top-deck Family Aventura District with an outdoor adventure area (including an overwater swing ride), water park, and an indoor space for rollerskating and bumper cars. Select ships offer arcades with a Formula 1 simulator and virtual reality attractions or the Robotron robotic-arm thrill ride. The line’s US–based ships also feature connecting cabins and family-friendly dining (the pizza and gelato are superb).

Families looking for an exclusive hideaway can book rooms in The Yacht Club, with access to a private restaurant, lounge, sun deck, and pool—all ages welcome.

Standout itinerary: 7-night Caribbean and Bahamas cruise on MSC World America sailing round-trip from Miami.

Royal Caribbean operates the world’s largest, most activity-laden ships, and its calling card is high-energy fun for all ages.

It has been revealed that families can rock climb, zip-line, ice skate, splash down waterslides, solve escape room challenges, and enjoy entertainment ranging from musical performances to acrobatic high-dive dance indicates without leaving the ship. The enormous Icon Class ships even have a dedicated family deck called Surfside, where kid-friendly restaurants, splash playgrounds, and a carousel are surrounded by cabins and suites designed to accommodate families.

On all ships, parents can steal away for adults-only fun when they drop the littlest cruisers at onboard nurseries run by professional caregivers. Kids can make crafts, play games, and do science experiments at onboard camps operating morning until late in spacious, tech-enhanced multipurpose spaces. Teens have their own hip hangouts for foosball, video games, and evening parties with newly introduced friends. The whole family can later reunite to share the day’s fun over Johnny Rockets burgers and shakes or perhaps a teppanyaki dinner with showman chefs.

Standout itinerary: 7-night Perfect Day CocoCay and Caribbean cruise on Icon of the Seas sailing round-trip from Miami.

Industry observers note that disney’s rapidly expanding cruise ship segment isn’t just for preschoolers reveling in their Frozen era. Its itineraries across the Caribbean, Alaska, and Europe offer family fun for a wide range of ages, including adults. Plus, its short itineraries pair nicely with a theme park visit.

Entertainment is a highlight, from live on-stage productions of classics like Moana and Beauty and the Beast to mealtime demonstrates themed around the Marvel universe and Coco. The ships’ movie theaters screen first-run flicks across the Disney-owned studios (not just animated classics), and the once-a-cruise Pirate Night is the only time you’ll ever see fireworks launched from a cruise ship.

Sources indicate that disney Cruise Line’s enormous youth facilities, also with nurseries and teen clubs, offer activities themed to Disney IP. Kids can design a superhero suit or theme park ride, pilot the Millennium Falcon, and join Olaf for virtual snowball fights. The line also treats adults very well with pools, sun decks, fine-dining restaurants (including ones by Michelin-starred chefs), bars themed around The Haunted Mansion and Star Wars, and cafés exclusive to travelers ages 18+.

Disney supports traveling families in less flashy ways, as well. Cabins feature extra berths for kids, split bathrooms with a toilet in one room and a sink in the other, and room-dividing curtains so grownups won’t distract would-be nappers. Waiters will purée baby food and cut up your kid’s dinner all while cracking silly jokes and performing magic tricks. When the travel logistics are handled, families can focus more on having fun.

Standout itinerary: 4-night Bahamas cruise on Disney Wish sailing round-trip from Port Canaveral.

Retirees rule the world of river cruising, but AmaWaterways has teamed up with Adventures by Disney (Disney’s escorted travel arm) to offer select Rhine and Danube cruises to families.

Disney’s onboard Adventure Guides handle all the logistics in port, from escorting tours in every destination to managing dietary restrictions and directing guests to the best restaurants and local treats. On board, they host movie evenings and kids-only dinners so parents can enjoy a leisurely meal with adult conversation.

Recent findings suggest that adventures by Disney swaps the history- and culture-focused walking tours typical of river cruise excursions for alpine coasters, amusement parks, river kayaking, and visits to chocolate factories. A selection of winery visits and slower-paced tours appeal to multigenerational families willing to split up childcare responsibilities ashore.

According to recent reports, amaWaterways, in turn, has specially built ships with more third-berth and connecting cabins than the typical river ship. It supplements its regional cuisine with kid favorites, while introducing the whole family to specialties like French macarons and German sausages.

Standout itinerary: 7-night Rhine River cruise from Basel, Switzerland, to Amsterdam, Netherlands.

A family cruise can be a nature-filled adventure to places like Alaska, the Galápagos, Baja California, Iceland, Greenland, and even Antarctica. For active families with curious kids and teens (and parents!), National Geographic-Lindblad Expeditions is a top choice.

The cruise line’s ships carry under 200 guests, so families can focus on each other without those significant-ship distractions. Though small, the ships do offer connecting cabins to accommodate groups and casual dining with plentiful options to suit all tastes.

On a National Geographic cruise, the destination is the draw, and family-friendly activities range from snorkeling and kayaking to hiking and biking. On select voyages, the cruise line offers its National Geographic Explorers-in-Training program for kids and teenagers, led by certified field instructors. The program focuses on nature, science, and storytelling, with activities like practicing smartphone photography in Alaska with a photo instructor, collecting and then observing plankton under a microscope in Baja California, and learning to drive a Zodiac.

Standout itinerary: 7-night Galápagos Escape cruise from Quito, Ecuador.

According to recent reports, luxury cruise ships aren’t built for kids, but select cruise lines make an effort to entertain junior cruisers during holiday and summer sailings in places like Alaska and the Caribbean. Regent Seven Seas Cruises’ ships might not offer a dedicated kids club on board, but the line’s longstanding Club Mariner Youth Program welcomes children ages 5 to 17 with a schedule of onboard activities.

Trained counselors make use of the ships’ public spaces to keep kids busy with mini-golf games, dessert decorating, karaoke parties, and movie nights. In Alaska, programming is destination-themed, and a youth-oriented enrichment speaker engages kids in learning about Alaska’s nature and wildlife.

Industry observers note that don’t underestimate your family’s ability to find fun on an adult-oriented ship. On Regent, kids can enjoy swimming in the onboard pool, joining a team for trivia, and playing board or card games in the library. Afternoon tea and evening shows may also become family attractions. You might find that complimentary room service from the main dining room menu coupled with movies on-demand in your suite is the perfect family activity to end your day.

Standout itinerary: 7-night Alaska cruise on Seven Seas Explorer from Vancouver, Canada, to Whittier, Alaska.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thepointsguy ↗ Open Full Page

Is air travel ready for Thanksgiving? The meltdown is over, but worries persist

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (769 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thepointsguy

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It appears air travel is back on track after one of the most chaotic weekends we’ve seen at airports in years.
  • According to recent reports, flight schedules returned to normal this week after a rare nationwide ground stop created a nightmare weekend for flying.
  • It’s not so much a safety question — industry experts steadfastly agree that air travel is still remarkably safe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It appears air travel is back on track after one of the most chaotic weekends we’ve seen at airports in years.

According to recent reports, flight schedules returned to normal this week after a rare nationwide ground stop created a nightmare weekend for flying. More than 18,000 flights were canceled between Friday and Sunday, affecting millions of travelers. It appears there will be no spillover from that meltdown into the big Thanksgiving travel week that’s on the horizon, though.

The bigger concern is long-term.

It’s not so much a safety question — industry experts steadfastly agree that air travel is still remarkably safe.

But there are plenty of worries about the possibility of another major air travel headache like we saw this weekend.

And that’s a stressful and costly reality whether you’re a passenger, a crew member, an airline executive or a front-line aviation worker.

In recent years, travelers have gotten one reminder after another about how strained our aviation infrastructure is.

For years, the Federal Aviation Administration has been plagued by both severely outdated technology and short staffing in air traffic control.

Those concerns have grown even louder in the wake of several recent incidents.

It has been revealed that after 9/11, the U.S. went more than 20 years without a nationwide ground stop like the one we saw on Friday.

We’ve now seen two happen since 2023. Both instances involved outages to critical FAA systems.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, the vital air traffic control workforce that directs the flow of planes in our airspace has been chronically understaffed. Controllers routinely work six-day weeks and mandatory overtime.

Together, these problems have fueled several of the most high-profile air travel disruptions in recent memory.

Last fall, ATC staffing was a major factor in the mass flight cancellations and delays we saw at the height of the government shutdown.

In 2025, equipment outages plus undermanned air traffic control centers contributed to the weeks of chaos travelers endured at Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR).

In the wake of the latest technology failure on Friday, FAA administrator Bryan Bedford was asked bluntly whether he could say for certain that there wouldn’t be a repeat of this past weekend’s chaos.

“I can say with certainty that the system is really, really old,” he told CBS News Tuesday.

According to recent reports, “Let’s not kid ourselves,” Bedford added. “This system has been fragile, and it does go down.”.

There has been momentum to fix both problems, which have festered for decades under the leadership of both political parties.

In recent years, the FAA has upped its air traffic control hiring efforts, in a push to reduce long-standing vacancies.

Meanwhile, Congress last year earmarked $12.5 billion for infrastructure upgrades.

The Department of Transportation has started that work, but states it needs a lot more money to make truly sweeping upgrades.

The travel sector has broadly supported that request: “They need to get to 100% staffing and to have the funds to modernize the technology,” United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby wrote in a social media post Sunday.

But securing that funding will hinge on political dealmaking in Washington, D.C., which in January will be led by a divided government.

And however that fight ends, these problems won’t be solved overnight.

It takes years to fully train air traffic controllers.

And to add to the complexity, overhauling aviation infrastructure while tens of thousands of flights operate each day is painstaking work with significant consequences — even if the money is there in the first place.

Look no further than last week’s FAA outage, where crews replacing a router apparently triggered a chain-reaction outage that upended air travel in the U.S. for days — a disruption American Airlines now counts among the most significant in its 100-year history.

According to recent reports, “The transition itself needs to be carefully analyzed and tested,” noted Capt. Shem Malmquist, a longtime Boeing 777 captain and visiting professor at the Florida Institute of Technology’s College of Aeronautics. “Otherwise, an upgrade intended to solve one problem can introduce another.".

Despite all the concerning headlines, industry experts largely agree:.

“Both things can be true,” Malmquist said, pointing to the many safety layers that allow planes to safely operate even when problems arise.

Keep in mind: Every plane that was in the sky during last week’s FAA disruption landed safely.

And the move to halt thousands of flights? That was ultimately meant to protect travelers, leaders have emphasized.

"Passengers experience delays and cancellations, but those restrictions help keep the system safe," Malmquist mentioned. “That doesn’t mean the underlying vulnerabilities are acceptable.”.

New FAA Meltdown Report Points To Disturbing Oversight Changes Under Trump

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1303 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The more we learn about the nationwide FAA ground stop, the less convincing the effort to blame old equipment and previous administrations becomes.
  • A CNN investigation describes a troubling gap between the oversight the FAA states occurred and what sources say actually happened.
  • Industry observers note that the matter concerns work by L3Harris at a radio communications facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, before the November 13 ground stop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The more we learn about the nationwide FAA ground stop, the less convincing the effort to blame old equipment and previous administrations becomes. Upcoming reporting points to an oversight policy changed under the current administration and a technician whose role apparently ended after letting a contractor through the door. Aging infrastructure required careful management. Instead, we appear to have received less of it.

A CNN investigation describes a troubling gap between the oversight the FAA states occurred and what sources say actually happened.

Industry observers note that the matter concerns work by L3Harris at a radio communications facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, before the November 13 ground stop. According to CNN, an FAA technician provided access to the building but understood that his responsibility ended there.

One source described the technician this way:.

“He was only there to unlock the door…there was no monitoring.”.

Recent findings suggest that FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford had said the installation was monitored. An agency spokeswoman subsequently explained:.

“The escort is not there while the technician is doing work”.

It has been revealed that those accounts require reconciliation, but strike me as irreconcilable. Opening a door and overseeing an installation are very different responsibilities.

In a recent development, A March 2025 FAA memo changed the process for contractor maintenance. Work previously submitted as requests requiring approval became notifications that could proceed without affirmative FAA approval. The policy retained a review role for FAA liaisons, but a small group was tasked with handling thousands of notifications.

The FAA disputes that the policy reduced oversight, but the questions remain:.

This is why I find the continuing effort to blame Biden or Buttigieg so absurd. Neither man was running the department when this policy changed or when this installation occurred. I have already written about the contractor questions surrounding this failure. The new reporting makes those questions more urgent.

Decades of deferred investment explain why modernization is necessary. They do not excuse weakening the supervision of the modernization itself. If anything, working with old infrastructure should make the government more careful about introducing latest equipment, not less.

The staffing matter deserves scrutiny too, also highlighted by One Mile At A Time.

In February 2025, the FAA fired hundreds of probationary employees during the administration’s government-cutting campaign. Duffy remarked no controllers or critical safety personnel were among those dismissed. The Professional Aviation Safety Specialists union later unveiled the reinstatement of the 132 terminated employees it represented.

That means we cannot necessarily a direct causation from those firings to this outage, though the broader approach remains fair game. An administration that celebrates eliminating positions needs to account for the work those people perform. If that work still needs doing, someone else must absorb it, a contractor must perform it, or it goes undone, a particular concern at an agency already struggling with staffing.

In its statement on the ground stop, PASS says the FAA’s May 2026 workforce initiative called for at least 750 additional certified professional technicians by 2030. The union says little progress has been made toward hiring them.

We can certainly agree that unnecessary government spending should be eliminated. But a smaller payroll does not demonstrate greater efficiency if the remaining organization cannot adequately supervise the work entrusted to it…the cost of a nationwide aviation disruption must enter that calculation too, especially now.

Meanwhile, Musk is distancing himself from the political movement he helped finance.

Speaking at the DealBook Summit on November 18, he mentioned:.

He described himself as politically moderate, rejected blind adherence to Republican policies, and expressed regret over his election spending:.

“I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it”.

Sources indicate that we joke about United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby adjusting his political posture with the prevailing winds. Apparently, he has company. I would welcome a sincere reassessment from Musk. But distancing himself from a label does not erase his role in promoting the administration or DOGE.

It also does not establish that he now recognizes the problems with the personnel policies he championed. Regretting an unsuccessful political investment is different from regretting how the government was managed. Still, when even Musk wants distance from MAGA, I think it is fair to ask whether the brand has reached its expiration date.

Recent findings suggest that my reading of the election is that Americans are tired of the performance. They want competent government and explanations they can believe. Being told that every success belongs to the president while every failure belongs to his predecessor wears thin and it goes well beyond right/left or Republican/Democrat divisions.

In a recent development, to be fair, Bedford has now offered something we have heard too little of. As ABC News reports, he mentioned Wednesday:.

It has been revealed that “I’m the guy they hired to get this done. So blame me. If we need to blame somebody, blame me.”.

I appreciate that. He also promised a transparent accounting of the technical findings. But accepting blame must lead to an explanation of the decisions that preceded the failure. It cannot simply shield Duffy or end the inquiry.

The incoming Congress should audit the maintenance policy, staffing records, risk assessments, and contractor communications. It should establish what oversight was required, what actually occurred, and whether the agency had enough qualified people to carry out its responsibilities.

Duffy wants another $50 billion. Perhaps the modernization program needs that money. But Congress should understand how the existing process failed before assuming that a larger appropriation will fix it…and maybe remind Duffy that instead of going on reality TV road trips he should have done the job he was hired to do.

Accountability must become something more useful than another round of political theater that both sides use to score political points. Trump remains president for two more years. The latest Congress will have to work with him to repair the damage and modernize this system.

Industry observers note that I find his vindictiveness and self-absorption deeply troubling. In his recent 60 Minutes interview with Ross Douthat, he remarked:.

“I do hate some of my enemies and I always will.”.

That is a miserable disposition for governing a country whose citizens will always disagree. Even so, waiting for him to become a different person is not a strategy. Congress should pursue practical agreements that restore adequate staffing and contractor oversight while funding necessary upgrades.

Sources indicate that if Trump needs to claim credit for a functioning aviation system, let him. I care far more about the result than denying him another chance to stoke his vanity. Congress can scrutinize the administration’s failures while negotiating legislation that begins to correct them. If the goal is to make things better, then we need to borrow the line from Ronald Reagan: “There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn’t mind who gets the credit.”.

According to recent reports, the latest reporting points toward an oversight failure under the current administration. The exact technical cause and the contribution of staffing decisions still require investigation, but blaming old equipment is plainly insufficient.

Modernizing a system this complex will involve difficulties. I would be much more understanding of an administration that acknowledged those difficulties, explained its mistakes, and corrected them. Instead, passengers have received conflicting accounts and political blame. The new Congress needs to insist on answers, then work with the president on repairs that outlast the next news cycle.

Americans need to be able to trust the people running their aviation system…to some extent, the past is in the past and today is a fresh day and a chance for course correction.

Sources indicate that kentucky Rep. James Comer, here talking to reporters on Capitol Hill in June, is running for governor. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

According to recent reports, kentucky Rep. James R. Comer, whose role as chairman of the House Oversight Committee gave him a powerful platform to investigate Democrats, including former Presidents Joe Biden and Bill Clinton, has launched a run for governor next year.

The Republican, who was just elected to a sixth full term representing Kentucky’s 1st District, is seeking to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear. Kentucky is one of three states holding off-year gubernatorial elections in 2027, alongside Louisiana and Mississippi.

In his announcement at a tele-town hall Monday night, Comey emphasized pocketbook concerns, pledging to eliminate the state income tax and boost job-creation in Louisville.

“If we get that income tax to zero, people are going to have more money to spend, and we're going to be able to attract more good-paying jobs to Kentucky, which will be able to keep our best and brightest in the state,’’ he stated.

In a recent development, as the leader of the House Oversight panel, Comer has been at the forefront in the fight over the release of records related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. (Last week, the committee released a report concluding that the federal government mishandled criminal probes into Epstein’s activities.).

Comer is a staunch ally of President Donald Trump, who carried Kentucky by 31 points in 2024, and his hard-nosed style of politics is conveyed in a soft-spoken Southern drawl.

Recent findings suggest that known back home as Jamie, Comer has deep roots in rural Monroe County, dating back to the late 1700s. Prior to coming to Congress, he operated a farm before serving 11 years in the Kentucky House. In 2011, he was elected as the commonwealth’s commissioner of agriculture.

It has been revealed that he made an unsuccessful run for governor in 2015, losing the Republican primary by 83 votes to Matt Bevin, who went on to win the general election. The following year, Comer easily won election to the House from his western Kentucky district, succeeding Republican Ed Whitfield.

Industry observers note that comer has moved rapidly to consolidate GOP support for his gubernatorial bid. He already has the backing of Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul and Sen.-elect Andy Barr. Michael Adams, Kentucky’s term-limited secretary of state who’d been seen a potential contender, gave Comer an early endorsement this summer.

It has been revealed that while Comer enters the race as the Republican front-runner, he won’t have the field to himself. Other declared hopefuls include local prosecutor Rick Hardin and distiller Charles “Bruiser” Martin, who appeared on the Discovery Channel show “Moonshiners: Master Distiller.”.

Sources indicate that while Kentucky has in recent decades grown reliably Republican at the federal level, the GOP has won just two gubernatorial elections there over the past half century. Two high-profile Democrats have already launched bids to keep the governor’s mansion in party hands: Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and former state House Majority Leader and Beshear adviser Rocky Adkins, who ran for governor in 2019.

In a statement Tuesday, the Democratic Governors Association dismissed Comer as “a job-killing, pro-war politician who looks down on everyday Kentuckians.”.

Recent findings suggest that my favorite thing about San Juan? You can have a morning that feels plucked out of a history book, an afternoon that commits you entirely to the beach, and a night that’s topped off with a frosty Medalla, sweet rum cocktail, and flirty bachata dance. It’s glitzy yet lush, historic yet ever-evolving, a city delightfully full of contrasts, and one I will never run out of reasons to revisit.

My father’s side of the family is from Puerto Rico, so I’ve been coming back to the island for years, and I love that there’s always another corner to get to know. There’s Old San Juan, with all its pastel-painted façades, galleries and shops, blue cobblestone streets, and tucked-away restaurants; Condado and Ocean Park for long, sea-salty afternoons by the ocean; and Santurce, where street murals, galleries, haute dining, and a lively bar scene bring a fresh, creative vibe to the city.

Sources indicate that of course, there’s no shortage of hotels in San Juan, but sometimes a vacation to the island’s capital calls for a little more room to sprawl, or a front door that opens onto a lush little neighborhood rather than a buzzy hotel lobby. The city’s best Airbnbs offer just that, along with wonderful amenities, whether it’s a private pool hidden behind swaying palms or a breezy courtyard for sipping on some local morning coffee.

Consider this your invitation to soak up the sun in Puerto Rico's capital for a few days. Read on for nine of the best Airbnbs in San Juan to consider for your next trip.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alaska Airlines will drop four destinations from its network in Portland, Oregon.

According to recent reports, the carrier confirmed it will end service from Portland to Baltimore, St. Louis, Fresh Orleans, and Jackson Hole, Wyoming.

Three of the connections rolled out only months ago. Portland-Jackson Hole came online in June, and service to Baltimore and St. Louis started in May.

In a recent development, “As we add new routes to our network, we constantly assess existing routes to ensure we’re using our aircraft in the markets our guests want most,” the carrier stated in a statement provided to AirlineGeeks. “As part of that process, we’ve made the decision to discontinue service between Portland and Baltimore, Jackson Hole, St. Louis, and New Orleans. We remain committed to Portland and will continue to invest in opportunities that strengthen our network there, including adding service in markets where we see the greatest opportunities for our guests.”.

Alaska serves over 60 destinations from Portland, and recently opened a newly introduced lounge there.

#53939. Latest Update: Delta Air Lines CEO Called Wi-Fi Essential, Now Indicates Passengers Don’t Choose Airlines For It

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1231 w)

Latest Update: Delta Air Lines CEO Called Wi-Fi Essential, Now Indicates Passengers Don’t Choose Airlines For It

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1231 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian once called connectivity essential to daily life and promised an onboard experience resembling what passengers enjoy on the ground.
  • Speaking with Fortune Editor-in-Chief Alyson Shontell at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum on November 16, Bastian defended Delta’s connectivity strategy.
  • “This is about the total experience, and customers are not choosing airlines based on the Wi-Fi.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian once called connectivity essential to daily life and promised an onboard experience resembling what passengers enjoy on the ground. Now, defending the decision to wait for Amazon Leo rather than install Starlink, he notes customers do not choose airlines based on Wi-Fi. I understand the argument he is trying to make, but Delta spent years teaching passengers to expect more from their internet connection. Some of us listened.

Speaking with Fortune Editor-in-Chief Alyson Shontell at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum on November 16, Bastian defended Delta’s connectivity strategy.

“This is about the total experience, and customers are not choosing airlines based on the Wi-Fi.”.

He acknowledged enjoying Starlink himself, explained that Delta and SpaceX could not agree on a business model, and expressed confidence that Amazon could deliver a competitive alternative. Bastian also defended the existing Viasat product, describing it as “pretty darn close” to Starlink.

We can debate his last point, but his broader claim about how customers choose airlines strikes me as far too dismissive, especially considering what he has said before.

Industry observers note that when Delta announced its free Wi-Fi initiative in January 2023, Bastian described connectivity in very different terms. Back then, he said:.

“At work, at home and everywhere in between, connectivity is essential to daily life, and your journey on Delta should be no different.”.

In the accompanying T-Mobile announcement, he added:.

“The ability to stay connected while seeing the world is simply foundational.”.

It has been revealed that I agreed with him. Delta made fast, free Wi-Fi part of its premium proposition. The message was that passengers could expect a more useful and enjoyable flight because they could remain connected.

Sources indicate that the airline has continued making that case. Its own explanation of why travelers should choose Delta includes fast, free Wi-Fi among the benefits it promotes.

Now that its primary competitor, United, is rapidly approaching a point in which it will have a superior internet product, the message sounds more like passengers should focus on everything else.

I tend to give people the benefit of the doubt and Bastian is no exception.

In a recent development, saying connectivity is essential does not necessarily mean passengers will select the airline with the fastest connection. Bastian could reasonably argue that Delta already provides sufficiently good Wi-Fi and that another improvement in speed will not overcome differences in schedules, service, or loyalty.

It has been revealed that but saying customers do not choose airlines based on Wi-Fi goes considerably further. Some certainly do. I am one of them. Delta cannot spend years promoting connectivity as part of what makes its product worth choosing, then expect no scrutiny when its CEO downplays connectivity as a reason to choose a competitor.

Perhaps Bastian has data showing that relatively few passengers have changed their booking habits. I would be interested in seeing it. His statement, however, leaves little room for customers whose behavior already contradicts it. He’s essentially inviting them to fly to United instead.

Not that I fly Delta often, but unlike some of my colleagues I’ve had very good experiences with Wi-Fi on Delta.

Recent findings suggest that the Viasat Wi-Fi I have used on both American Airlines and Delta has generally been fine for the work I do. I can work on the blog, handle email, and complete other tasks without needing the fastest connection available.

Starlink or Viasat, I just need my connection to work and I should not have to wonder whether it will (one reason there are many aircraft on United, like the 757-300, that I avoid like the plague). If Viasat lets me accomplish what I need to accomplish, that flight remains productive and I’m a happy passenger. I am not going to pretend otherwise simply because I prefer Starlink.

It has been revealed that but Starlink has raised my expectations. It is objectively faster and more responsive and it more closely resembles working from the ground…always. When I have comparable options, that influences my decision. I have already explained how I try to improve my odds of finding Starlink on United Airlines.

That does not mean I would accept any fare or routing to get it, but it means connectivity enters the calculation alongside departure time and price, particularly on a daytime flight. For someone whose work travels with him, several productive hours onboard have immense value…and I cannot relax on a plane if there is work to be done (that miserable United 777 flight from SFO-EWR comes to mind).

Bastian is right that passengers evaluate the total experience, but the internet connection is part of that experience and increasingly a critical part of the experience as passengers expectations evolve.

A good crew and comfortable seat are welcome and in some ways foundational, but so is being able to finish work before landing rather than spending the evening catching up instead of spending it with my family.

Sources indicate that different passengers will assign different values to those things. Someone taking a vacation may be delighted to disconnect. Someone traveling during the workday may be far more concerned about whether the connection will support the tasks waiting on a laptop. I do not expect Bastian to concede that every passenger should leave Delta for United, which is just a stupid argument. But recognizing that connectivity can influence a booking would hardly undermine the rest of Delta’s product…Bastian suddenly sounds defensive and tone deaf.

It would simply acknowledge how some customers use their time onboard….

I have defended the commercial logic behind Delta choosing Amazon Leo. An airline has legitimate reasons to consider control over its passenger interface and the broader business relationship when selecting a technology partner. We should also welcome competition for Starlink. Having another capable provider would be good for airlines and passengers.

According to recent reports, but Delta prepares to begin installing Leo on an initial 500 aircraft in 2028. That leaves time for competitors to establish new expectations, even if Amazon ultimately delivers an excellent product. As I discussed earlier this week, the failed launch carrying 40 Amazon satellites illustrates the execution risk involved in waiting for a network still being built, even if Delta has multiple back-up options.

Sources indicate that delta may have made the right long-term choice: only time will tell. But that does not mean passengers will ignore what competitors offer in the meantime and I’m fairly comfortable in saying Delta will lose a fair number of customers due to its Wi-Fi disparity with United.

Bastian once described connectivity as essential and foundational. He was right then, making his recent remarks puzzling, even when taken in context. I also concede that the Viasat service on American and Delta has generally worked well for my needs. This is not a case of Starlink being the only usable internet in the sky.

But reliable Wi-Fi now influences which flights I book, and Starlink increasingly gives me another reason to choose one departure over another and specifically, to choose United Airlines over others. Delta helped make connectivity something passengers expect. It should not be surprised when passengers begin choosing airlines based on who delivers it best.

    Latest Update: American Airlines Passengers Find Bags Covered In Brown Sludge, But Airline Claims It Was Peanut Butter

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Waiting more than two hours for your checked bag is frustrating.
    • Passengers aboard American Airlines flight 2609 from Miami (MIA) to Atlanta (ATL) on November 16, 2026, reported an unpleasant surprise at baggage claim.
    • Passenger Derick McCallum recorded the scene and later questioned the airline’s explanation:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Waiting more than two hours for your checked bag is frustrating. Watching it emerge covered in a brown substance that looks like human waste is considerably worse. That is what American Airlines passengers reported in Atlanta this week, though the airline says the mess had a much less revolting explanation: peanut butter.

    Passengers aboard American Airlines flight 2609 from Miami (MIA) to Atlanta (ATL) on November 16, 2026, reported an unpleasant surprise at baggage claim. Travelers waited more than two hours before their luggage appeared on carousel eight at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport. When the bags arrived, passengers saw a brown substance smeared across them and naturally feared the worst.

    Passenger Derick McCallum recorded the scene and later questioned the airline’s explanation:.

    In a recent development, “Even if somebody did pack peanut butter? How much peanut butter does somebody pack to cover that many bags?”.

    (my mind goes to Diddy Combs and AstroGlide…).

    It has been revealed that american later said that liquefied peanut butter had leaked from a passenger’s checked bag, affecting nearby luggage. The airline said an environmental inspection confirmed its explanation.

    “Unfortunately, a food item from a customer’s checked bag leaked during the flight, affecting several bags nearby.”.

    I would certainly prefer peanut butter to the alternative passengers feared. But I would still be rather unhappy about finding someone else’s sandwich spread having spoiled my suitcase.

    It isn’t clear how much peanut butter was involved, how it was packaged, or exactly how it spread…feel free to speculate.

    Passengers complained they were left cleaning their luggage with disinfecting wipes and tissues. American apologized and mentioned it would work directly with affected customers to resolve the situation. Since the baggage was delayed two hours anyway, did the stuff look even worse before? Or did a baggage handler throw the peanut butter bag and thereby cause the apparent explosion in the first place?

    I check bags when necessary, particularly when traveling with my family. But stories like this reinforce why I prefer to keep my belongings with me when possible. Even if you carefully pack your own suitcase, you have no control over what someone else puts in theirs. While that’s true in a shared overhead bin too, it’s much less likely to be a problem.

    There is some dark humor in a baggage carousel full of passengers trying to determine whether what that brown stuff was all over their bag, but I’m sure there was nothing to laugh about if that was your bag covered in brown.

    Industry observers note that american Airlines states peanut butter leaking from a checked bag caused the brown mess passengers discovered on their luggage in Atlanta. Better than the alternative, I suppose, but I hope American follows through promptly on cleaning or otherwise resolving the damage for affected passengers. Yuck!

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Artificial intelligence could be playing a role in the cascade of high-profile technology failures seen over the last week, U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin noted Monday.

    Mullin told FOX News’ Sean Hannity that he spoke with someone in the tech industry, “one guy who is very smart with tech,” who identified AI as a possible culprit.

    “He remarked, ‘I believe that it’s the SI, because the programs aren’t designed to work as fast as SI is,'” he said.

    The individual suggested that the technology’s ability to move fast and fix itself created “ripple effects” that overwhelmed older conventional systems. The secretary stated that theory “kind of makes sense to me.”.

    The Trump administration uses the term “super intelligence,” or SI, in place of AI.

    Mullin remarked his source did not want to be identified but ruled out at least one famous personality from the tech sector.

    Multiple large, U.S.-based networks have crashed over the past week, including the FAA’s air traffic control communications system, United’s internal applications, Microsoft’s business services, and software used by banks such as JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo.

    Mullin said there is no indication from the intelligence and cybersecurity communities that the outages are part of a cyberattack.

    The FAA has blamed Friday’s nationwide ground stop on a faulty or improperly installed router, which flooded other routers with data and ultimately crashed the system.

    • According to recent reports, the carrier said Wednesday that it will introduce its first-ever Premium Economy cabin on 10 refurbished Airbus A330s.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Aer Lingus is moving to upgrade the widebody aircraft operating its transatlantic network.

    According to recent reports, the carrier said Wednesday that it will introduce its first-ever Premium Economy cabin on 10 refurbished Airbus A330s. The aircraft will also get upgraded Business Class seats – now enclosed as suites – and an improved Economy section.

    It has been revealed that “[This] is a transformation of the entire experience across our A330 fleet, elevating Business Class, Economy, and, for the first time in Aer Lingus history, introducing Premium Economy,” CEO Lynne Embleton said in a news release. “We want to give our customers greater choice, comfort, and connectivity while creating an experience that feels unmistakably Aer Lingus.”.

    The airline’s Premium Economy section will feature 28 Recaro R4 seats in a 2-3-2 configuration. Each seat will have a 38-inch pitch, eight inches of recline, enhanced cushioning, an integrated footrest, and wings for privacy. The Premium Economy experience also comes with upgraded three-course dining, complimentary drinks, bedding, an amenity kit, and noise-reducing headphones.

    The upgraded Business Class will have 28 Collins Elevation suites in a 1-2-1 configuration, giving each passenger direct aisle access. Each seat will have a fully flat bed, a closing door, enhanced bedding, and “well-being amenities.” A self-service snack and refreshment bar will also be available.

    The carrier will also roll out newly introduced Economy seats with more personal space and six-way adjustable leather headrests.

    According to recent reports, latest interior elements will tie the three cabins together, officials said. Prepares call for mood lighting, artwork reflecting Irish landscapes, and custom fabrics in colors inspired by the sea.

    It has been revealed that all seats will have larger 4K high-definition entertainment screens, Bluetooth headphone connectivity, USB-C charging ports, and access to Starlink wireless internet. Starlink is already available across all of Aer Lingus’ transatlantic routes.

    It has been revealed that the first of the overhauled A330s will reenter service in October 2027, flying between Dublin and New York-JFK. The new cabin experience will become available on additional North American routes as work on the remaining A330s is completed.

    Aer Lingus serves a total of 20 destinations across the U.S., Canada, and Mexico, including Boston, Newark, New Jersey, Miami, Los Angeles, Toronto, and Cancún.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American Airlines intends to refresh and expand its three Admirals Club lounges at Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport.

    The carrier said Tuesday that it will add seating, upgrade amenities, and improve food and beverage service across all three spaces in Terminal 4.

    In the near term, the Admirals Club lounge in Concourse A between gates A19 and A21 will get a latest servery area, infrastructure enhancements to support expanded food and beverage offerings, and facility updates to improve the overall customer experience.

    Sources indicate that longer-term aims call for nearly tripling the combined footprint of the Concourse A lounges, the other being above gates A7-A9. New furniture and finishings will be brought in, and seating capacity will expand by 150%.

    The lounge in Concourse B, between gates B5 and B7, will get a new self-service food and beverage area and have its seating capacity increased by 20%.

    Industry observers note that “Phoenix continues to be an important hub in our network, and these investments reflect our commitment to giving customers more space, comfort, and convenience when they travel through PHX,” American Chief Customer Officer Heather Garboden mentioned in a news release. “While we look forward to the development of the fresh West Terminal, these enhancements will help create an even more seamless travel experience for the millions of customers who pass through Phoenix each year.”.

    In a recent development, the planned West Terminal will be built on the west side of the airport between Terminal 3 and Taxiway U. American is expected to serve as the terminal’s primary carrier.

    According to the airport’s timeline, the project should be finished by 2033.
