    #53927. Why The Boeing 737 MAX Is Often Heavier Than Its MTOW At The Gate

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1387 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Why The Boeing 737 MAX Is Often Heavier Than Its MTOW At The Gate

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1387 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that on a commercial airliner, every pound weighs profit against physics.
    • In a recent development, because rolling on the ground and flying place different pressures on the frame, an airplane has two distinct weight restrictions from an engineering perspective.
    • It has been revealed that takeoff demands a lower limit called Maximum Takeoff Weight (MTOW), which drops the allowance to 182,200 pounds (82,644 kilograms).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that on a commercial airliner, every pound weighs profit against physics. Financial margins are thin in today's aviation industry, and narrowbody aircraft like the Boeing 737 MAX frequently fly close to their maximum carrying capacity. Airlines employ a clever regulatory provision to fit every passenger, bag, and drop of fuel onto an aircraft without violating safety regulations. Extra fuel is dispensed at the gate as temporary fuel that will burn off prior to takeoff.

    In a recent development, because rolling on the ground and flying place different pressures on the frame, an airplane has two distinct weight restrictions from an engineering perspective. When a jet sits at the gate or taxis slowly on flat concrete, only the tires, wheels, and landing gear support the load. Because the plane moves at a walking pace, engineers certify a higher ground limit called Maximum Taxi Weight (MTW), allowing a 737 MAX 8 to weigh 182,700 pounds (82,871 kilograms) at pushback.

    It has been revealed that takeoff demands a lower limit called Maximum Takeoff Weight (MTOW), which drops the allowance to 182,200 pounds (82,644 kilograms). When pilots advance the throttles to accelerate down the runway, the wings, engines, and brakes take over the workload. The aircraft must be light enough to lift off safely or climb away if one engine fails. That 500-pound (227-kilogram) difference lets dispatchers load extra taxi fuel on top of a full cabin, burning off the surplus before takeoff.

    Aviation safety laws clearly distinguish between rolling slowly on pavement and accelerating down a runway. When taxiing at around 15 knots, a jet experiences slight vertical pressures that rarely exceed 1.2 times normal gravity. The primary frame and large landing gear may readily handle extra mass during this slow roll. Because the wings are not yet lifting the aircraft, engineers allow a higher ground-weight restriction without jeopardizing the aircraft's structural integrity.

    For basic safety of flight, a substantially lower weight limit is mandated while taking off at high speed. If an issue arises before liftoff, the tires and brakes must be able to safely stop the aircraft once it is positioned on the runway. Additionally, the aircraft must be light enough to maneuver over surrounding hills or buildings with just one engine in the event that the other fails. The lower takeoff limit is set by these stringent safety regulations.

    In a recent development, the amount of weight a plane can safely lift off the ground is further restricted by local weather and runway conditions. Hot summer air and high-altitude airports make the air thinner, which reduces wing lift and engine power. Wet or icy pavement also makes it much harder for the brakes to stop a heavy jet during a canceled takeoff. Because conditions change every day, pilots cannot exceed the strict takeoff limit by even a single pound.

    Sources indicate that airlines make good use of this weight differential on crowded flights. A Boeing 737 MAX 8, which weighs about 99,360 pounds empty, hits its zero-fuel limit of 145,400 pounds when 172 passengers, luggage, and freight are added. In order to carry the required flight fuel and weather reserves without bumping paying customers, dispatchers load the aircraft to its legal takeoff limit before adding 500 pounds of specialty taxi gasoline on top.

    To handle this extra weight, the flight crew employs precise ground procedures and fuel monitoring. The cabin air conditioning and electronics are powered by a small tail generator that burns about 100-200 lbs (45-90 kg) of gasoline per hour prior to pushback. The engines gradually use up the remaining buffer when the crew starts both main engines and starts taxiing. Pilots closely monitor the onboard computer weights and fuel gauges during the taxi to the runway.

    Crew expertise becomes critical whether airport traffic moves faster or more slowly than expected. Pilots must hold short of the runway and burn off excess fuel before advancing the throttles if air traffic control permits the aircraft to take off right away, before the 500-pound buffer is gone. On the other hand, lengthy ground delays force the crew to closely monitor fuel levels to ensure they never run out of what is required for the actual flight.

    Pilots must make a difficult choice if a traffic bottleneck on the taxiway consumes all of the buffer and begins depleting flying reserves. Before trying to fly, they had to leave the departure line and return to the gate for more fuel. Passengers experience annoying delays when returning to the terminal, but it guarantees the aircraft never takes off without the legally mandated reserves needed to reach its destination without incident.

    Sources indicate that only when airport traffic moves at a typical speed does the overloaded ground fuel approach succeed. A jet consumes about 250 pounds of fuel during a normal 12-minute taxi at a busy hub, easily lowering its weight below the permitted takeoff limit. A sudden air traffic control shortcut that shortens the drive to under four minutes leaves the aircraft hundreds of pounds too heavy because both engines consume roughly 20 pounds of fuel per minute when idle.

    Strict federal safety regulations prohibit pilots from starting their takeoff roll even one pound over the certified takeoff weight. When an unexpectedly fast taxi leaves the jet overweight, the flight crew faces an awkward choice. They must either turn down an immediate takeoff clearance or pull aside onto an open concrete pad to burn off the extra gas while holding the wheel brakes.

    To shed that surplus weight as fast as possible, pilots advance the throttles slightly and turn the cabin air conditioning systems up to full power. The irony is clear to anyone watching from the terminal. Modern airliners operate so close to their strict structural limits that crews sometimes have to waste valuable time, runway slots, and expensive jet fuel sitting still simply because they reached the runway too early.

    It has been revealed that when compared to its primary European competitor, the 737 MAX's narrow weight gap is much more pronounced. Pilots have an 882-pound taxi fuel cushion, while a typical Airbus A320neo is rated for a 174,165-pound takeoff and a 175,047-pound ground limit. Boeing's 500-pound limit is almost doubled on larger aircraft like the A321neo, allowing pilots to manage congested taxiways or lengthy gate waits without depleting crucial flight reserves.

    When revising the 737 design, Boeing engineers had far less flexibility. The MAX ended up roughly 7,000 pounds heavier than the older 737 model because of stronger wing supports, added fire barriers, and massive new engines mounted higher and farther forward on the wing. That extra base weight squeezed every remaining pound of structural margin out of the classic airframe.

    Maximum Takeoff Weight (At Runway).

    Because Boeing could not heavily reinforce the landing gear mounts without altering the jet's low ground stance, engineers locked the ground-to-takeoff-weight gap at just 500 pounds. Keeping that buffer slim preserved valuable passenger seats and cargo space on paper. However, it leaves flight crews managing razor-thin fuel margins whenever they fly the jet at its maximum range.

    Sources indicate that stretching a 1960s body design to fly long cross-country routes creates hidden trade-offs in passenger comfort. When cruising at 41,000 feet, the cabin pressure inside a 737 MAX feels like standing on an 8,000-foot mountain because its classic aluminum skin can't handle as much internal pressure. Newer rivals maintain a lower cabin altitude, around 6,500 feet, leaving MAX travelers with slightly less oxygen and noticeably more fatigue after landing.

    Cabin moisture is another victim of that traditional metal construction. Because aluminum frames can corrode if moisture collects inside the wall insulation, engineers cannot pump extra humidity into the air system. During long five-hour flights at maximum takeoff weight, cabin humidity drops to roughly 10%, making the air drier than most deserts and leaving passengers feeling dehydrated.

    Industry observers note that pushing the 737 MAX to its absolute ramp weight limit allows airlines to carry nearly 180 passengers and cross-country fuel on a single-aisle jet. Those impressive economics keep ticket prices competitive and routes profitable for carriers. However, that efficiency comes at a physical cost, asking travelers to endure a drier, higher-altitude cabin than newer jets flying the same routes.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This article is part of a new series, On Tour, in which we talk to touring artists about life on the road.

    On Halloween, a bouncing crowd of skateboarders, witches, ghosts, and ghouls slowly coalesced in Newly introduced York City's Tompkins Square Park. They were there for a quintessentially East Village pop-up concert headlined by the Melbourne-based post-punk band Radio Free Alice (followed by an after party at Niagara). The band's debut album, What’s In Between, was just released the day prior, blending the high energy of ’80s new wave with biting social satire and a healthy dose of cheek. Having picked up a following in Australia and Europe, the four-piece group has built an underground reputation on guerrilla gigs like this one—held everywhere from beneath London railway bridges and Melbourne’s former Pentridge Prison to suburban backyards in Austin, Texas.

    According to recent reports, that’s what makes the album title so apt: The young Aussies are caught between cities and countries, trying to make sense of everyday life while the road itself starts to feel like home. They’re in the thick of their own coming-of-age story, and one that's unfolding on an international stage. Fresh off the first dates of a nearly sold-out European lineup, tickets are now on sale for their What's In Between North America tour, which will kick off in San Francisco on February 24, 2027.

    It has been revealed that earlier this month, vocalist and guitarist Noah Learmonth picked up my call from a Sprinter van somewhere in Germany, on the road from Copenhagen to Berlin. With the wit, gumption, and on-stage vocals of a Gen-Z Morrissey, his devilish grin fills the screen as he tells me he spends 99% of his time in the window seat behind the van’s little table, facing forward. His preferred seat is currently occupied by guitarist Jules Paradiso. He gives me a 360-degree tour of their ecosystem, where everyone has settled into their own version of life on the road. Drummer Lochie Dowd has claimed a small sleeping nook near the back. Michael Phillips, bassist and resident reader, sits with his Kindle, having just finished Christos Tsiolkas’s The Slap. As for who’s running the show? “Fuck, no one,” the still-grinning Noah notes. “There’s a man up front called Ben, our tour manager, who’s a crazy man. He’s the one who leads the blind. We’d all be fucked otherwise.”.

    What’s everyone’s travel personality on tour? Who’s running the show?

    According to recent reports, yeah, [I'm] type D. I’m sort of in my own world when I’m traveling—headphones on, that kind of vibe. Jules is really easy manufacturer. He’s a valuable asset to have in the world. Michael’s pretty chill, too. He’s looking at me now as I summarize his personality. Lochie likes to sleep in this little nook. That’s a major part of his tour experience: finding that little nook.

    When we met Ben, we just fell in love with him and his crazy methods, his madness. The thing about Ben is he gets our sound right every time. It’s really annoying when someone else does the sound and you watch the videos back and go, ‘Oh my God, what the fuck? Why is there no bass in the synth? Why do we sound like Duran Duran? What’s going on? I sound like Sonic Youth.’ That’s not at all what we were going for. Two of my favorite bands, though. But Ben gets exactly the sound we’re going for, and he’s a real empath. We’ve spent so much time on the road together. He’s our guy.

    Where do you stay while you're on the road?

    According to recent reports, when we’re touring Europe, we’ll stay in budget hotels. Either an Ibis or a Travelodge. In America, it’s more motel-type places—Motel 6 kind of things. It’s very cliché, but kind of sick in a way. Each morning when you wake up, you set your alarm for half an hour before you have to leave, get up, have a shower, smash your clothes into your backpack, and run down to the lobby so you’re not late and Ben doesn’t give you a verbal spanking.

    Sources indicate that terrible. I just had McDonald’s. I don’t even like McDonald’s. You literally don’t have an option. You pull into a service station and the only food there is McDonald’s. Jules is a Big Mac guy, though. I know that.

    Sources indicate that I’m personally notoriously light. I just have this yellow North Face backpack that I’ve had since I was about seven years old. My auntie gave it to me for my birthday. My trusty yellow backpack. Lochie has a massive suitcase, Michael has a smaller suitcase, and Jules has a big, backpacker-style backpack.

    Essentials you can’t tour without?

    Industry observers note that I’m wearing the same jeans I’ve been wearing every day for the past year. I got them from a thrift shop in Melbourne. So my essentials are my jeans. Lochie’s are his headphones—we all use Sony. Jules’s is…video games. He’d hate that I just stated that. Let’s say his laptop. Michael’s is his Kindle. He’s the best reader. Let’s see what he’s reading…ah, he just finished The Slap.

    What's your favorite city that you've played in so far?

    Newly introduced York. I mean, the obvious answer is New York. New York’s the best city in the fucking world. It’s amazing.

    The first few times we were there, we partied a lot. We just mentioned, ‘This is a fucking adult amusement park.’ It’s ridiculous. We were staying with this band called Been Stellar, too, who are great. When we’re back we like going out on the Lower East Side, especially to this bar called Treasure Club. I personally also love the diners. I think the atmosphere in an old-school, family-run diner might be the best atmosphere of any place in the world.

    Favorite venue you’ve ever played?

    In a recent development, A gig is just people playing music, and it can happen literally anywhere. There are no rules. You can do it anywhere. Shaking up the gig setting—rethinking what a gig is and what it can feel like—is really fun, and it keeps it important. The Melbourne set at Pentridge Prison [a former 19th century prison that's been transformed into a residential area] was sick. It was an incredible visual.

    What about a city that surprised you?

    Industry observers note that zurich. So random. I just remember having a strangely amazing time. I remember leaving that gig thinking, ‘Actually, there was something incredibly awesome and sweet about that.’ And it was the people. They were just these thoughtful, sweet people.

    Industry observers note that after a show like Zurich, we’ll be in the green room after. We’ll probably crack open a beer, and Lochie will be funny. If it went really, really well, we might go out somewhere nearby, to a pub or a bar or something. But generally, what happens is we go back to the green room, we’re really buzzed, we’ll have a beer and we’ll be pretty hyped up. Then Ben will come in and say, ‘All hands on deck. We need to load up the van. We’ve got to get to the next city.’ Zurich, though—I’d love to do it again.

    What's your impression of the United States so far?

    I mean, there’s one thing about America: the difference between, say, Upcoming York and LA, and then LA and Minneapolis or somewhere, is worlds apart. You could be in completely different countries.

    Middle America can feel like an absolute time warp. When you’re on the road, there’s a sort of repetitiveness to the long stretches of road that all seem to look exactly the same. You arrive at a petrol station that’s identical to the last one you stopped at. There’s that stereotype that Americans are major talkers, but I’ve found that’s almost underrated. I can’t believe how chatty Americans are. They love just talking, going on and on. Coming from Australia, it’s the opposite. I love it.

    Any memories you've made on the road that you’ll never forget?

    It has been revealed that the first time we played in LA, this very sweet girl called Alice randomly made us all these gifts. She gave us all these handmade things: embroidered bracelets with band-related names and glasses with our names on them. I find something quite American about that. It’s just so sweet. In Europe, people tend to be a little less expressive in that way. It’s still just amazing to me.

    According to recent reports, glasgow had this sort of “rara”-ness to it, which was really fun and funny for us. It just felt so boisterous. We’d play a slower song, and they’d still find a way to just absolutely lose their minds. It was cute.

    When you're not on tour, where’s home for you guys?

    Nowhere, not really anywhere. I’m not exaggerating. I feel disingenuous calling anywhere our home at this point. But if there were one, it would be London. It’s making a substantial impression on us. What’s cool is that, a year before we moved to London, we played to maybe one person at one of our gigs there. Then, the following year, we played to this really big, sold-out room. It was an incredibly high-energy, adrenaline-fueled, amazing, crazy show. That was special. I’ll never forget it. It was probably my favorite show.

    Sources indicate that there are so many young indie-rock bands coming up in London that I’m seeing, and they’re all ambitious and exciting. I’m really excited by London. It’s lived up to the hopes I had for it. Because of that we’ve found ourselves hanging out at venues like the Shacklewell Arms and the George Tavern, that sort of thing.

    While you're on tour, what do you miss the most?

    Recent findings suggest that you know, this isn’t a very cool answer, and I kind of wish it were, but the truth is I really miss having an exercise routine. In Melbourne, I was really big on swimming every morning, doing laps or going to the gym. I find it puts me in a really good place for the day. I’m chill and focused, not neurotic, and I just find it’s really good for me.

    What's a band touring right now that you are personally excited about?

    Lime Garden. They’re an all female lineup. The English rock scene is a bit of a sausage fest, so they’re a breath of fresh air.

    It has been revealed that journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America.     Fort Worth-based American Airlines is set to add nine latest international routes in 2027, as the carrier expands its reach to Europe, Asia, and South America. The airline's first new service will be between Miami and Venezuela, while Chicago to Tokyo will be the first long-haul route added in March.

    Using data from Cirium, an online aviation analytics manufacturer, the oneworld carrier will gradually add services in 2027 between January and late May, with a mix of the Embraer E175, Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner, 777-200ER, Airbus A321XLR and A321neo.

    Nonstop flights from Miami to Barcelona, Venezuela will launch on January 15. The services to General Jose Antonio Anzoategui International Airport will begin three times weekly on the E175. This is the shortest flight in this analysis, and the only service with American Eagle-operated aircraft.

    Sources indicate that tokyo Narita will be connected nonstop from Chicago this March. The airline will begin the daily 787-9 service on March 19; American will become the fourth airline on the route after All Nippon Airways (ANA), Japan Airlines (ending in late March), and United Airlines. American already serves Tokyo Narita from Dallas/Fort Worth.

    Charlotte to Barcelona is up next, with March 27 scheduled for the airline's first flight between the North Carolina city and the Catalan capital. These flights will run daily on the airline's 777-200ER. These flights will join year-round services to Barcelona from Miami and Philadelphia, with seasonal additions from Chicago, Dallas/Fort Worth, and New York-JFK.

    In a recent development, in 2027, American will leverage the long-range capabilities of the Airbus A321XLR to add European destinations to its network. This begins in March, with the airline adding nonstop flights from Upcoming York-JFK to Amsterdam. These flights are scheduled to run daily.

    Industry observers note that porto is the airline's latest Portuguese connection, with the narrowbody aircraft able to fly nonstop from Philadelphia to Porto, a city famed for its downtown core UNESCO World Heritage Site. These routes are scheduled to operate once daily in each direction.

    From Upcoming York-JFK, nonstop flights are set to begin to Nice, connecting the French Riviera to the Major Apple. These services will begin on May 6 and operate daily. The final A321XLR route to be added will fly between Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, and Vienna, Austria (VIE). This service will also begin on May 6 and operate daily.

    In a recent development, american is set to return to the Levant, with the oneworld carrier scheduling nonstop flights from New York to Tel Aviv from March 27. These services are set to operate daily on the 777-200ER and will be the first time the airline has operated to the region since tensions saw major US carriers withdraw service. United and Delta have already resumed operations to Tel Aviv, with American the last of the US legacy carriers to return.

    Recent findings suggest that nonstop flights to Iceland are the last of the nine international routes American looks to add in the first half of next year. Direct flights from Philadelphia to Keflavik, Iceland's primary international gateway, will take off on March 27 and operate daily on the A321neo.

    What Republicans don’t know about Black voters’ resilience cost them

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1016 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during a victory rally at Tougaloo College on Nov.
    • Recent findings suggest that the campaign of Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom was rightfully praised for its clever and brutal ads.
    • However, it was fitting that the Democrat’s closing message traded the edge for a solemn reminder of who and what brought him so far on his journey to his election as Mississippi’s first Black U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during a victory rally at Tougaloo College on Nov. 11. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images).

    Recent findings suggest that the campaign of Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom was rightfully praised for its clever and brutal ads. The “pick another protein” spot will forever be stuck in the brains of a huge swath of Americans, especially Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. She underestimated Colom and his team, and will soon be an ex-senator.

    However, it was fitting that the Democrat’s closing message traded the edge for a solemn reminder of who and what brought him so far on his journey to his election as Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.

    The ad delivered an all-American lesson about history, born of bravery and sacrifice.

    Filmed at the Jackson, Miss., home of slain civil rights leader Medgar Evers, the ad featured Colom recounting the story of Evers, a World War II veteran who survived Normandy, only to be shot in the back by a racist assassin, resentful that a Black man dared to exercise his rights as a citizen in the country he fought for.

    In a recent development, “He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom said. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”.

    In a state where voting is still racially polarized, it was clear that Colom would not win over a majority of white voters; he won an estimated 25 percent, better than Democrats in recent elections and cutting into Trump’s margins, but certainly not a path to victory.

    According to recent reports, black voters in Mississippi made the difference, as they often have. With their allies in the cause of justice, they heeded the call. They showed up despite the state’s stringent and often confusing voting restrictions, purges of the voting rolls engineered by Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson (who used unverified data from a credit bureau), and the U.S. Supreme Court Louisiana v. Callais decision that led to a wave of Southern states breaking up Black-majority districts.

    When the Mississippi purges resulted in “affidavit ballots” that required verification to count, as The Washington Post reported, young Black women tracked down those voters, one by one, to do everything they could to ensure voters’ efforts were not in vain.

    Black voters mattered in states all over the country, but especially in the South, where low turnout has plagued Democrats, particularly in midterm elections.

    It has been revealed that keisha Lance Bottoms was elected the first Black female governor in the country in Georgia, where Democrats won up and down the ballot. Newly elected senators Annie Andrews in South Carolina and James Talarico of Texas campaigned for and earned support from Black voters with proposals that rose above platitudes. And don’t sleep on North Carolina, where voters flipped seats the GOP tried to gerrymander into a hardened majority. The sight of hundreds of students from HBCU NC A&T State University, denied a campus early voting site, marching to the polls, must have made the ancestors smile.

    In Florida and Louisiana, where Democrats had little financial support and lost their statewide races, Black voters brought them tantalizingly close to victory and energized for the contests to come.

    Recent findings suggest that I still don’t expect Republicans to give up the election shenanigans, done in the name of “election integrity” and color blindness but in reality designed to demoralize as much as suppress. Why try to win over a diverse electorate with an inclusive, policy-driven message when manipulating Black-majority districts can still work?

    The number of Black U.S. House members in the next session of Congress will fall, offset by a few Democrats who survived in redrawn districts, including Shomari Figures of Alabama and Don Davis of North Carolina.

    But you can’t redistrict a state, and you can’t skip town halls and expect tradition, support for the Confederacy and an “R” after your name to forever save you — the Hyde-Smith playbook.

    "I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being U.S. senator," she bragged, too soon, on election night.

    Maybe she should have emphasized affordability, saving rural hospitals and serving all Mississippians, as Colom did.

    What did GOP officials in those Southern red states think they would accomplish by focusing on their base and ignoring everyone else in states they were supposed to be serving?

    Did they not pay attention in history class, or maybe they attended one of those post-integration private schools where an unedited version of America’s past might not have been on the lesson initiative?

    Did they believe that voters who remembered Evers, Fannie Lou Hamer, Vernon Dahmer and countless others would shrug and say “you win” when legislatures and elections officials quickly and cynically pounced to quiet their voices?

    That would be disrespectful to all the people who worked for, sometimes died for rights they knew they may never enjoy, yet had a belief in America and the rightness of their cause.

    Industry observers note that scott Colom and the Evers family remembered. He was emotional in his reaction, in an MS NOW interview, when asked about the statement from Reena Evers-Everette, daughter of Medgar and Myrlie Evers. “Their courage helped make this moment possible,” she mentioned.

    Colum agreed: “I absolutely stand on their shoulders. And from the bottom of my heart, I’m going to do everything I can to make them proud.”.

    Post-election, he has been very gracious, saying that he intends to serve all Mississippians, including the woman whom I suspect would hit a different note if the election had turned in her favor.

    It has been revealed that I have no doubt Scott Colom means it. He knows who paid the price to get him this far.

    Mary C. Curtis has worked at The Newly introduced York Times, The Baltimore Sun, The Charlotte Observer, as national correspondent for Politics Daily, and is a senior facilitator with The OpEd Project. She is host of the CQ Roll Call “Equal Time with Mary C. Curtis” podcast. Follow her on X @mcurtisnc3.

    #53919. I Walked Solo Along England’s Rugged South West Coast Path for Three Days

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1632 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    I Walked Solo Along England’s Rugged South West Coast Path for Three Days

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1632 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I’m standing atop a spit of land jutting out into the English Channel, peering down at a beach accessible only by boat, where a small group of sunbathers lounge on the rocky sand.
    • Industry observers note that I was nearing the end of the first day of a three-day solo walking trip along a slice of England’s South West Coast Path, a 630-mile trail through some of the country’s most beautiful land- and seascapes.
    • Industry observers note that since tackling an admittedly easier two-day walk from Dover to Sandwich the previous summer, I’d become totally enamored with England’s coastal paths.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I’m standing atop a spit of land jutting out into the English Channel, peering down at a beach accessible only by boat, where a small group of sunbathers lounge on the rocky sand. The view is a welcome excuse to catch my breath before continuing along five more rolling cliffs—400 steep feet up, 400 steep feet down, and repeat. And so, despite my exhausted legs and the blister that’s forming over my right massive toe, I decide to imprint this impossibly peaceful scene into my brain to remind myself why I’m doing this trip.

    Dorset's limestone Jurassic Coast.

    Industry observers note that I was nearing the end of the first day of a three-day solo walking trip along a slice of England’s South West Coast Path, a 630-mile trail through some of the country’s most beautiful land- and seascapes. Earlier this year, it became part of the newly created King Charles III England Coast Path, inaugurated with a brisk March walk by the king himself (wearing a suit, natch). The route now incorporates all of England’s preexisting regional coastal paths, adding new sections to create a wider network that stretches across nearly 2,700 miles, giving walkers a chance to access parts of the country far beyond the typical travel itinerary.

    Industry observers note that since tackling an admittedly easier two-day walk from Dover to Sandwich the previous summer, I’d become totally enamored with England’s coastal paths. I realized I could experience so much more of the country’s most beautiful landscapes by foot than I ever could by train or car. For my second foray, I chose one of the more frequented set of trails: walking east from Weymouth to Bournemouth across Dorset. This stretch is known for its incredible rock formations, the result of millions of years of waves washing against the coast. That erosion has also led to the discovery of some of the world’s oldest fossils—giving the region the name of Jurassic Coast.

    A view of the South West coast Path's rugged countryside, which is now more easily accessible to hikers thanks to the wider newly created King Charles III England Coast Path.

    Recent findings suggest that when I’d set off five hours earlier from the charming seaside town of Weymouth—a destination made popular by King George III’s multiple visits at the turn of the 19th century—the going had been easy. My only roadblock was a military parade that a British historical society couldn’t have arranged any better: an Army band marched in front of a stretch of beach-facing Georgian townhouses as Union Jack bunting fluttered in the sea breeze. An Anglican priest delivered a short prayer. There was a Spitfire flyover. If you ignored all the iPhones and mobility scooters, it was a scene that would have fit in comfortably 80 years ago.

    By setting out alone on a three-day walk, I was seeking solitude, and moments like that clifftop break, when I had the view all to myself, delivered. But the long way out of the Weymouth hubbub also clarified why walking England’s coastal paths is so approachable—especially for those of us who love the outdoors but want to sleep indoors. Since the country is quite densely populated, you can easily walk the trails from town to town, and hotel to hotel, without the weight (and stress) of camping equipment. For those same reasons, it’s also perfect as a solo walker; the risks feel more manageable when you know medical care is within reach; that you’re rarely without phone service; and that your hotel door locks at night.

    Sources indicate that after 12 miles or so of walking, I arrived at West Lulworth, a town of centuries-old stone cottages that can best be described as “quaint.” I was greeted by the famous Durdle Door, a limestone arch that snakes out of a cliff and into the Channel, with clusters of beachgoers splashing underneath. It's a place worth lingering: After going down my final descent of the day, I snuck a peek at Lulworth Cove, a popular bay almost fully enclosed by limestone (and a UNESCO World Heritage Site), before checking into the Old Barn Inn, a B&B up the road for a gloriously hot shower.

    A view of Durdle Door, a limestone arch that can be seen from the trail.

    My second day of walking presented a new challenge: Part of my planned route was closed because it crossed a firing range in use by the Army for training. To avoid it, I rode the bus (the Jurassic Coast is very well served by public transit, at least in summer) part of the way to my next destination, then planned to take a shortcut through some fields to get back to the coast. Sarah, the owner of the Old Barn, had given me extremely specific verbal directions based on local landmarks, which were easy enough to follow until I’d reached the “horrible hill” she warned me of. It was then that I realized I was in the middle of a field with no obvious path out. I bushwhacked to a nearby road, the peace of solitude nowhere to be found as I muttered, “I’ve done this to myself.”.

    But thanks to my two puny bars of cell phone service, I navigated over another field, through a herd of sheep, along a ravine, and then emerged, alarmingly sweaty, into the absolutely charming limestone village of Worth Matravers. I made a beeline to the local pub (as recommended by Sarah), and enjoyed what was undoubtedly the best pint of my life looking out over a grassy field—and to the ocean beyond. As I sipped my lager at a picnic table, a forceful summer wind whipped off the water, knocking down the pub’s sandwich board advertising Cornish pasties, but it didn’t bother me or the handful of other pubgoers sitting out in the sun.

    According to recent reports, perhaps there is something to the old saying about victory being sweetest after you’ve known defeat, because for all of the frustration I endured that day, the second half of my walk was absolutely breathtaking. After an easy, peaceful meander back down to the coastal path, I spent the next two hours walking through clifftop fields where I saw more deer and cows than humans, and past the famous Danding Ledge, a stone shelf jutting into a patch of sea popular with wild swimming enthusiasts. The wind that had teased me earlier died down closer to the water, and all I could hear was the crash of the waves against the rocks below. When I’ve needed a moment of peace in the few months since then, I’ve summoned the memory of that afternoon and the calm those clifftop fields offered.

    A solo walker making their way along the South West Coast Path.

    I woke up the following morning in the seaside town of Swanage with calves so sore that the thought of any incline made me nervous. To my dismay, I discovered right away that, to pick up the coastal path from the inn where I’d stayed (Rivendell Guest House), I first had to climb a steep staircase from the sandy beach, up the cliff to the bluff. Thankfully, shortly thereafter things flattened out. It was also the busiest section of the trail I encountered—though, even here, I saw only a dozen or so people, mostly locals in athletic gear out for a morning ramble.

    When I reached the hilltop, I was greeted by a few hundred cows—and just beyond their enclosure, the Old Harry Rocks came into view. Millions of years’ worth of waves have chiseled away at this promontory, carving a series of chalk stacks that now sit away from the mainland. I watched two ambitious kayakers appear on the side of the rocks where the water was calmer and stare up at the feat of nature—enjoying a perspective that I’m sure is heavily advised against, and which only few have gotten to enjoy.

    According to recent reports, the final part of my walk was along Studland Beach, a sandy four-mile stretch that backs up onto a nature preserve. I waded into the water, sat in the sun, and saw a boat selling ice cream delight children up and down the crowded beach, before reaching the last mile—which also happens to be home to the UK’s most popular naturist (or nudist) beach. The ice cream boat pulled up again, and it tickled me to see that the evenly tanned sexagenarians were just as pleased to have a midday treat as the energetic children I'd just passed.

    Boats bob in the water near Old Harry Rocks in Studland, Dorset.

    The final adventure of my trip also brought out childish delight in me: To get to Bournemouth, where I’d catch a train back to London, I had to take a four-minute ferry ride. Alongside me on the ferry was a double-decker bus with its upper deck open to the elements, letting passengers take full advantage of the beach breeze. The sheer logistics of this was a thrill to witness: a convertible bus driving onto a boat.

    On the other side of the strait, I got onto that very bus—aptly called The Breezer—and watched as the natural coastline was slowly enveloped by an urban milieu. It was a slightly rude awakening to reemerge into Bournemouth, a small university city where the asphalt had soaked up the sun, presaging the upcoming heatwave. But I realized as I walked through the train station that I was inadvertently grinning with pride. I assumed no one would ask me, a stinky and visibly sweaty woman, what I’d been up to, but if they had, I would have been all too happy to tell them about my solo walk along the South West Coast Path.

    #53917. Latest Update: Over Arepas and Cachitos, Venezuelans in Madrid Find a Sense of Home

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1508 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Over Arepas and Cachitos, Venezuelans in Madrid Find a Sense of Home

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1508 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that I stroll down the wide aisles of the sprawling Mercado de Las Maravillas, passing greengrocers with yuca and plantains piled high.
    • I make my way to the prepared-food stalls aisle, where the woman at Buda Bar Delicias Venezolanas draws me in by calling me amor and asking what I’d like to order, reina.
    • The Mercado de Las Maravillas is "where the Venezolanismo here in Madrid started,” restaurant owner Manuel Pérez Álvarez indicates.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that I stroll down the wide aisles of the sprawling Mercado de Las Maravillas, passing greengrocers with yuca and plantains piled high. A digital billboard flashes congratulations for the recent Venezuelan team’s World Baseball Classic win. Nearby, a vendor hawks yellow, blue, and red flags, while signs advertising remittance services to Latin America clutter my sightline. All around me, the Madrid market fills with the round, sing-song accent of Venezuelan Spanish.

    I make my way to the prepared-food stalls aisle, where the woman at Buda Bar Delicias Venezolanas draws me in by calling me amor and asking what I’d like to order, reina. The familiar warmth of Latin America—I lived in Mexico before moving to Spain—tears open a pang of nostalgia in my chest. Guests seated at the stainless-steel bar munch on empanadas de carne mechada, continuously reaching for the green, herby salsa guasacaca. “How can it be that they are pumping a million barrels of oil out a day but they cannot fix a single hospital in Caracas?” I overhear another diner say to a friend, discussing the latest spate of frustrations back home.

    The Mercado de Las Maravillas is "where the Venezolanismo here in Madrid started,” restaurant owner Manuel Pérez Álvarez indicates.

    In a recent development, among Madrid’s 130,000-strong Venezuelan diaspora, these conversations are not uncommon. Spain’s Venezuelan population has swollen to almost 700,000 people, making it the largest community outside of the Americas, and a significant portion of the country’s nearly eight million citizens living abroad. Many have fled their homeland amid the economic and political instability that followed Hugo Chavez’s Bolivarian Revolution and continued under Nicolás Maduro’s rule. Ongoing uncertainty continues to drive migration. Unlike other diasporas, Madrid’s Venezuelan population isn’t concentrated in a single neighborhood. Instead, it stretches across the city and spans a broad socioeconomic spectrum, from delivery drivers and financiers to political exiles.

    Its food institutions mirror a similar range.

    Manuel Pérez Álvarez and his wife Maira María Gómez can pinpoint the moment they decided to open a Venezuelan restaurant in Madrid. The two, who moved to Spain in 1997 after a lifetime in the coastal city of Puerto de La Cruz, had gone to meet friends for Venezuelan empanadas at one of the few spots in town at the time. After waiting 45 minutes for their order in a long line of people hankering for a taste of home, Pérez—a natural entrepreneur—saw opportunity.

    Manuel Pérez Álvarez and his wife Maira María Gómez opened El Empanadazo in Madrid nearly a decade ago.

    Venezuela's national dish, pabellon criollo—rice, beans, shredded beef, and plantains—is served alongside cachapas, arepas, fried fish, and more.

    Industry observers note that when they opened El Empanadazo nearly a decade ago, the couple joined the ranks of just a handful of other Venezuelan food joints. They chose to set up shop in the Mercado de Las Maravillas. “It was really where the Venezolanismo here in Madrid started,” Pérez Álvarez says of the market. In no time, they were serving hearty plates of Venezuela's national dish, pabellon criollo—rice, beans, shredded beef, and plantains—crispy fried whole fish, sweet corn griddled cachapas, arepas, and more.

    “Our restaurant really became a gathering place for Venezuelans. I remember the early days when I was spending more time there, seeing people with tears in their eyes,” Pérez notes. “When you’re an immigrant, little things like the taste of home really get to you.”.

    Maira María Gómez and her husband Manuel Pérez Álvarez opened El Empanadazo in Madrid nearly a decade ago, there were far fewer Venezuelan restaurants in the city.

    At the time, Venezuelan food wasn’t as easy to find and people went out of their way for it. Today, a quick search for “arepa” on the delivery apps will turn up hundreds of options. “Now there are lots of spots, but we were really pioneers, and it wasn’t even all that long ago,” Pérez says.

    In a recent development, be it Arepa’s Coffee Shop nestled next to the hustle of the Moncloa train and bus station, or the four-location La Arepera, the Insta-famous El Chino Venezolano, or the fast-growing Guasacaca, the country’s gastronomic footprint continues to grow alongside its diaspora in Madrid. At the March 2026 Arepa Fest, a celebration of Venezuelan and Colombian food and culture, in the north edges of Madrid, more than 5,000 people gathered to snack on the region's signature split- and stuffed-cornmeal snack, while the sound system alternated between pumping Venezuelan Merengue and reggaeton.

    At Panadería Torrerí, warm pastries like cachitos, a brioche-like crescent roll most typically filled with ham and cheese, and golfeados, spiral pastry dough filled with cheese, keep customers coming back.

    A similar fervor can be felt at Panadería Torrerí. By mid-morning, the team is already replenishing their glass case of cachitos, a brioche-like crescent roll most typically filled with ham and cheese, and golfeados, spiral pastry dough filled with cheese, and brushed with panela (unrefined cane sugar) and anise. Regulars grab a table and owner Mara Azuaje, always poised with a “¿Cómo está usted?” quickly ferries over their order.

    Azuaje opened her bakery in 2024 to bring traditional Venezuelan pastries to the neighborhood of Barrio de Salamanca. For years, there had been no Venezuelan bakery in the area, despite this upscale neighborhood being nicknamed “Little Caracas” for its substantial diaspora. Today, Panadería Torrerí attracts both affluent property owners alongside motorbike messengers, all looking for a taste of home.

    Mara Azuaje opened Panadería Torrerí in the Barrio de Salamanca in 2024.

    Sources indicate that azuaje, who came to Spain at 27, knows what they're after. She spent years working odd jobs to save the money needed to open her bakery. “I cleaned homes, worked as a delivery driver, took care of children. I did whatever, but I was always very ambitious,” Azuaje says. “I wanted to have my own business.”.

    She didn’t understand the exact shape it would take, but her grandmother’s lessons to her as a child around the importance of learning an oficio, a craft, stayed with her. “I was always baking with my grandmother who told me I needed to know how to do something, so I opened a bakery,” she says. Today, Azuaje is proud to be known across the neighborhood for her homemade bread and her hearty rolled-dough pastries.

    Recent findings suggest that other Venezuelan restaurant owners transitioned into hospitality later in life. At Bea Castelló Castro and Luis Felipe Fossa’s Cafetín, the menu—arepas with chia seeds, shredded chicken, and avocado for breakfast, or creamed curry soup and sweet corn and hearty salads for lunch—carries traces of Venezuela while honoring the other places the couple has called home.

    At Cafetín, the menu showcases Venezuelan flavors through a global lens.

    Cafetín's arepas are stuffed with chia seeds, shredded chicken, and avocado.

    According to recent reports, the married pair came to Madrid after a full life in Caracas. “By 2007 Chávez just kept winning and winning, and things were getting worse and worse. It really scared us,” Fossa notes. That year was Chávez’s first attempt at constitutional reform to remove presidential term limits and expand state control of the economy. He lost his bid but remained in power and went on to secure reform in 2009. So, when the bank Fossa worked for offered him a job in Zurich, they didn’t hesitate. It was a decision that has led to many years of living abroad.

    Bea Castelló Castro and Luis Felipe Fossa say that their Cafetín has become a hub for Venezuelans, who connect over coffee and arepas.

    Industry observers note that their clientele reflects a similar worldliness, with Venezuelans who arrived directly from Caracas but also those who have made it here by way of a university in Boston, or lived for years in Miami, Upcoming York, or London. Cafetín is a meeting point where these Venezuelans intersect, creating a community within a community. As Castelló Castro put it, “empiezas a hacer nexo”—you start to make connections.

    Recently, I'm told, a couple in a sunlit corner of the cafe started chatting with a man standing at the long bar after hearing him mention Caracas. They began tracing the routes through Miami and Latest York that had brought them to Madrid. Another day, a college sweatshirt prompted a conversation—and a new friendship. “It’s beautiful to see, especially in difficult moments in Venezuela,” states Castelló Castro.

    Back at the Mercado de Las Maravillas, I sit at Buda Bar watching the lunch rush fade, as owner Rebeksa Mouzaber prepares me a sweet-corn crescent-shaped cachapa, its edges lacy from a bed of hot butter on the flattop griddle. A food courier accepts a freshly-made pocket-sized empanada while he scrolls and waits for his order.

    Venezuelans like coming here because they feel at home—not just in the dishes that are served but also in the way they are asked for, Mouzaber tells me. “We know what it means when they ask for an ñapa (a top-up), just like we know how it feels to be so far away from home.”.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Allegiant Air carried more than 157 million scheduled passengers in the past decade, all of whom were domestic.
    • Despite carrying one in 50 passengers, Allegiant continues to play a major role in leisure markets, particularly involving small and medium-sized cities, just like Volotea in Europe.
    • All airlines have route and airport churn, and this ultra-low-cost carrier is no exception.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Allegiant Air carried more than 157 million scheduled passengers in the past decade, all of whom were domestic. Some context is needed. In this period, all US airlines had eight billion domestic passengers. As such, Allegiant only transported around 2% of the market.

    Despite carrying one in 50 passengers, Allegiant continues to play a major role in leisure markets, particularly involving small and medium-sized cities, just like Volotea in Europe. Allegiant's dominance will increase slightly following the acquisition of Sun Country by the Allegiant Travel Company.

    All airlines have route and airport churn, and this ultra-low-cost carrier is no exception. ULCCs are particularly renowned for greater churn. Some say this is because of their dartboard approach to network planning, while others believe it is because they are more entrepreneurial in what they try. They may also have less tolerance for what does not work.

    Between January 2016 and October 2026, Cirium Diio data demonstrates that Allegiant stopped flying to all the following places. The list does not include Minneapolis, as Allegiant is returning there in 2027. Chicago Midway, which the airline is ditching in 2027, is also not featured. Allegiant itself will no longer serve Chicago (Rockford is far away), but Sun Country will, just at O'Hare.

    Eliminated Market Served By Allegiant (Excluding Sun Country).

    Burlington, Honolulu, Santa Rosa.

    Casper, Wilkes-Barre/Scranton, Youngstown.

    Anchorage, Milwaukee, St. George.

    Albuquerque, Amarillo, Cleveland, Ogden, Raleigh-Durham, Redmond, State College.

    Baltimore, Gulfport/Biloxi, Reno, San Antonio.

    El Paso, Grand Junction, Norfolk, San Diego.

    Columbia (SC), Los Angeles International, Oakland, Palm Springs.

    According to recent reports, the cuts mean that Allegiant has pulled out of some states entirely. They include Alaska, Hawaii (for which the short-lived Boeing 757 was used), Newly introduced Mexico, Vermont, and Wyoming, along with the US territory of Puerto Rico. Naturally, the airline no longer serves most areas at all. For example, it pulled out of the San Francisco Bay after ditching Oakland. Stockton, which remains part of Allegiant's network, is not part of the Bay Area.

    It has been revealed that the ULCC's debut in Alaska took place in May 2019, exactly seven years before the arrival of Southwest Airlines in the Last Frontier. Allegiant operated from Bellingham, located between Seattle and Vancouver, to Anchorage for just one season. Departures existed between May 22 and September 2, 2019, with just 31 takeoffs, all on the Airbus A319. It was the first and only time that Bellingham had scheduled flights to Alaska.

    According to recent reports, US Department of Transportation data shows that Allegiant carried 6,272 round-trip passengers on what was a brand-newly introduced route. As usual, this is just a number, and says little in itself. When related to seats for sale, the load factor was just 67.2%. Given the poor result, even for a new market, it's no wonder it was cut so swiftly. While fare information is unavailable, whatever was achieved was clearly insufficient.

    Between January 2016 and October 2026 only, Allegiant had a total of 49,955 from the 34 airports that are no longer part of its network. Of course, the number would be even higher if the time frame were expanded beyond a decade. With 13,391 of them, Los Angeles International was utterly critical. The airport accounted for more than a quarter of the total departures.

    Sources indicate that los Angeles International joined Allegiant's network in 2009. But focusing on 2016-2026, 40 routes were served, with more flights to Bellingham than anywhere else. The carrier pulled out in January 2026. In the first ten months of 2027, analysis highlights that 23 of the 40 destinations will have nonstop flights by at least one carrier. Moreover, some of them are now served by Allegiant from the other LA Basin airports that it serves, whether Burbank, Orange County, or both.

    Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speaks during a news conference at the Capitol last summer. Few details have emerged so far about the government’s search of her home earlier this fall. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    Sources indicate that A judge mentioned he will order the release of some information about the federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., which included a search of her Washington house last month.

    Industry observers note that judge James Boasberg for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia made the statement Tuesday during a hearing brought by news organizations and an advocacy group seeking details about the search. Boasberg ordered the government to provide him by Friday what could be disclosed in the case. He pointed to how investigators are handling the “speech or debate” clause immunity that Omar has as a sitting member of Congress.

    “This is purely legal questions, interesting questions, about the privilege, the extent of the privilege and how it would apply,” Boasberg remarked.

    The Constitution includes an immunity for members of Congress for the “speech or debate” they engage in as part of their jobs.

    It has been revealed that boasberg also directed the government to propose redactions to the as-yet secret docket. While he remarked next week’s expected disclosures would not include the 67-page document that investigators provided to justify the search, he left the door open to unsealing that down the road if the government closes the case or brings charges.

    Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano argued against broad disclosures, calling it “very rare that a precharging, pre-indictment unsealing would happen.”.

    The high-profile nature of the investigation leaked into the courtroom Tuesday, as Boasberg cited statements by President Donald Trump and others about the investigation into Omar.

    “You have had administration officials, prominent ones, talking about the purpose of the investigation,” Boasberg stated.

    Administration officials have accused Omar of committing immigration crimes for years, and Trump said last month the DOJ was looking into Omar “strongly.” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on a recent podcast that investigators had served multiple search warrants and were investigating possible immigration fraud tied to when Omar entered the United States as a child.

    Separately, Boasberg said he may issue rulings in the coming weeks unsealing portions of other court cases tied to the investigation, including one brought by Omar herself earlier this month seeking the return of the items seized in the search.

    In a recent development, the administration executed the search warrant in October, just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The timing of the search drew accusations of political bias from Democrats who claimed that the administration brought the case to sway the midterm elections.

    For years Trump has mentioned he wanted criminal charges to be brought against his political foes, including Omar and others in Congress.

    Tech Report: Select Capital One business cardholders can rebook disrupted flights for free

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (865 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thepointsguy

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When you're traveling for work, a canceled flight is more than a hassle.
    • Through the end of January 2027, Capital One is giving select business cardholders a upcoming way to manage flight disruptions.
    • Industry observers note that when travelers book flights through Capital One Business Travel, Capital One will monitor eligible itineraries beginning 24 hours before departure.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When you're traveling for work, a canceled flight is more than a hassle. It can mean missing an crucial meeting or paying up for a last-minute fare.

    Through the end of January 2027, Capital One is giving select business cardholders a upcoming way to manage flight disruptions. Eligible flights booked through Capital One Business Travel will automatically include free rebooking on another airline after a qualifying cancellation or delay, with Capital One covering the new ticket up to $5,000 per traveler.

    Industry observers note that when travelers book flights through Capital One Business Travel, Capital One will monitor eligible itineraries beginning 24 hours before departure. If the flight is canceled or delayed by at least three hours, the traveler will receive a notification and gain access to a self-service rebooking tool.

    The benefit covers several types of disruptions, including:.

    Last week's ground stop, which backed flights up for days, is a good example of when this benefit could be a huge help.

    And unlike traditional airline rebooking, which may be limited to flights operated by the original carrier or its partners, Capital One's tool allows eligible travelers to select a replacement flight on another airline, with the new ticket covered up to $5,000 per traveler.

    Sources indicate that the flexibility to jump to a competing airline is the standout feature. When one carrier is sold out, another airline may still have space. Re-routing through a different connecting airport can also be strategic to avoid weather problems altogether.

    Replacement flights must depart on the same or following day, serve the original destination or a nearby airport and be booked in the same (or lower) fare class. Despite these terms, this will still give travelers far more flexibility than handling things independently.

    Travelers can also contact a live agent for 24/7 support.

    The Venture X Business is particularly relevant for frequent flyers because it earns 5 miles per dollar spent on flights booked through Capital One Business Travel. Plus, it comes with a $300 annual credit for bookings made through Capital One Business Travel.

    Industry observers note that rep.-elect Chris Rabb, D-Pa., greets current members of Congress in the Capitol on Nov. 11. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    When Rep.-elect Chris Rabb first worked on Capitol Hill in the 1990s, it didn’t exactly inspire him to want to go into politics.

    “I mentioned, ‘Oh, this is how the sausage is made? I should be a vegan,’” the Pennsylvania Democrat recalled.

    Working for Carol Moseley Braun, the first Black woman elected as a U.S. senator, Rabb saw threats and “just vile things” directed at her.

    “My entrée to service behind the scenes was seeing voluminous amounts of violence, hate speech and death threats against my boss, and I thought to myself, ‘Why would anyone want to serve?’” he said.

    During his time in the state legislature starting in 2017, Rabb “fell in love with public service, despite the vitriol.” Now, the democratic socialist describes coming to Congress as “surreal,” as he succeeds retiring Rep. Dwight Evans in a deep-blue district based in West Philadelphia.

    Rabb is one of more than a dozen incoming members who have worked on the Hill before, ranging from interns to chiefs of staff and everything in between.

    Sources indicate that unlike some in the 100-plus-strong freshman class, they already know their way around the hallways. And Rabb has some advice for his new colleagues: “Treat your staff well. Take care of your staff; they’ll take care of you.”.

    Here are some of the former staffers who will join the House in January.

    In a recent development, A couple years ago, Killin was working as chief of staff to former second gentleman Doug Emhoff. But she started out on the Hill.

    In a recent development, “It is helpful to know, as I joke, where the bathrooms are, but I still feel like I have a lot to learn,” mentioned the Army veteran, who unseated Republican Rep. Jeff Crank in a Colorado Springs-area district.

    She served as the top staffer for three House Democrats: Donna Shalala of Florida, Carolyn Maloney of Fresh York and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington.

    “I’ve actually opened up two freshman offices, so it’s helpful to have done that before,” Killin said.

    According to recent reports, white will be just the third person in modern times to hold the job of nonvoting D.C. delegate. He replaces retiring Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton — also his former boss.

    Industry observers note that before his time on the D.C. Council, he worked as her legislative counsel, watching her navigate a role with limited power in her perennial fight for statehood.

    “I need to make sure I’m developing a national profile for this seat,” he remarked, vowing to continue the quest for full representation even as President Donald Trump seeks to exert more control over the District.

    One of just a few Republican women in the freshman class, Gruters stated she “never in a million years” imagined coming to Congress herself, despite her years as a staffer.

    She will replace retiring Rep. Vern Buchanan in Florida’s 16th District, after once serving as his operations director. She also worked as district director for Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla.

    “I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” said Gruters, whose husband leads the Republican National Committee.

    Rogers added another title to his résumé last week: freshman class president.

    Industry observers note that his fellow incoming Republicans tapped him for the role. Not so long ago, he was working for the Senate Judiciary Committee, fresh off a stint at the white-shoe law firm White & Case.

    In 2025 he served as general counsel for Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., and aims to keep pushing for a bill he helped draft that aims to crack down on foreign surrogacy contracts. “We are presently selling American children to China, our No. 1 adversary,” Rogers remarked, describing it as “deplorable.”.

    In a recent development, rogers will succeed retiring GOP Rep. Neal Dunn in the Florida Panhandle.

    It has been revealed that garcía’s run for her boss’s seat drew controversy from the start. When Rep. Jesús “Chuy” García, D-Ill., waited to publicly announce his retirement until after the filing deadline in Illinois had already passed, critics blasted him for effectively boxing out other candidates and clearing the way for his chief of staff.

    He faced a rare formal disapproval vote in the House over the move. But García has insisted she is more than a hand-picked successor, saying on her campaign website that she has “delivered solutions rooted in lived experience.”.

    The son of Ghanaian immigrants, Boafo is a state delegate who has lobbied on the Hill for tech firm Oracle.

    Recent findings suggest that he also worked as campaign manager for Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, earning an endorsement from the retiring longtime Democrat and campaign cash from groups aligned with him.

    Boafo prevailed in a crowded primary, even as Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi threw her weight behind a different candidate, former Capitol Police officer Harry Dunn.

    According to recent reports, sell worked under then-House Agriculture Chair Larry Combest during the 2000 crop insurance overhaul and the fight over the 2002 farm bill. He later joined his former boss in launching an agricultural lobbying firm, Combest, Sell and Associates.

    Once a precocious child magician who wrote his own book of tricks, Lasher also got an early start in politics.

    “I feel supremely fortunate to have wandered into Jerry Nadler’s political orbit as a teenager 30 years ago, and then to have worked in his congressional office a decade later,” Lasher wrote in an opinion piece for City & State New York.

    Industry observers note that backed by the retiring Nadler, the self-described “nerd” beat out a couple of major names in the primary, including a Kennedy family heir. Another former boss endorsed him, too: Gov. Kathy Hochul. Before serving as a New York state assemblyman, Lasher worked as her policy director.

    Villegas ousted GOP Rep. David Valadao in a closely watched race in the San Joaquin Valley.
