    #53911. Why United Airlines Is Betting On Premium To Bring Revive Popularity Of 50-Seater Jets

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1793 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Why United Airlines Is Betting On Premium To Bring Revive Popularity Of 50-Seater Jets

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1793 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • United Airlines is attempting something that might have seemed unthinkable a decade ago: making the widely disliked, aging 50-seat regional jet attractive to passengers again.
    • It has been revealed that the resulting CRJ450 represents an unusual strategy in an industry focused on larger regional aircraft and premium-heavy cabins.
    • United's decision to introduce the CRJ450 is primarily about making its regional network more profitable without sacrificing connections to smaller communities.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    United Airlines is attempting something that might have seemed unthinkable a decade ago: making the widely disliked, aging 50-seat regional jet attractive to passengers again. Instead of abandoning the 20-year-old Bombardier CRJ200, the Chicago-based carrier is transforming it into a substantially more luxurious aircraft, complete with a first class cabin, extra-legroom seating, and high-speed satellite internet.

    It has been revealed that the resulting CRJ450 represents an unusual strategy in an industry focused on larger regional aircraft and premium-heavy cabins. But why is United investing in an aircraft with just 41 seats when other airlines have been moving away from 50-seater jets? The answer involves pilot union agreements, regional connectivity, the CRJ550's success, and United's ambitions to attract higher-paying passengers even on its smallest routes.

    United's decision to introduce the CRJ450 is primarily about making its regional network more profitable without sacrificing connections to smaller communities. The aircraft is a heavily reconfigured Bombardier CRJ200 operated by SkyWest Airlines under the United Express brand. Rather than purchasing an entirely newly introduced aircraft, United is giving an existing regional jet a different commercial purpose by replacing its traditional 50-seat economy configuration with a 41-seat, three-cabin interior. The move also demonstrates that the airline believes there is still a place for smaller regional aircraft when the onboard experience is sufficiently attractive.

    Industry observers note that timing is notable because 50-seat regional jets have struggled with passenger perceptions for years. Frequent flyers have often nicknamed the CRJ200 the Devil's Chariot, reflecting its cramped cabin, limited overhead storage, and relatively uncomfortable experience. Its narrow fuselage and 2-2 seating arrangement leave little room for the amenities passengers expect, particularly those traveling in premium cabins. According to The Points Guy's coverage of the CRJ-450 and Runway Girl Network, United intends to address these shortcomings through a comprehensive interior redesign.

    According to recent reports, however, the CRJ450 is not an attempt to make an old aircraft a private jet with flamboyant luxury. Its introduction reflects a structural limitation affecting United's regional operations: agreements with its pilots limit how many larger regional jets it can deploy. This raises the question of why United cannot simply replace its smallest aircraft with larger jets.

    According to recent reports, the explanation lies in pilot scope clauses: contractual provisions negotiated between major US airlines and their pilot unions. These agreements regulate the number and characteristics of aircraft that regional partners can operate on behalf of mainline carriers. United faces particularly restrictive limitations on larger regional aircraft, while its contractual framework provides considerably more flexibility for 50-seat jets. Consequently, retiring every smaller regional aircraft would not necessarily be practical, even if larger jets offered better passenger economics.

    United previously demonstrated how it could work around this limitation with the CRJ550, introduced in 2019. Based on the larger Bombardier CRJ700, the aircraft was reconfigured from its conventional 70-seat arrangement into a 50-seat aircraft with three cabins. It offered eight First class seats, 16 Economy Plus seats, and 26 standard economy seats, along with additional luggage storage. The strategy lets United offer a more premium experience while keeping the aircraft in the 50-seat category. The Points Guy explains the contractual advantage in its analysis of United's CRJ-450 business case.

    The CRJ-450 takes the same principle further, this time using the smaller CRJ200 airframe.

    Converted into the 41-seat CRJ450.

    Converted into the 50-seat CRJ550.

    Conventional regional operation.

    United may not be choosing the CRJ450 over a larger aircraft solely because of passenger capacity. Instead, it is opting for the aircraft category that offers the greatest contractual flexibility. Still, keeping 50-seaters in the fleet only makes commercial sense if passengers are willing to fly on them. The CRJ450's redesigned cabin could help make that possible.

    Industry observers note that one of the biggest changes to the CRJ200 is in the cabin, not the engines or airframe, which remain the same. United is removing nine seats from the original 50-seat layout to create three cabins: seven United First seats, 16 Economy Plus seats, and 18 standard economy seats. The fresh layout changes how the aircraft is marketed, giving passengers the option to buy a first class seat on one of United's smallest regional aircraft.

    The first class cabin is arguably the most interesting part of the redesign. United is removing the overhead bins above these seats and replacing them with a dedicated luggage closet, creating a more open environment with a higher perceived ceiling height. Three of the seven first class seats will be individual seats arranged in a 1-1 configuration, giving passengers more privacy. Meanwhile, the Economy cabin will feature larger overhead bins that can accommodate standard rollaboard carry-on bags, addressing one of the CRJ200's most common passenger complaints. The airline has also included free high-speed Starlink WiFi for MileagePlus members.

    Dedicated First Class luggage closet.

    Larger rollaboard-friendly bins.

    Not part of original configuration.

    The redesign follows the philosophy behind the CRJ550, although United is making more substantial changes to the passenger experience on the smaller aircraft. According to Upgraded Points' CRJ450 cabin tour and Live And Let's Fly, the objective is to make the aircraft feel considerably more spacious despite retaining the narrow CRJ200 fuselage. However, removing nine seats raises another question: can the additional premium revenue offset the reduction in passenger capacity?

    United's decision becomes easier to understand when viewed against the airline's extensive history of regional aircraft operations. United Express has relied on numerous aircraft families over the decades, ranging from small turboprops to larger regional jets. These aircraft have allowed the airline to serve communities that could not consistently support mainline Boeing or Airbus services while feeding passengers into major hubs.

    Sources indicate that historical United Express fleets have included aircraft such as the ATR 42 and ATR 72, British Aerospace BAe 146 and Avro RJ, BAe ATP, Jetstream 31 and 32, Jetstream 41, Dornier 328, de Havilland Canada Dash 8, Embraer EMB-120 Brasilia, and Saab 340. United Express also operated several generations of regional jets, including the Bombardier CRJ100, CRJ200, and CRJ700, as well as the Embraer ERJ-135, ERJ-145, E170, and E175. Each type served a different operational need, based on route demand, aircraft availability, and the economics of connecting smaller markets.

    Planespotters.com's United Express fleet overview illustrates the range of aircraft operated over time. It lists 901 historic aircraft across the regional fleet categories and 480 right now in service. Of those, 78 are Bombardier CRJ200s. These figures show that the aircraft family remains part of the regional aviation network.

    In a recent development, with 50 seats, the CRJ200 enabled regional operators to connect smaller cities with major hubs without relying on the passenger demand required to fill larger aircraft. United later expanded its regional operations with the ERJ145 and CRJ700, while the E170 and E175 offered more capacity and a newer passenger experience. The CRJ550 demonstrated how an existing airframe could be adapted for a premium product. Now, the CRJ450 applies that approach to the smaller CRJ200, potentially giving the aging aircraft family another role in United's network.

    In a recent development, but the aircraft's historical importance is only part of the story. Its real value will depend on where United deploys it and whether smaller communities can generate enough premium demand.

    United intends to use the CRJ450 to connect smaller communities with its major hubs, particularly Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD) and Denver International Airport (DEN). These airports are key connection points for passengers traveling beyond the airline's regional network, including those connecting to domestic transcontinental and international services. The CRJ450 will do more than move passengers between two smaller cities: it will help United sell premium itineraries that begin or end in markets with limited air service.

    Industry observers note that connecting major cities with smaller communities remains critical to the airline's network. The first CRJ450 is expected to enter passenger service through Chicago O'Hare in December 2026, with smaller destinations such as Akron-Canton and Fort Wayne among the potential markets The Points Guy discussed. SkyWest will operate the aircraft under the United Express brand, with a multi-year agreement covering the first 40 aircraft.

    The commercial argument is compelling for passengers connecting to international flights. A business traveler departing from a smaller Midwestern community could purchase a single itinerary featuring United First on the regional segment and United Polaris on a subsequent long-haul flight. Previously, the regional portion of that journey might have involved a cramped, economy-only CRJ200. United is effectively extending its premium positioning to the first and last stages of the journey rather than concentrating its investment exclusively on larger aircraft.

    The CRJ450 also fits into United's wider premium expansion strategy. In March 2026, the airline announced plans to add more than 250 aircraft over the following two years, alongside newly introduced premium configurations for its Airbus A321neo and A321XLR fleets and its Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners. United reported that premium seats per North American departure had increased by 40% since 2021. Nevertheless, converting older regional jets introduces another challenge: the aircraft must remain economically viable despite its reduced seating capacity and substantial interior modifications.

    The CRJ450's biggest advantage is that United does not need to develop an entirely upcoming aircraft to introduce the product. It can use existing CRJ200 airframes, after the necessary interior modifications. This provides an alternative to purchasing new regional aircraft, although conversion costs, maintenance requirements, and the age of the underlying airframes will remain crucial considerations.

    It has been revealed that skyWest is targeting approximately 50 CRJ200 conversions by 2028, while its agreement with United covers 40 aircraft. The first two conversions were still underway in November 2026, and SkyWest expected subsequent modifications to take about two to three weeks per aircraft. According to Aviation Week, the regional operator sees the program as a longer-term investment in a premium product. SkyWest executives have also suggested that demand for converted aircraft could eventually extend beyond the initial United program.

    The financial test will be whether the additional revenue from seven First class seats and 16 Economy Plus seats offsets the nine fewer passengers the aircraft can accommodate. Lower passenger capacity also means less weight, which SkyWest's management identified as a potential fuel-related advantage. United will additionally have to demonstrate that passengers are willing to pay premium fares on relatively short regional journeys, rather than simply appreciating the improved cabin without generating additional revenue.

    The CRJ450 is an unusual attempt to extend the commercial life of an aircraft that many passengers would rather avoid. Its success could encourage further regional aircraft conversions, particularly as airlines search for ways to offer differentiated products without waiting for entirely upcoming aircraft programs. Whether United can turn the Devil's Chariot into a genuinely desirable premium product will become clearer once the aircraft begins operating regularly across its regional network.

    JetBlue is growing its presence in Central America and the Caribbean.

    In a recent development, for the first time ever, the carrier will serve the Honduran capital of Tegucigalpa. Starting Feb. 25, 2027, flights from Fort Lauderdale, Florida, will arrive at Palmerola International Airport in Comayagua, which serves Tegucigalpa.

    Currently, JetBlue’s only destination in Honduras is San Pedro Sula, in the country’s northwest.

    On Feb. 23, the carrier will launch service between Fort Lauderdale and George Town, Grand Cayman, in the Cayman Islands.

    Both routes will operate daily, using a mix of Airbus A320 and A220 aircraft.

    Sources indicate that jetBlue will also offer limited-time daily service from Fort Lauderdale to Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago, between Jan. 29 and Feb. 15. The connection will help travelers reach the islands during Carnival, the airline stated.

    Industry observers note that “We’re grateful for the way customers across South Florida continue to embrace JetBlue, and we’re committed to delivering even more of the destinations and travel options they’re looking for,” Daniel Shurz, JetBlue’s senior vice president of revenue, network, and enterprise planning, stated in a news release. “With latest international service to Honduras and Grand Cayman, we’re strengthening Fort Lauderdale’s role as a key gateway to Latin America and the Caribbean, making it easier for customers to reconnect with loved ones, explore new places, and travel across our growing network.”.

    Recent findings suggest that american has prioritized Latin America as demand from U.S. markets, especially Miami, grows. The carrier just recently launched service to Barranquilla and Cali in Colombia and will add Barcelona, Venezuela, to its network in January.

    • Recent findings suggest that southwest and French Bee are joining forces to expand international travel options for passengers not only on both sides of the Atlantic, but also the Pacific.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that southwest and French Bee are joining forces to expand international travel options for passengers not only on both sides of the Atlantic, but also the Pacific. The two carriers announced a fresh interline partnership that will allow travelers to combine flights on both airlines under a single ticket.

    Recent findings suggest that the agreement connects French Bee’s international network with Southwest’s extensive domestic network in the U.S. The partnership will provide connections through French Bee’s three U.S. gateway airports that Southwest also serves: Los Angeles, Miami, and San Francisco.

    French Bee also flies to Newark, Upcoming Jersey, but Southwest does not offer service there.

    Passengers will be able to connect between French Bee’s international flights and Southwest domestic flights without having to purchase separate tickets for each airline or recheck bags at each airline.

    French Bee operates an all-Airbus A350 fleet, with its primary hub located at Paris-Orly Airport, and operations to North America and destinations in the Indian Ocean and South Pacific.

    Southwest passengers will gain access to French Bee destinations not only from Paris, but also Tahiti in French Polynesia, which the French carrier flies to from San Francisco. The partnership will also offer one-stop French Bee connections from Paris to the Maldives and Sri Lanka, scheduled to launch in December 2026, along with current flights to Reunion Island.

    For French Bee customers, the new arrangement provides access to a much larger network of domestic destinations throughout the U.S. Southwest’s network includes cities such as Las Vegas, Chicago, Dallas, Denver, Nashville, Austin, San Diego, Phoenix, and multiple destinations in the Hawaiian Islands.

    The agreement represents another step in Southwest’s expanding international connectivity strategy, as the airline continues to develop relationships with overseas carriers rather than rely exclusively on its own international operations with its all-Boeing 737 fleet.

    Tickets for connecting flights are now available through French Bee’s website.

    Latest Update: Earning World Of Hyatt Elite Nights & Status With Credit Cards: Worth It?

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Chase and Hyatt have two co-branded credit cards — the World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more) and World of Hyatt Business Card (learn more).
    • According to recent reports, one of the awesome things about Hyatt’s two credit cards is that they can earn you elite nights, making it easier to qualify for status in the World of Hyatt program.
    • Chase and Hyatt have both the World of Hyatt Credit Card (a personal card) and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (a business card).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Chase and Hyatt have two co-branded credit cards — the World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more) and World of Hyatt Business Card (learn more). I’d consider these to be among the more lucrative hotel credit cards out there, particularly the personal version of the card.

    According to recent reports, one of the awesome things about Hyatt’s two credit cards is that they can earn you elite nights, making it easier to qualify for status in the World of Hyatt program. In this post, I’d like to get into the nitty-gritty of how earning Hyatt elite status with credit cards works, and discuss whether it’s worth it.

    Chase and Hyatt have both the World of Hyatt Credit Card (a personal card) and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (a business card). Both cards have valuable benefits, though I think the personal card is considerably more compelling than the business card. Let me start by just briefly recapping the perks of the two cards.

    The World of Hyatt Credit Card has a $95 annual fee and offers:.

    It has been revealed that this means that you’re getting five elite nights toward status and a Category 1-4 free night award every year just for having the card. To me that more than justifies the annual fee, by a long shot (I consistently get $250+ of value out of the free night certificate alone). That doesn’t even factor in the incremental perks you can get for spending on the card.

    The World of Hyatt Business Credit Card has a $199 annual fee and offers:.

    It has been revealed that the business version of the card isn’t quite as rewarding as the personal version of the card, especially if you’re not a big spender. However, for businesses that spend quite a bit on credit cards, this can be the best card for earning elite status.

    Sources indicate that both the World of Hyatt Credit Card and World of Hyatt Business Credit Card offer the ability to earn elite nights. However, the ways in which you earn elite nights differ between the two cards, so let’s go over those details.

    Recent findings suggest that the World of Hyatt Credit Card offers qualifying nights toward Hyatt status in two ways. First of all, the World of Hyatt Card offers five elite nights annually just for having the card. There’s no spending required to earn these five elite nights, and you receive them for each calendar year in which you have the card, including the year in which you open the card.

    Recent findings suggest that beyond that, the World of Hyatt Card offers two elite nights for every $5,000 spent on the card (in other words, that’s up to one elite night per $2,500 of spending). There’s no limit to how many elite nights you can earn this way, and the elite nights earned through spending on this card aren’t in any way tied to the calendar year. In other words, if you spent $2,500 on the card in 2026 and then spend $2,500 on the card in 2027, you’d earn two elite nights at that point.

    Recent findings suggest that the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card offers five elite nights for every $10,000 spent on the card in a calendar year (in other words, that’s up to one elite night per $2,000 of spending). On this card, the spending counter resets at the beginning of the calendar year. In other words, if you spent $8,000 on the card in 2026, you’d still have to spend a full $10,000 in 2027 to earn five elite nights.

    As you can see, this card offers elite nights for spending at an accelerated rate, though unlike the personal card, it doesn’t offer the five elite nights annually just for having the card.

    How soon do elite nights post from the World of Hyatt Credit Card and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card?

    While the above covers the basics, I’d like to now analyze the overall value proposition of earning World of Hyatt elite status by spending on the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Card, including addressing some of the most common questions and scenarios that come up.

    With Hyatt, not all elite perks are tied directly to having status, but rather some require earning a certain number of elite nights in a year, known as the Milestone Rewards program. The Milestone Rewards program is how you earn perks like suite upgrade awards, club access awards, Guest of Honor awards, and more.

    Hyatt elite nights earned through Hyatt credit cards would count toward Milestone Rewards the same as any hotel stays would, which adds further value to credit card spending.

    One of the perks of both Hyatt credit cards is that you receive Discoverist status for as long as you have the card. Discoverist status ordinarily requires 10 elite qualifying nights or 25,000 base points per year. As a reminder, here are World of Hyatt’s elite thresholds:.

    According to recent reports, one common point of confusion is that people assume these cards really come with up to 15 elite nights per year. They assume you already get Discoverist status, and that any elite nights are on top of that. Note that while these cards offer Discoverist status, you don’t get the elite nights that correspond to that.

    This means that if you have a Hyatt credit card, you’ll receive Discoverist status on an ongoing basis (and five elite nights every year if you have the personal card), but you’ll still need to qualify for Explorist or Globalist status based on the full criteria.

    Hyatt’s lifetime Globalist status is based on earning one million base points in the program. World of Hyatt members earn five base points per dollar spent on Hyatt stays, meaning you essentially have to spend $200,000 at Hyatts to earn lifetime Globalist status.

    In a recent development, credit card spending, and any elite nights earned through Hyatt credit cards, won’t count toward lifetime Globalist status. That’s because the qualification criteria is based solely on base points, and not based on elite qualifying nights (in which case it would count).

    World of Hyatt Globalist is my favorite top tier hotel status, and what I love is that Hyatt’s co-branded credit cards make it easier to earn that. Let’s look at the best strategy for earning Globalist status with the card. Hyatt Globalist status ordinarily requires earning 60 qualifying nights in a year. So how much would you have to spend on a Hyatt credit card to earn that status?

    On the World of Hyatt Credit Card, you’d need to spend $140,000 to earn Globalist status:.

    Meanwhile on the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card, you’d need to spend $120,000 to earn Globalist status:.

    As you can see, the personal credit card offers more elite nights upfront, while the business credit card offers elite nights at a faster pace for spending (assuming you can reach the thresholds).

    Sources indicate that when you’re analyzing the value of spending your way toward status, don’t forget that even beyond the general status perks, the Milestone Rewards perks could really add up. For example, if you make it to 60 elite nights, you could select five suite upgrade awards and four club access awards, and would also receive a Category 1-7 free night award, a Category 1-4 free night award, and three Guest of Honor awards.

    Then on the personal version of the card, you also receive an additional Category 1-4 free night award when you spend $15,000 on the card in a year. The value of all of those perks really adds up.

    Hyatt counts award nights toward status, and just for having the World of Hyatt Credit Card, you get a free night every year, plus the opportunity to earn a further three free nights for spending $15,000, earning Explorist status, and earning Globalist status.

    On top of that, presumably you want to earn Globalist status because you actually intend to stay at Hyatts with some frequency. Hotel status is worthless if you don’t actually stay at that brand.

    Sources indicate that to be realistic, let’s assume that long term you’re earning 30 elite nights per year through actual stays. There are so many great Globalist benefits to use (like suite upgrade awards and free night awards), so if you’re staying at Hyatts less than that I question whether Globalist is worth it for you.

    If you earned 30 of the required 60 elite nights through credit card spending, you’d need to spend the following:.

    Given all the incremental perks you’re picking up with Milestone Rewards, I’d say the math could really check out.

    It has been revealed that when deciding if it makes sense to spend money on the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Credit Card, consider the opportunity cost of the spending. For easy math purposes, I tend to consider the opportunity cost of credit card spending to be around 3.4%.

    Recent findings suggest that that’s because based on my valuation of miles & points, most transferable points currencies are worth 1.7 cents each, and you have some cards offering 2x points per dollar spent. Meanwhile I value World of Hyatt points at 1.4 cents each.

    If we were to theoretically assume you’re spending $60,000 on a Hyatt credit card per year (give or take) in order to earn Globalist status, what’s the opportunity cost of that spending? By my math, you’re looking at an opportunity cost of up to 2% (the spread between a 3.4% return and 1.4% return). That’s around $1,200, if you value things the way that I do. But that’s not factoring in the value of all the other perks mentioned above:.

    For many, I think the above perks could more than justify the difference in return on spending otherwise.

    According to recent reports, there are many things to love about the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Card, though the ability to get a fast track toward status is probably my favorite perk. I absolutely love Hyatt Globalist status, and credit cards have historically helped me requalify for status. If you’re a Hyatt loyalist and don’t yet have the hotel group’s co-branded credit cards, they’re seriously worth considering.

You need to manually check account history and cross reference against when your last 2 EQN cleared, and even then it might only be an approximation because you won't know where in that month's statement you actually crossed the line. They could peg it to the calendar year but at this point that'd be a perk devaluation because you'd lose any residual rollover spend past a $5000 milestone within a calendar year. A good compromise could be 1 EQN per $2000 that resets every calendar year. Or they could just add a $#&%ing tracker on their app. If and when Hyatt eventually revamps their card offerings and perks, they need to fix this. It's ridiculous.

    I've got both cards. Just hit $30K on the biz card, and that plus the 5 nights from the personal card have trimmed the Globalist threshold to 40 nights, which I can usually hit. My current role has far less travel travel than former ones, so I need a little boost!

    According to recent reports, I just checked and I put $50K!! on the Hyatt card this year to maintain Globalist status. Only $6K were Hyatt charges. By the end of the year, I'll spend 34 nights in Hyatts and only 18 nights that I would have chosen Hyatts independent of chasing Globalist. 9 nights were suite upgrades. 8 nights were at Mr & Mrs Smith hotels with no Globalist perks. So, I got 10 nights x 2 people = 20 free breakfasts. Let's say the suite upgrades were generously worth $100/night and $20/breakfast. So by your calculations, I lost about $1000 by using the Hyatt card instead of another to get $1300 in "free" benefits. I'm off the hamster wheel in 2027.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Frontier Airlines is now offering its GoWild All You Can Fly Pass for 2027, letting travelers take to the skies at a deep discount for an entire year (and potentially longer).
    • According to recent reports, for a limited time, flyers can purchase a GoWild Pass good through 2027 for just $399.
    • While that's not quite as good as some offers we've seen in past years (but better than some in other years), it can add up to significant savings if you fly the airline a lot.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that it's here! Frontier Airlines is now offering its GoWild All You Can Fly Pass for 2027, letting travelers take to the skies at a deep discount for an entire year (and potentially longer).

    According to recent reports, for a limited time, flyers can purchase a GoWild Pass good through 2027 for just $399. Members of the airline's Discount Den can score the pass for $349.

    While that's not quite as good as some offers we've seen in past years (but better than some in other years), it can add up to significant savings if you fly the airline a lot. You must be a Frontier Miles member to purchase one.

    Sources indicate that keep in mind that passholders pay $0.01 in airfare plus applicable taxes, fees and charges at the time of booking, so the pass gets you out of the regular airfare, but you're still on the hook for taxes and fees as well as other charges for things like optional seat selection and bags. While taxes on domestic legs are low, international ones can incur $60-$110 each way, depending on the destination.

    Sneak peek: Frontier's newly introduced first-class seats are finally on sale, set for March debut.

    Multiple passholders can book travel at the same time, but you can't mix and match passholders with non-passholders on the same reservation.

    Likewise, different types of fares can be combined each way on itineraries as long as all passengers hold a valid GoWild Pass at the time of booking and the primary passenger holds a Discount Den membership if Discount Den fares are selected.

    According to recent reports, one other big caveat: GoWild passes autorenew, so if you want to cancel when your current pass expires, you'll need to contact the airline to do so. Your renewal date will be stated in your confirmation email when purchasing the pass.

    The GoWild Pass is valid for flights to over 100 destinations across Frontier's route network, including both domestic gateways and international cities in Mexico, the Caribbean and Central America. The airline's route network changes frequently, though, so stay on top of it to make sure your route will be in service when it's time to book.

    Industry observers note that travel begins after purchase (meaning as soon as today) and is available through Dec. 31, 2027, meaning potentially over a full year of flying.

    There are no blackout dates, like we've seen in some past instances, but on peak dates, you can expect to pay $59-$199 extra per segment.

    Industry observers note that here's the kicker: Standard bookings for eligible GoWild fares begin a day before departure for domestic flights and 10 days before departure for international flights. If your return flight is outside that window, then you'll have to try to make an additional booking when the window opens for that flight.

    If you do want to book more in advance than that, however, you can pay an additional charge to do so, though this can vary based on the date and the route.

    Also keep in mind that just because a seat is open on the flight you want does not mean it's eligible for a GoWild booking.

    You can earn Frontier Miles on the purchase of the pass as well as any extras, like seat assignments, bag fees or priority boarding that you purchase.

    If you hold elite status with Frontier, you are still eligible for your benefits, including free seats and bags, so that can be a great way to save on optional fees that non-elites have to pay.

    Sources indicate that all-you-can-fly airline passes are a rarity these days and come with lots of limitations. Frontier Airlines' GoWild All You Can Fly Pass is no exception.

    Recent findings suggest that still, if you fly the airline a lot, have flexibility (and a bit of spontaneity) in your plans and don't need a ton of extra amenities like preferred seats or checked bags, these fares can be a good way to save a bit on flights you'd be taking anyway ... or perhaps some fun last-minute fares you wouldn't be able to take advantage of otherwise.

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025.
    • In a recent development, outgoing Montana GOP Rep.
    • The gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Rep. Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    In a recent development, outgoing Montana GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.

    The gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug. 31 from Zinke’s leadership political action committee to the nonprofit Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation, campaign finance records show. The donation is more than the foundation has reported receiving in any year since it was founded nearly two decades ago.

    Zinke’s wife, son, and sister presently serve on its board of directors, according to the foundation’s annual filing with the state of Montana.

    In a brief interview, Zinke denied that any portion of the money transferred to the foundation will directly benefit him or any of his family members who sit on the board of directors. “No, no, never," he said when asked if any family members will draw a salary from the gift.

    The money will instead go to building a storage barn and kid’s sledding park on the property controlled by the foundation, Zinke said.

    None of the records indicate Zinke violated the law or directly benefited from the gift to his foundation.

    “While it's not uncommon for a politician to transfer leftover money from a political war chest to charity, it is pretty rare for a politician to transfer leftover political funds to a charity that they or a relative controls,” said Michael Beckel, director of money in politics reform at Problem One, a bipartisan group that seeks to reduce influence of money in politics.

    Instead, outgoing members typically transfer remaining campaign cash to local party committees or candidates, Beckel added.

    Ethics experts say Zinke’s move highlights ongoing concerns over the broad latitude campaign finance law gives leadership PACs in how they spend money.

    “I definitely think it is something to be concerned about,” noted Stuart McPhail, director of campaign finance litigation at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit watchdog.

    “Leadership PACs are really nothing more than personal slush funds under today's rules,” he mentioned, noting that unlike regular campaign committees, member leadership PACs are not prohibited from donating to charities or organizations that could directly benefit the member or relative.

    Zinke, a former Navy SEAL who commanded special forces during the Iraq War, converted his traditional campaign committee to a leadership PAC — Commander Zinke Leadership Fund — in March 2026, shortly after announcing he would not run for reelection. It last reported having $1.4 million cash on hand in October of this year.

    It marks the second time one of Zinke’s political committees made a payment to the organization. In 2019, the committee Zinke ran during his earlier years in Congress — he served one term in the House before being tapped as Trump’s first-term Interior secretary — gave over $11,000 to the foundation before winding down operations.

    In a recent development, the Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation was founded by Zinke and his wife in 2007 in his hometown of Whitefish, Mont., with intends to provide winter recreational activities for children. Its latest tax filing reports revenue of $15,000 and roughly equal expenses in 2024 for snow plowing and park maintenance.

    Zinke’s dealings with the organization were the subject of an ongoing inspector general investigation when he resigned as Interior secretary in January 2019.

    Investigators ultimately did not find that Zinke violated conflict-of-interest laws, but they concluded that he failed to comply with federal ethics obligations and “misused his official position in violation of federal regulations.” The Justice Department declined to prosecute Zinke.

    Zinke stepped down from the foundation in 2017, shortly after his Senate confirmation. But investigators found that he continued to represent the organization in negotiations with the developers of a commercial project adjacent to the foundation’s land and lied to an ethics agent about his involvement in the project.

    The project’s investors included David Lesar, then-chairman of oil services company Halliburton.

    Another Zinke-tied leadership PAC has previously raised eyebrows in Washington.

    Sources indicate that supporting Electing American Leaders PAC — known as SEAL PAC — where Zinke serves as chairman, has been marred by accusations that it funneled money to political consultants instead of candidates. A 2022 CQ Roll Call analysis found that 87 percent of the PAC’s spending went to operating expenses.

    The PAC also made recurring monthly payments to a manufacturer registered to Zinke’s son, Wolfgang Zinke, and based at a Zinke family-owned home in Whitefish.

    Sources indicate that SEAL PAC’s executive director, Rob Catron, maintained that the payments constitute a consulting fee to Wolfgang Zinke for management of the PAC website, among other tasks. “He earns every penny of it,” Catron said.

    According to recent reports, since May 2022, the PAC has given roughly $270,000 to Wolfgang Zinke’s tech giant, FG Solutions, for mailing and printing, records show — more than any individual candidate or committee supported by the PAC. The company also received $5,000 from a related super PAC, SEAL PAC USA, which can solicit unlimited contributions for independent expenditures but can’t donate directly to candidates.

    Montana corporate records show Wolfgang Zinke founded FG Solutions – which says it provides services including “personal assistant and any lawful purpose” – just 10 days before it received its first payment from the PAC in 2022.

    Catron defended how the PAC spends money on veterans running for the House, arguing that it takes money to raise money.

    “We raise a lion’s share of our funding through national direct mail fundraising, which is very expensive to do,” he remarked, citing the PAC’s use of a national text message fundraising campaign as a major expense.

    SEAL PAC raised about $9.6 million this election cycle, distributing about $1.1 million to GOP lawmakers and candidates, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Most of the committee's funds went to operating expenses, including over $3 million paid to Direct Support Services, a Washington-based vendor, for direct mail postage.

    Zinke’s not the only lawmaker to face scrutiny over how they spent surplus campaign cash in recent years.

    Sources indicate that in 2023, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., set off alarm bells for transferring $200,000 from his campaign committee to The Sanders Institute, a nonprofit founded by his wife and stepson, following a $350,000 donation from his 2020 presidential campaign coffers.

    The organization briefly shut down during Sanders’ presidential run in 2019 to avoid the appearance of impropriety.

    Sanders’ stepson, David Driscoll — a former executive at Nike and snowboard manufacturer Burton — is listed on the think tank’s website as its executive director, drawing a six-figure annual salary according to tax filings.

    It’s unusual, though not unheard of, for campaign committees to pay family members of the candidate for bona fide work.

    “If [Wolfgang Zinke] is actually performing this work, he’s qualified to do it, and this is his typical market rate for this kind of contract, then it would be permissible, even if this was a campaign account,” McPhail said about SEAL PAC's payments.

    But the payments could present a legal “gray area” over whether personal-use restrictions apply to certain PACs, according to McPhail.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that in late 2023, we saw the opening of the Felipe Carrillo Puerto International Airport (TQO), in Tulum, Mexico. For those not familiar, Tulum is located on the eastern coast of the Yucatan Peninsula, and for years, it was a growing tourist destination.

    While it could previously be accessed via Cancun International Airport (CUN), the hope was that by opening a latest international airport, visitor numbers would expand massively. Unfortunately what has actually happened is exactly the opposite, as airline after airline has pulled out. What exactly is going on here? I think it makes for an interesting story, and thanks to TravelinWilly for flagging this.

    It has been revealed that in 2023, we saw airline after airline announce flights to Tulum. Among US carriers, we saw American, Delta, JetBlue, and United, all launch flights to Tulum, while Spirit unveiled flights, but never released them.

    That was only a small part of the overall international service to the airport, as we also saw flights to Tulum on Air Canada, Air Transat, Avianca, Copa, Discover, and WestJet, along with flights on domestic carriers like Aeromexico, Mexicana de Aviacion, Viva, and Volaris.

    Sources indicate that less than three years after the airport opened, where do things stand? When it comes to international year-round service, we’ve now gone from service to 12 airports, to service to four airports, which is an absolutely massive reduction:.

    In a recent development, just to put this into numbers, in the first half of 2026, the airport saw a 33.2% reduction in passengers. June 2026 was the worst month to date, with a 44.8% drop, as there were just 47,600 passengers, compared to 86,200 passengers the year prior.

    It goes without saying that for a newly built airport, this is rather catastrophic, and not what you hope to see.

    In some ways, it feels like the whole concept behind Tulum Airport was sort of unnecessary. That’s also easily explained by the fact that the airport was well over a decade in the making, so while I can see how it might’ve seemed like a good idea at some point, tourism trends do evolve over time.

    The reality is that there was a point where Tulum was cool, edgy, and a bit off the beaten path, compared to… whatever it is now. But when it comes to the struggles that airlines have had with flying to Tulum, it seems like the problems have been endless:.

    It’ll be interesting to see if Tulum can reverse any of these trends, and regain visitors….

    It has been revealed that A few years ago Tulum Airport opened to some fanfare, as a good number of airlines rushed to add service there. Unfortunately the excitement didn’t last long, as the airport has gone from a dozen year-round international routes, to just four.

    This reduction in demand particularly evident from the United States, as soon there will just be nonstop service on American and Delta, and even that will be with reduced frequencies and routes.

    It has been revealed that tulum Airport is facing endless challenges, not the least of which is a decline in visitors to Mexico from the United States, combined with increasing competition for those fewer visitors. Mexico just isn’t a value destination in the way that it used to be in places like Cancun, Tulum, Los Cabos, etc., and that’s understandably impacting demand.

    I’m curious if Tulum can find a way to turn things around, but it’s not a good situation.

It’s not Starlink caliber but it’s pretty darn close.”.

    “This is about the total experience, and customers are not choosing airlines based on the Wi-Fi.”At the #F500Innovation Forum, @Delta CEO Ed Bastian told @ajs that the airline helped Elon Musk’s satellite Wi-Fi “get started in aviation,” but the two sides “just couldn’t come to… pic.twitter.com/xmSERJNjjH.

    When Bastian formally unveiled intends for free Wi-Fi at CES 2023 in Las Vegas, he noted the following:.

    Industry observers note that “At work, at home and everywhere in between, connectivity is essential to daily life, and your journey on Delta should be no different. Our vision has long been to deliver an experience at 30,000 feet that feels similar to what our customers have available on the ground.”.

    According to recent reports, “We didn’t just want free Wi-Fi to offer base-level service – we wanted it to be transformative for the entire onboard experience. It is imperative all customers onboard can enjoy their favorite content just as they would at home, and we’ve put this system through meticulous tests to make that possible.”.

    Any reasonable person could agree that:.

The issue isn’t that people will stop flying Delta altogether. The issue is that Delta has built its entire brand on being the industry leader, and on being on the forefront of technology.

    There’s no denying that this sentiment among the public changes over time, because inflight Wi-Fi is easily one of the top amenities that passengers notice nowadays. And I think anyone who thinks a major Wi-Fi disadvantage lasting for years isn’t part of what contributes to consumer sentiment is lying to themselves.

    Delta CEO Ed Bastian is now downplaying the importance of inflight Wi-Fi. He’s arguing that “customers are not choosing airlines based on Wi-Fi,” which in isolation, is probably true.     Rescue Missions: The Untold History Of The Boeing 747's Unique 5th Engine Mounting

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1505 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that picture a legendary widebody aircraft thundering down a runway with five massive powerplants bolted beneath its wings, where only four of them are burning fuel and generating thrust.
    • Sources indicate that such an extraordinary capability centered around the Boeing 747's unique fifth-engine mounting system, an engineering marvel designed to rescue stranded airframes when conventional global supply chains failed.
    • When the 747 entered commercial service in 1970, early high-bypass turbofans like the Pratt & Whitney JT9D and Rolls-Royce RB211 were revolutionary in fuel efficiency but notoriously temperamental compared to today's powerplants.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that picture a legendary widebody aircraft thundering down a runway with five massive powerplants bolted beneath its wings, where only four of them are burning fuel and generating thrust. It may seem like an engineering experiment or a futuristic testbed flight, but this was a real logistical lifeline used during the height of the classic jet age. When a commercial airliner suffered a catastrophic engine failure at a remote airport thousands of miles from home, operators did not wait weeks for maritime freight or transport charters; instead, they simply strapped a spare, fully assembled jet engine directly under the wing and flew it there themselves.

    Sources indicate that such an extraordinary capability centered around the Boeing 747's unique fifth-engine mounting system, an engineering marvel designed to rescue stranded airframes when conventional global supply chains failed. Why did Boeing incorporate a dedicated structural hardpoint specifically for hauling dead-weight turbofans across oceans, and how did flight crews manage the immense aerodynamic penalties of a multi-ton pod?

    When the 747 entered commercial service in 1970, early high-bypass turbofans like the Pratt & Whitney JT9D and Rolls-Royce RB211 were revolutionary in fuel efficiency but notoriously temperamental compared to today's powerplants. If a widebody suffered a catastrophic engine failure at a remote international outstation, such as a distant hub in Asia, Africa, or the Middle East, airlines were met with a huge logistical problem. Standard cargo aircraft of the era frequently lacked the main-deck cargo door dimensions or payload capacity needed to transport a fully assembled, multi-ton turbofan core across continents.

    In a recent development, the incompatibility created crippling Aircraft on Ground (AOG) delays that could strand a flagship aircraft out of service for weeks while awaiting maritime shipping or rare charter flights. To overcome this vulnerability, aviation pioneers drew upon operational precedents established during the dawn of the jet age. Analysis from Simple Flying notes that as early as 1959, Qantas began outfitting its Boeing 707 fleet with external mounting hardware to ferry replacement powerplants across international networks, a resourceful practice later adopted by operators of the Douglas DC-8 as well.

    Sources indicate that recognizing that the much larger 747 would encounter identical outstation risks on expanding global routes, Boeing engineered a permanent solution directly into the aircraft's baseline wing architecture. They did so by building a dedicated hardpoint into the port wing so that the Queen of the Skies could act as its own heavy-lift delivery truck.

    Mechanically, the fifth-pod system was based on a precision-engineered hardpoint located exclusively on the port wing, positioned inboard between the fuselage and the number two engine pylon. This location was deliberately chosen because it placed the massive secondary weight close to the aircraft centerline, minimizing structural stress on the outer wing spars. Technicians secured the replacement powerplant to a dummy strut designed to withstand extreme shear loads during takeoff, cruise, and landing without distorting the wing's aerodynamic profile.

    Unlike the aircraft's active operating engines, the fifth-pod unit was entirely non-functional and carried purely as dead-weight freight. It featured zero plumbing, no fuel feed lines, no electrical wiring, and no hydraulic connections, meaning it contributed nothing to forward propulsion.

    In order to prevent catastrophic windmilling and structural bearing damage from oncoming airflow, ground crews removed the forward fan blades or locked them securely, wrapping the core in streamlined aerodynamic fairings and nose-cone caps.

    Positioning the multi-ton spare engine close to the fuselage root, engineers minimized dangerous center-of-gravity shifts that could compromise aircraft stability. Despite that, even with the weight efficiently distributed, strapping an exposed turbofan shell under one wing created a significant amount of parasitic drag that massively altered the aircraft's aerodynamic balance.

    It has been revealed that when an unpowered turbofan is slung beneath the port wing, the resulting parasitic drag creates a persistent yawing tendency that flight crews must actively manage from takeoff to touchdown. The fifth pod sits exclusively on the left side, so the aircraft naturally wants to pull to the left, needing constant rudder deflection and precise trim adjustments to maintain coordinated flight. The reality was that even though the sheer mass of the airframe dealt with much of the disturbance, the asymmetric resistance needed unyielding pilot attention during initial climb phases and crosswind approaches.

    Industry observers note that to keep the aircraft flying straight and level within safe structural envelopes, flight manuals mandated strict operational limitations, including a maximum cruise speed reduction to around Mach 0.78 or lower to prevent aerodynamic buffeting around the mounting pylon, as noted in discussions from PPRuNe. Furthermore, the added weight of roughly 13,228 lb (6,000 kg) combined with increased drag penalized fuel consumption by 10% to 15%, slashing normal range capabilities.

    For multi-thousand-mile rescue operations, this heavy fuel burn resulted in using strategic refueling stops, such as touching down at Perth Airport (PER) before attempting the long Indian Ocean crossing to Johannesburg, as noted in Qantas newsroom breakdowns.

    The huge operational penalty made many of these standard delivery routes become carefully choreographed logistical hurdles, which not every airline ended up being able to manage. So which global airlines actually mastered this intricate procedure, and how did they complete the most famous rescue missions of the classic jet era?

    The technical and aerodynamic penalties were, of course, formidable, though only a select group of international legacy operators mastered the fifth-pod procedure. During the classic widebody era of the 1970s, 1980s, and 1990s, airlines such as British Airways, Singapore Airlines, South African Airways, Aer Lingus, and Trans World Airlines kept certified engineering protocols to haul spare engines across their far-flung networks. Among these operators, Qantas emerged as the absolute master of the craft, making use of its geographical isolation at the bottom of the world to perfect fifth-pod logistics across decades of 707 and 747 operations.

    The defining modern case study of this capability occurred on January 6, 2016, when Qantas deployed Boeing 747-438 registration VH-OJS on flight QF63 from Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport (SYD) to Johannesburg O.R. Tambo International Airport (JNB). Making a crucial technical refueling stop at Perth Airport (PER), the aircraft carried a massive Rolls-Royce RB211 turbofan tucked beneath its port wing to rescue a grounded sister aircraft, registration VH-OJU, which was stranded without heavy maintenance support in South Africa. The meticulous operation skipped weeks of complex maritime shipping and unavailable cargo freighter charters, demonstrating the unmatched operational agility of a passenger jet acting as its own heavy-lift supply truck.

    Even as flight QF63 proved that an airline could successfully rescue a stranded widebody using its own passenger fleet, the global aviation landscape was undergoing a transformation in the background. We no longer see these engine ferry flights, mainly because newer aircraft were never designed with the ability to attach an engine like this, so why is that the case?

    The decline of the fifth-engine ferry system is a direct testament to the extraordinary reliability of modern aviation powerplants. In the 1970s, early turbofans experienced frequent mechanical hurdles that necessitated self-rescue solutions at remote international outstations. Today, advanced high-bypass turbofans achieve dispatch reliability rates exceeding 99.9%, as detailed in Simple Flying analysis, making mid-route engine failures at isolated hubs vanishingly rare and shifting airline operational risk profiles entirely.

    Sources indicate that furthermore, the globalization of heavy air cargo networks ended the logistical necessity of external wing transport. Purpose-built super-transporters and modern nose-loading freighters, such as the Boeing 747-8F and the Antonov An-124, can easily accommodate fully assembled fan cases and engine cores within their main cargo decks.

    It is also vital to distinguish these utilitarian cargo ferry pods from dedicated engine testbed aircraft, such as Pratt & Whitney's famous Boeing 747SP testbeds, which mount active powerplants on the forward fuselage or tail for in-flight engineering trials rather than commercial cargo transport.

    Eventually, twin-engine widebodies came to dominate global long-haul routes and passenger 747s faded into retirement, and so the underwing hardpoints vanished from active airline fleets. Now that modern aviation looks toward ultra-long-range point-to-point networks, how will operators handle rare logistical emergencies when support is thousands of miles away?

    Recent findings suggest that the disappearance of the fifth-pod capability is really showing the end of an era when long-haul flight operations required sheer mechanical improvisation. When an aircraft could strap a six-tonne jet engine beneath its wing and power across oceans to rescue a stranded sister ship, it demonstrated an aviation philosophy built on frontline self-reliance. Today, that raw frontier spirit has been supplanted by predictive maintenance algorithms, digital supply chain tracking, and global logistics networks that move parts faster than any passenger flight ever could.

    With passenger 747-400s being phased out of commercial service among operators, and modern twinjets like the A350 and 777X lacking any structural provision for external wing cargo, the hardpoints that once defined jumbo jet versatility exist now only in aviation museums and archival photographs. Comparing and contrasting this era and the current era of modern engine manufacturing really highlights how far safety and design excellence has come, and leaves us wondering where the industry may head next.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., arrives at the Rayburn Building for a House Judiciary Committee hearing in February.
    • Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the upcoming year, making the most of their coming majority.
    • Industry observers note that that means staffing up major committees.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., arrives at the Rayburn Building for a House Judiciary Committee hearing in February. He will be a key player in leading oversight efforts next year — and so will Democratic staff. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the upcoming year, making the most of their coming majority.

    Industry observers note that that means staffing up major committees. And for the dozens of attorneys and other aides preparing to take on a belligerent Trump administration that has cast Democratic oversight as potentially criminal, the job will come with extra scrutiny.

    In a recent development, arya Hariharan, former chief oversight counsel to Sen. Richard J. Durbin on the Senate Judiciary Committee and now a partner at Holland & Knight, said the pressure will be on from day one.

    “Are you prepared to not sleep very much and know that every single thing you do is going to be scrutinized, every footnote, every comma?” Hariharan noted.

    Still, the way Hariharan sees it, serving on the Hill is worth it. “I hope they all fall in love with it because it’s a lovely place to work,” she says of staffers headed there for the first time.

    Recent findings suggest that the work done by attorneys and other staff in oversight probes can swiftly become part of constitutional law. When Trump adviser Peter Navarro defied a subpoena from Democrats investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, it touched off debates about executive privilege and contempt of Congress. Probes of Hunter Biden led to similar court fights.

    It has been revealed that some questions have gone all the way up to the Supreme Court, like in Trump v. Mazars, when the House fought to access Trump’s business records during his first administration in furtherance of toughening up government ethics laws.

    In a recent development, there’s every indication that pressure will continue in the latest Congress. James Melendres, a partner at Snell & Wilmer, said Democrats are poised for aggressive oversight efforts, even if they know it could be tough to make headway against litigation resistant administration officials.

    In a recent development, “Democrats are going to have less than two years to show results. I think they are going to move really fast,” Melendres mentioned.

    Democrats will likely soon start to send out preservation letters to private companies, institutions and others they intend to probe in the newly introduced year, if they haven’t already, Melendres said.

    “There may be significant pushback from the administration, from agencies and individual government officials who receive requests. I think third-party, nongovernment agencies and individuals are going to be high on the list for these committees,” he said.

    In a recent development, in addition to the hiring that happens over the next few weeks, House Democrats will have major decisions to make about chamber and committee rules for the new Congress, including who will hold subpoena authority. And off-Hill observers will be watching closely.

    “For companies, for individuals and their counsel, mapping all of that is going to be a significant part of the job between now and early January,” Melendres remarked.

    Lawmakers need to nail down funding levels for congressional committees and staff — the amount of money involved can make a big difference in how big investigations get. Major committees, and major investigations, take a large amount of staff and expertise to get going.

    Sources indicate that for instance, the special House panel that investigated the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol spent about $14 million in less than 18 months, including for dozens of staffers.

    Recent findings suggest that standing committees, such as Oversight and Judiciary, take a good chunk of change, too. In 2025 the House spent $12.9 million on the House Oversight and Government Reform panel, and $13.1 million on the House Judiciary Committee.

    Those expenditures mean dozens of staff working long hours to review documents, send letters, send subpoenas and conduct interviews. Judiciary ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who is expected to serve as chair next year, stated he wouldn’t get into specifics yet about how many resources the new Congress may devote to oversight efforts.

    “But we are talking about the most corrupt administration in the history of the United States, and this is an overwhelming and daunting task that faces us,” Raskin noted.

    The Trump administration itself has already signaled it intends to push back forcefully on congressional oversight efforts.

    Earlier this month, President Donald Trump described Democrats’ vows to investigate his administration as “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”.

    Days later, the White House counsel sent a letter saying that subpoena threats from House Oversight ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., and others “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”.

    U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz for the Southern District of Texas followed up with letters of his own to Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.; Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.; and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., urging them to preserve documents tied to their promised oversight.

    “The American people are entitled to freely associate without their elected officials terrorizing them with aggressive, harassing government action,” Reitz’s letter to Warren said.

    Members of the incoming majority have signaled they intend to defend themselves and their probes, and Blumenthal remarked he won’t be deterred by the letter.

    Recent findings suggest that “There’s no way that I’m going to be intimidated or bullied. It would be laughable and ludicrous, but it is a clear abuse and misuse of prosecutorial powers and weaponization by the Department of Justice,” said Blumenthal, who serves as the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

    As for Raskin, he called the White House counsel letter and other missives “absurd on its face.”.

    “I’m sure they would love to get into a whole series of letters and counter-letters and litigation. They’re trying to distract everybody from the fact that they just lost the worst landslide electoral repudiation in at least a half century in America, and so they’re going to pick a fight,” Raskin told reporters.

    Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely incoming speaker, told reporters last week that he intended oversight efforts in his chamber to be led by Raskin and Garcia.

    Industry observers note that “We haven’t ruled anything in. We haven’t ruled anything out. We’re going to follow the facts. We’re going to apply the law. We’re going to be guided by the Constitution, and we’re going to let the chips fall where they may,” Jeffries said.

    Democrats have already publicly listed a handful of job postings for oversight staff and counsel, ranging from the Science to Armed Services to Judiciary panels, set to start early next year.

    It has been revealed that beyond those hires, House Democrats will have to make one major pick they haven’t yet revealed — the House counsel. The position, first created in the 1970s, is hired by the majority and advocates for the chamber in court. That attorney, along with a group of bipartisan House leaders controlled by the majority, will steer the chamber’s legal strategy.

    Sources indicate that in prior Democratic Congresses, that office has been active in court; Doug Letter frequently argued on behalf of the Democratic House majority seeking to enforce subpoenas on behalf of congressional committees. The position is held by Matthew Berry in the current Republican-controlled House.

    “I mean, I think a lot of people are interested in that job,” Raskin remarked.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that A very small international airline aims to add long haul, international flights to the United States as of next spring, and I feel pretty confident in saying that 99% of people have never heard of this airline (I had to look it up after seeing one of their planes at an airport several weeks back, and I know a thing or two about identifying airplanes). 😉.

    Industry observers note that as reported by AeroRoutes, as of May 1, 2027, Parata Air will launch daily nonstop flights between Seoul Incheon (ICN) and Los Angeles (LAX). The flight will operate with the following schedule:.

    WE301 Incheon to Los Angeles departing 12:00PM arriving 7:20AMWE302 Los Angeles to Incheon departing 9:50AM arriving 3:20PM (+1 days).

    Industry observers note that parata Air will operate the route with an Airbus A330-200, featuring 260 seats, including 18 business class seats and 242 economy seats. The 5,944-mile flight is blocked at 11hr40min eastbound and 13hr30min westbound.

    In a recent development, tickets on the flight are now on sale, and I see fares starting at around $670 one-way in economy, and around $2,500 one-way in business class. Those aren’t exactly terribly attractive fares for a newcomer that appears to have a pretty lackluster onboard product.

    In a recent development, for those not familiar with Parata Air, the airline debuted operations back in 2019, but it has a fleet of just a handful of planes, including three Airbus A330s and two Airbus A320s. This will be the carrier’s first service outside of Asia. As I hinted at in the headline, I imagine this is a fully unknown player to most people, and I had never heard of the airline until a few weeks ago.

    Random thought — can anyone think of a smaller international airline (in terms of fleet size) that added long haul flights to the United States? I know that’s very specific, but I can’t think of another one… it’s possible I’m missing something, though!

    The airline acquired its three A330s secondhand from different sources, with the planes having flown for Garuda Indonesia, Hainan Airlines, and Thomas Cook (though that plane doesn’t have business class).

    Industry observers note that the Seoul Incheon to Los Angeles market is pretty well served in terms of capacity, but not so well served in terms of competition. That’s because no US carrier flies between Los Angeles and Seoul Incheon, and with Korean Air having acquired Asiana, there’s now only one South Korean flag carrier.

    If you look at the market, you’ll see that Korean Air operates up to four daily flights, and Air Premia operates up to two daily flights. Now we’ll see a third airline from the country operating in the market, though with the lowest capacity, and arguably the worst product.

    It has been revealed that it’ll be interesting to see when we see some competition here on the US side. Delta might operate the route eventually, but that doesn’t actually increase competition, since the airline has a joint venture with Korean Air. American has (smartly, probably) given up on Los Angeles as a long haul hub. So that leaves United, and I could definitely see the airline eventually adding service in the market, as a competitive response against Delta and Korean Air, if nothing else.

    Recent findings suggest that as of May 2027, Parata Air will be launching a newly introduced nonstop route between Seoul Incheon and Los Angeles, representing the carrier’s first service outside of Asia. The airline will be operating daily in the market with Airbus A330s. With this, there will be three South Korean carriers flying this route, though no airlines from the United States.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The busy Thanksgiving travel season is just about to kick off as millions take flight around the country. You can expect crowded terminals, long security lines and potentially surge-priced rides to and from the airport.

    The good news is that major ride-hailing players Uber, Lyft and Blacklane all have introduced Thanksgiving offers, including one that is exclusive to our TPG members.

    Here's how to make the most of your holiday ride transport.

    Related: Here’s what Thanksgiving foods you can bring in your carry-on and what has to be checked.

    Through Nov. 30, Uber is running a promotion called "From Bad Seats to Better Rides." If you get squeezed into a middle seat with no armrest or end up in the last row by the lavatory, you could receive up to 30% off your Uber ride home from the airport.

    To take part, register your flight and seat details on Uber's Thanksgiving promotion page. Uber provides several examples of undesirable seats but has not published a complete list of what qualifies as undesirable. Individual savings vary, and terms apply, so check the offer added to your Uber account before booking. In our testing, you will not be required to submit a boarding pass or an image of your undesirable seat to receive a discount.

    Industry observers note that TPG tip: Link your Delta SkyMiles and Uber accounts and select Delta as your earning partner before you travel. You will earn 1 mile per eligible dollar on UberX airport rides, 2 miles per eligible dollar on Uber XL, Uber Comfort, Uber Black and Uber SUV rides and 3 miles per eligible dollar on Uber Reserve rides in the U.S. Note that taxes, fees, mandatory charges and tips do not earn miles.

    Related: From Starbucks to Uber: Airline and hotel partnerships that earn points and miles.

    Uber One Member Days run through Dec. 1, where Uber indicates members can unlock up to $500 in savings across rides, deliveries, hotels and other offers. Some deals are targeted, so check your email and your Uber app to see if you are eligible, but offers may include:.

    No purchase is necessary to enter either sweepstakes.

    TPG tip: Link your Marriott Bonvoy and Uber accounts and select Marriott as your earning partner. You will earn 3 Marriott Bonvoy points per eligible dollar on Uber XL, Uber Comfort, Uber Black and Uber SUV rides in the U.S., including those booked with Reserve and 2 points per eligible dollar on UberX rides booked with Reserve. Members who have not linked the two accounts can also earn 1,000 bonus points for linking by Nov. 24, plus another 1,000 points after completing an eligible premium or Reserve ride by the same date.

    You can link both Delta and Marriott to Uber, but only one can be selected as the earning partner for a ride at a time, so choose which currency is more useful to you.

    Related: Marriott unveils Uber partnership changes: The good, the bad and the totally worthless.

    In a recent development, united MileagePlus members can earn 8 United miles per eligible dollar on scheduled airport rides with Lyft through Nov. 30, twice the standard rate of 4 miles per dollar. Link your MileagePlus and Lyft accounts and select United as your active rewards partner before booking.

    Industry observers note that the offer applies to eligible rides requested, completed and paid for in the U.S. or Puerto Rico.

    Make sure you schedule your ride in advance, because unscheduled airport rides only earn 3 miles per eligible dollar, while most standard personal rides earn 1 mile per eligible dollar.

    Note that taxes, fees, tolls and tips do not earn miles.

    TPG tip: Shift your rewards up a gear by paying with the (see rates and fees) or (see rates and fees), and you will earn 5 total Chase Ultimate Rewards points per dollar on qualifying Lyft purchases through Sept. 30, 2027. Both cards earn 1 point per dollar on purchases outside their bonus categories.

    Recent findings suggest that sapphire Reserve cardholders also receive a $10 monthly in-app Lyft credit through Sept. 30, 2027. Unused credit expires at the end of each calendar month.

    Related: How to easily earn extra rewards on Lyft rides.

    In a recent development, if you would rather avoid a crowded airport pickup zone, why not treat yourself to Blacklane? The global luxury chauffeur service operates in more than 500 cities across more than 60 countries, and its fixed prices include standard taxes, tolls, tips and fees.

    According to recent reports, TPG members can currently receive an exclusive $80 credit toward two chauffeur journeys in the U.S. To claim it, sign in to or create a TPG account through the TPG Member Offers page, then click through to Blacklane from the offer.

    Industry observers note that TPG tip: Bilt members can redeem Bilt Cash toward Blacklane rides each calendar year: up to $50 for Blue and Silver members, $100 for Gold members and $150 for Platinum members. Blacklane rides booked through Bilt also earn 1 Bilt Point per dollar.

    Related: No surge, no scramble: Why I loved using Blacklane for my latest airport transfer.

    Thanksgiving airport rides can be expensive, but this holiday season you may be able to reduce the cost and/or increase your rewards.

    Recent findings suggest that uber's bad-seat offer is the most straightforward discount if your aircraft seat qualifies and is a fun and lighthearted way to reward those whose seat allocation is unfortunate. Uber One members should also check their accounts for targeted airport and hotel offers, while the Lyft promotion is an easy way to earn double United miles on a ride many travelers will book anyway.

    Link your loyalty accounts, select the right earning partner and check your card benefits before traveling to ensure a happy and rewarding holiday.
