    Delta SkyMiles Blue Amex Review: Is The No Annual Fee Card Worth It?

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2141 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that american Express and Delta have had a close relationship for many years, and as part of that, they issue seven co-branded Delta Amex cards.
    • Link: Learn more about the Delta SkyMiles® Blue American Express Card.
    • Before I get into the full Delta Blue Amex Card review, here’s an overview of the card’s main features, from its welcome bonus and earning rates, to other benefits:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that american Express and Delta have had a close relationship for many years, and as part of that, they issue seven co-branded Delta Amex cards. This is my in-depth Delta SkyMiles® Blue American Express Card review, as this is the entry-level personal Delta credit card with no annual fee (Rates & Fees), and probably the least talked about card in the lineup. It’s far from the most rewarding Delta credit card, but if you want to earn Delta miles and only fly the airline occasionally, it could be worth a look.

    Link: Learn more about the Delta SkyMiles® Blue American Express Card.

    Before I get into the full Delta Blue Amex Card review, here’s an overview of the card’s main features, from its welcome bonus and earning rates, to other benefits:.

    Beyond that, here are my thoughts on the pros and cons of the Delta Blue Amex:.

    In a recent development, when applying for a credit card, the welcome bonus, eligibility rules, and fees, are obviously major factors that people consider. With that in mind, let’s take a look at those details for the Delta Blue Amex Card. As you’d expect for this card, the lack of fees largely comes at expense of a smaller welcome offer.

    According to recent reports, the Blue Delta SkyMiles Amex has a welcome offer of 10,000 bonus SkyMiles after spending $1,000 within the first six months of your card membership. Based on my latest points & miles valuations, Delta SkyMiles are worth 1.1 cents each, making this bonus worth $110. We’ve seen this card’s bonus go a bit higher, but not by a huge amount.

    The bonuses on all other Delta Amex cards are significantly higher, which isn’t a surprise, since cards with annual fees often have better bonuses than cards without annual fees. It’s hard to get excited about that offer, but I guess something is better than nothing?

    Sources indicate that the welcome offer on the Delta Blue Amex Card is “once in a lifetime,” so it’s not available to you if you currently have the card, or if you’ve had the card in the past. The rules go beyond that, though.

    Recent findings suggest that you’re actually not eligible for the bonus on the card if you have or have had any of the more premium versions of the Delta Amex card portfolio, at least among the personal cards. This is true across the portfolio, and the idea is that you’re always eligible for the bonus on a more premium card, but not eligible for the bonus on a less premium card.

    So if you do want to pick up multiple Delta Amex cards, you’ll want to first apply for the Delta Blue Amex, then the Delta Gold Amex, then the Delta Platinum Amex, and then the Delta Reserve Amex (or at least you’ll want to move in that general order).

    Beyond that, Amex’s general card application restrictions apply, including that you can typically have at most five credit cards from Amex at a time (that doesn’t include hybrid cards).

    Let me emphasize once again that the Blue Delta Amex has no annual fee. It’s great to see a trend whereby we’re seeing more airline credit cards with no annual fees, since it’s a nice option for someone who wants a co-branded credit card, but doesn’t want to pay an annual fee.

    You can also add additional users to the card at no extra cost.

    Sources indicate that there’s no doubt that card issuers are moving toward offering more no annual fee cards with no foreign transaction fees, though it’s still not the standard. The Blue Delta Amex has no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees), which is awesome, since most Amex no annual fee cards do still have these fees.

    When it comes to earning rewards, the Blue Delta SkyMiles Credit Card offers:.

    For a no annual fee product, it’s nice to see a card offering a bonus on dining. While some bonus categories are better than none, I don’t find the bonuses to be particularly compelling, as there are still better cards out there for airfare purchases and restaurant purchases.

    Sources indicate that while Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles. You can redeem SkyMiles for flights on Delta or on Delta’s SkyTeam partners, like Air France, China Airlines, and Korean Air.

    Sources indicate that partner award flights can be an especially good option if you focus on flights that don’t touch the United States, since flights that do are more expensive and get you less value for your miles. I’ve also seen some good award prices for Delta One (business class) awards, specifically for booking roundtrip rather than one way.

    In a recent development, the Delta Blue Amex is a decent no annual fee card in the sense that it offers 2x miles at restaurants and has no foreign transaction fees, but how are the perks on the card? Not surprisingly, this is an area where the card lags, and where the cards with annual fees offer significantly more value.

    Nonetheless, there are some perks to the card that may prove valuable to the occasional Delta flyer.

    In a recent development, if you have the Blue Delta Amex, then you can save 20% in the form of a statement credit for eligible pre-purchased meals, and in-flight purchases of food or alcoholic beverages, on Delta flights. Allow 8-12 weeks for the statement credit to post.

    Industry observers note that having the Blue Delta Amex makes you eligible for the Delta Pay With Miles program. What is that? This allows those with co-branded Delta Amex cards to redeem miles for one cent each towards a Delta flight purchase (in increments of 5,000 miles per $50). That’s not the best deal in the world, though this is a feature that’s exclusively available to those with an eligible card.

    Some people find this to be useful since they can redeem their miles towards flights, and then they still earn elite miles for taking those flights.

    It has been revealed that in other words, the 10,000 miles available as part of the welcome offer can be redeemed for a minimum of $100 worth of travel on Delta. This is obviously the lowest cost option for unlocking that benefit.

    According to recent reports, the Delta Blue Amex includes access to dedicated entrance lanes and fast lanes at stadiums and arenas that participate in the Amex Venue Collection program. As part of this benefit, you can also get 10% back on qualifying concessions purchases, up to $250 back per calendar year. (Enrollment required).

    Amex Offers is a program that offers discounts for purchases with all kinds of retailers. There’s huge value to be had in getting as many Amex cards as possible, so that you can get these offers on multiple cards.

    The ideal situation is to have a no annual fee card (like this one), so you can get access to these offers without paying an annual fee to get access to this.

    It has been revealed that amex Offers could save you hundreds of dollars per year. You can access these offers by logging into your account and scrolling down to the bottom of your account summary page.

    The Delta Blue Amex comes with some basic travel and purchase protection benefits:.

    There are some coverage limits and exclusions to be aware of, so you’ll want to review the full details in the card’s benefits guide before assuming you’re insured.

    Sources indicate that car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Tech giant. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc. Extended warranty and purchase protection: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

    Many people who like Delta as a brand may be tempted to pick up the Delta Blue Amex — it allows you to earn miles with Delta, it has no annual fee, and it offers some perks that could add value (20% off inflight purchases, Amex Offers, access to Delta Pay With Miles, etc.).

    However, in general, I wouldn’t recommend outright applying for this card:.

    Let me address both of those points below.

    If you’re considering the Delta SkyMiles Blue Amex, let me make the case for applying for the Delta SkyMiles® Gold American Express Card (learn more) instead, which right now has the limited-time offer:.

    Recent findings suggest that you can always get the Gold Delta Amex, and then if you don’t find it to be worth the annual fee, you can downgrade it to the Blue Delta Amex after a year. That would allow you to maintain the card account, and you wouldn’t pay the annual fee when you downgrade (and you’d still get the elevated perks and bigger bonus for the first year).

    At a minimum, it really is worth trying the Delta Gold Amex to see if you like it and to take advantage of the better bonus, and then you can downgrade at a later point if you find it’s not worthwhile.

    If you are looking to earn Delta SkyMiles through credit card spending then consider using a card earning Amex Membership Rewards points. That’s because these points can be transferred to Delta SkyMiles at a 1:1 ratio, and you can in many cases earn points at a much faster rate.

    For example, the American Express® Gold Card (learn more) offers 4x points at restaurants worldwide (on up to $50,000 in purchases per calendar year and then 1x) and at U.S. supermarkets (on up to $25,000 in purchases per calendar year and then 1x), and 3x points on flights booked directly with airlines or at AmexTravel.com. That’s a much better return than you’ll get on this card, and it’s also quite easy to make the math on the card work.

    If you’re absolutely committed to having a no annual fee card and want to maximize your return on spending, there are lots of excellent no annual fee cards to consider.

    My favorite is the Citi Double Cash® Card (learn more). The card earns 1% cash back when you make a purchase, and 1% cash back when you pay for that purchase (in the form of ThankYou points).

    But it gets even better than that — rewards earned on this card can be converted into ThankYou points at a 1:1 ratio and can be moved to partner programs at the best possible ratio, assuming you have the card in conjunction with one earning premium ThankYou points, like the Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more).

    That means the card earns two ThankYou points per dollar, and I value those points at 1.7 cents each, so that’s like a 3.4% return on everyday spending.

    In a recent development, I appreciate that American Express and Delta offer a no annual fee option with the Delta Blue Amex. For someone absolutely committed to getting a Delta Amex Card and not paying an annual fee, this is the best/only option.

    The card has no foreign transaction fees, offers 2x miles on dining, and gives you access to Pay With Miles and 20% discounts on inflight purchases.

    #53895. Industry News: Would Alaska-Hawaiian 12-Year Widebody Captains Really Earn $493.41 An Hour Under The Tentative Pilot Contract?

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1476 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Would Alaska-Hawaiian 12-Year Widebody Captains Really Earn $493.41 An Hour Under The Tentative Pilot Contract?

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1476 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that after more than 600 days of negotiations, Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines came to a tentative Joint Collective Bargaining Agreement with the Air Line Pilots Association International (ALPA).
    • It has been revealed that that rate is only the starting point for 2027 and is scheduled to rise annually, reaching $539.16 per hour by 2030, according to Aero Crew News.
    • Industry observers note that the terms ALPA agreed to on November 10 will be put to a vote on December 1 for the 4,600 union membersto collectively ratify, according to Airline Geeks.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that after more than 600 days of negotiations, Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines came to a tentative Joint Collective Bargaining Agreement with the Air Line Pilots Association International (ALPA). The terms now dictate that a 12-year widebody captain will earn an eye-popping base rate of $493.41 an hour starting in early 2027. Most mainline airline pilots credit between 800 and 1,000 flight hours per year, meaning a $493.41 rate translates to roughly $395,000 to $493,000 in base flight pay.

    It has been revealed that that rate is only the starting point for 2027 and is scheduled to rise annually, reaching $539.16 per hour by 2030, according to Aero Crew News. The Black Box Aviation Podcast reported that rates will be adjusted annually to match the average of American, Delta, Southwest, and United on comparable aircraft, or increase by at least 3%, whichever is greater. Alaska Air Group will also contribute 18% directly to 401(k) accounts, alongside a performance-based program with 5% annual payouts.

    Industry observers note that the terms ALPA agreed to on November 10 will be put to a vote on December 1 for the 4,600 union membersto collectively ratify, according to Airline Geeks. If approved, the new pay scales take effect on January 31, 2027. The new contract represents an immediate raise from $86.41 to $102.41 per hour, or a 21.2% to 26.2% pay bump.

    Sources indicate that the agreement is a long-awaited resolution following Alaska Air Group’s $1.9 billion acquisition of Hawaiian in September 2024. While the Federal Aviation Administration approved the financial merger and granted a single operating certificate in October 2025, aircrews remained divided. Formal joint negotiations introduced in February 2025, aiming not only to set uniform pay rates but also to establish an operational framework to reorganize the pilots and jets of the combined fleet.

    ALPA negotiators built the newly introduced agreement on Alaska’s existing contract framework while preserving legacy Hawaiian protections. Until the unified labor contract is official, management cannot freely assign pilots across both of the newly combined networks or readily swap aircraft to new airfields based on changing demand.

    Captain Drew Coyle, the Alaska Airlines MEC chair, commented on the negotiations.

    According to recent reports, “Our Joint Negotiating Committee remained focused on the priorities of both pilot groups while working through some of the most complex challenges facing our combined membership. Nothing about this process was easy. Now it’s our pilots’ turn to review the agreement, ask the tough questions, and decide whether it meets their expectations.”.

    The tentative agreement also clears a major labor hurdle to Alaska’s long-haul expansion and Hawaiian's $600 million modernization plan. Alaska is expecting up to 17 new Boeing 787 Dreamliners that will launch 12 new overseas routes. Meanwhile, Hawaiian’s fleet overhaul in Honolulu will retrofit all 24 Airbus A330-200 widebodies with new Leihōkū lie-flat suites and premium economy cabins. Still, flying two dozen midlife A330s alongside new 787s forces the airline to maintain separate supply chains, training programs, and maintenance programs.

    Passing this contract is only half the battle because Alaska and Hawaiian pilots still cannot fly each other's jets until their seniority lists merge. Under federal law, a neutral arbitrator must combine both pilot rosters into a single master list. Because seniority controls everything from captain upgrades to holiday schedules, pilots must stay separated on their legacy fleets until that process finishes.

    Before seniority talks even wrap up, all 4,600 member pilots must approve the four-year agreement itself. Union voting runs from December 1 through December 22. If a majority votes yes, the upcoming pay rates and scheduling rules officially take effect on January 31, 2027, locking in labor stability through January 30, 2031, while eliminating the old pay gap between both workforces.

    Captain Larry Payne, the Hawaiian Airlines MEC chair, also remarked on the agreement.

    “This joint collective bargaining agreement represents an important milestone for both pilot groups. The decisions made throughout these negotiations will shape our pilots’ careers and quality of life for years to come. If approved, this agreement will establish the foundation for future contracts as we move forward together as one pilot group.”.

    According to recent reports, once seniority lists finally combine, Alaska Air Group can unleash the full scheduling flexibility it bought with the merger. Management will be able to shift crews seamlessly between Hawaii's refreshed narrowbodies and Seattle's growing Dreamliner fleet as seasonal travel shifts. That operational freedom was impossible after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) granted a single operating certificate in October 2025, merging safety rules but leaving cockpits divided.

    Ultimately, locking in $493.41 an hour for widebody captains proves Alaska is serious about competing alongside major legacy airlines on global routes. Yet paying top-tier wages across both fleets raises the stakes for every flight across the Pacific. The carrier's long-term financial success now hinges on whether it can fill those upgraded cabins at profitable fares against tough domestic and international rivals.

    It has been revealed that as part of the merger, Alaska took over Hawaiian's 787 Dreamliner orders and rebranded its existing 787s to construct an international gateway at its historic Seattle-Tacoma International (SEA) base. To make the increased $493.41 widebody pay rate financially viable, Alaska is dividing its twin-aisle jets across the combined fleet's two unique hubs. Thus, Hawaiian maintains its legacy A330-200s in Honolulu to meet established island leisure and regional Pacific demand.

    Hawaiian originally sought the 787-9 in 2018 to upgrade its fleet and increase capacity on long-haul Pacific routes. Hawaiian even canceled a prior order for six A330neos because the Dreamliner had superior fuel efficiency, longer range, and more business-class seating in densely populated markets such as Tokyo and New York. Hawaiian eventually increased its commitment to 12 Dreamliners before merging with Alaska.

    Alaska now has widebody jets, experienced pilots, and foreign operating certificates, which it lacked as a primarily narrowbody airline before acquiring Hawaiian. From Seattle, Alaska deploys the 787-9 on ultra-long, high-demand routes to Tokyo Narita, Seoul, London, Rome, Paris, and Athens. The Dreamliner’s range and fuel efficiency are an ideal fit for these business and luxury travel corridors where higher ticket prices offset premium pilot wages.

    It has been revealed that in January, Alaska placed a historic order for 105 737 MAX 10s and five more 787-10s, pushing its total Boeing order book past 240 planes. This international push fits naturally with the airline's identity as a fiercely loyal, all-Boeing mainline operator based in Boeing’s backyard. By folding Hawaiian’s Dreamliners into an all-Boeing fleet, Alaska avoids the high cost of training crews and stocking parts for Airbus widebodies.

    It has been revealed that back in Honolulu, Hawaiian’s A330-200 fleet anchors core flights to Tokyo Haneda, Osaka, Sydney, Papeete, and Pago Pago, alongside major West Coast cities. Starting in 2028, Hawaiian will upgrade all 24 jets with upcoming Leihōkū lie-flat suites and premium economy cabins. Although older A330s lack the Dreamliner’s range and fuel efficiency, their lower ownership costs bring costs down to make economy vacation airfare more affordable.

    It has been revealed that the narrowbody crews of the combined Alaska-Hawaiian fleet are about to undergo a significant fleet makeover, much like the widebody pilots who fly long ocean trips. Hawaiian is retiring its outdated 717s, which are frequently used for interisland flights between Honolulu and nearby islands. As part of the expanded narrowbody business in the continental US, Alaska Air Group is moving some 737-800s to Hawaii and bringing its own newly introduced 737 MAX 8 and MAX 10 aircraft.

    Recent findings suggest that under the latest deal, 12-year narrowbody captains are paid $401.09 per hour. That's $92.32 less than widebody captains. Despite the lower hourly pay, narrowbody pilots perform significantly more takeoffs and landings every shift. This is especially true for crews doing 30-minute island hops. Replacing the 128-seat 717 with larger 737s will add dozens of additional seats per flight while also updating the flight deck, saving fuel on each sortie, and decreasing fleet maintenance. The pilots will have to train on a larger airframe, but the airline will be able to transport more passengers without recruiting additional workers.

    Industry observers note that switching to an all-737 narrowbody fleet simplifies pilot training and spare parts across both airlines. Instead of maintaining separate cockpit ratings for 717s, A321neos, and 737s, pilots can eventually fly a single narrowbody type across West Coast and island routes. This standardization lets management smoothly shift crews between mainland and island flying whenever seasonal travel demand spikes or dips.

    Recent findings suggest that still, operating larger 737s on short interisland routes brings clear economic and mechanical trade-offs. Because the 737-800 is much heavier than the 717, it burns more fuel per trip and puts extra wear on brakes and landing gear during frequent landings. However, the higher seat capacity lowers the cost per passenger, helping the airline offset those added baseline expenses.

    Surprise: Aer Lingus Unveils First-Ever Premium Economy, Coming To 10 A330s

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (660 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Aer Lingus is getting on the premium economy hype.
    • This is quite a significant change, and one that should give it a leg up in the highly competitive trans-Atlantic market.
    • The cabin will feature just four rows with 28 seats in a 2-3-2 configuration.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Aer Lingus is getting on the premium economy hype. The Irish flag carrier has today announced it will introduce the cabin for the first time on 10 of its Airbus A330s, which will also feature new business and economy cabins (the product won’t be coming to the Airbus A321LR/XLR fleet).

    This is quite a significant change, and one that should give it a leg up in the highly competitive trans-Atlantic market.

    The cabin will feature just four rows with 28 seats in a 2-3-2 configuration. That’s about average when compared to other premium economy cabins. The narrow fuselage of the A330 means there’s only room for three seats in the middle section, rather than the four many other airlines offer.

    Recent findings suggest that in terms of specs, the 18-19 inch wide Recaro R4 seats will offer 38 inches of pitch and eight inches of recline. In addition to footrests, a staple of any decent premium economy, the seats have been designed with fixed headrest wings to provide a sense of privacy.

    As for the soft product, Aer Lingus promises three-course dining, drinks throughout the flight, a pillow and blanket, an amenity kit, and noise-reducing (not noise-canceling) headphones.

    I actually really like the design and color scheme. It’s modern, looks elegant and premium, and most importantly of all for the airline of the Emerald Isle, the colors are quintessentially Irish.

    Sources indicate that aer Lingus says premium economy fares will start from 700 Euros one-way, putting a return trip at around 1,400 Euros. That works out to around $1,534, and a few hundred dollars cheaper than United’s nonstop fares from Newark (EWR) to Dublin (DUB).

    We’ll have to wait until October 1 next year to try Aer Lingus’ new premium economy out for ourselves. The airline hasn’t yet announced which routes will get the product first, but we should find out in the coming months.

    The good news is, they’ll operate on many of the airline’s 18 nonstop routes from Dublin to the United States.

    Sources indicate that as a small, almost boutique-style airline with just 63 aircraft, Aer Lingus must remain competitive, especially in the saturated transatlantic market in which it predominantly operates. The addition of premium economy bridges the large gap between economy and business, and should open the airline up to a potential upcoming customer base who’ve never flown it before.

    I’ll be attending an event in Dublin tonight, so I should be back with more images and extra info soon!

    What do you make of Aer Lingus’ newly introduced premium economy?

    Breaking: Latino Democrats celebrate midterm gains, with warning for party

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (685 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that california Rep.
    • Latino voters moved sharply away from Republicans this year, and a record number of Latino Democratic candidates were elected.
    • Sánchez has a warning for her fellow Democrats.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that california Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, here at a 2020 news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center, is the chair of BOLD PAC. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Latino voters moved sharply away from Republicans this year, and a record number of Latino Democratic candidates were elected.

    But California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez has a warning for her fellow Democrats.

    “Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” said Sánchez, who leads the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.

    Failure to address rising costs and push back against President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda could once again scramble the political calculus and spark another realignment in two years, noted House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar of California.

    “While Latinos shifted towards Democrats and … gave us this mandate as a party, Democrats must continue to earn their trust, not just every two years, but every single day,’’ he said.

    In a recent development, leaders of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus joined newly elected Latino members on Tuesday for a news conference to celebrate the recent wins and the role the group played in securing the House majority for Democrats. The caucus will boast 55 members in the next Congress, its largest roster ever, according to Sánchez.

    BOLD PAC, the caucus’ campaign arm, invested heavily in Latino candidates this year, including in primaries.

    California Rep. Salud Carbajal noted that BOLD PAC raised more than $18.5 million this cycle, which helped candidates leverage outside money.

    Working-class majority-Latino districts in South Texas, Arizona and California were among the areas that provided Democrats with their biggest wins. Democrats capitalized on voter dissatisfaction over rising costs, the very issue that helped Trump and the GOP make significant gains among Hispanic voters just two years earlier.

    But the wins weren’t limited to districts with sizable Latino populations.

    Rep.-elect Denise Powell, who flipped a swing seat in Nebraska, credited BOLD PAC for playing a key role in her win.

    “Yes, there are Latinos in Omaha, and those Latinos actually helped decide this race,’’ she noted. “BOLD believed in me as a candidate, but they also believed in our community.”.

    Rep.-elect Bobby Pulido, who came to politics after a successful career as a Latin Grammy-winning Tejano singer, flipped a redrawn South Texas border district that Trump would have carried by 18 points in 2024.

    “A lot of people feel like they don't belong to either party. But there's one thing about Latinos is we belong to each other,’’ Pulido noted. “It's very hard to be a Latino right now in this country. … I expect to see us united, more united than ever, because it's a tough time right now.”.

    Recent findings suggest that several of the winning candidates deployed novel strategies to reach voters. Pulido famously began performing at quinceañeras after his Republican opponent dismissed him as a performer.

    Colorado Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, who flipped a battleground district north of Denver, attended World Cup and Broncos watch parties. “If people don't hear our message, then it doesn't matter,’’ he mentioned.

    The candidates “met those voters where they were,’’ Sánchez said. “They went into those communities and interacted in a very real and meaningful way. That's something I think that strategists or consultants don't always get. It's not just about pumping out lots of television commercials.”.

    Amid those successes for Latino Democrats, Florida, home to one of the largest Latino electorates in the country, was a different story. Republicans held all three majority-Latino districts in the Sunshine State, though former news anchor Eliott Rodriguez, the son of Cuban immigrants, came within half a percentage point of unseating GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar in a district that backed Trump by 15 points in 2024.

    BOLD PAC did have a victory to celebrate in Florida, with Rep. Darren Soto, the deputy chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, narrowly prevailing in a district that Republicans redrew as one that no longer had a Latino majority.

    “The redistricting wars ended up failing because of the investment by BOLD PAC,’’ Soto mentioned.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It’s not just Aer Lingus’ premium economy stealing the headlines in Ireland today. Expected to fly passengers for the first time on October 1, 2027, the new cabins are part of a comprehensive Airbus A330 tip-to-tail retrofit that will include new business and economy cabins. We covered the premium economy cabin in a separate article story.

    According to recent reports, the same 10 Airbus A330s that will get the airline’s fresh premium economy will also get a swanky new business class. The airline’s Airbus A321XLRs aren’t included in this cabin update.

    Aer Lingus is also introducing a self-service bar stocked with snacks and drinks. I wonder if this will include Champagne….

    The airline will also serve up a whole latest in-flight dining experience featuring dishes inspired by both Irish ingredients and its transatlantic destinations.

    It wouldn’t be a full retrofit without sprucing up economy.

    Per the renderings, Aer Lingus has done a great job again with the cabin’s look and feel. The emerald green Shamrocks are a lovely touch.

    Seats are configured in the A330’s classic 2-4-2 configuration — a favorite for those traveling in pairs.

    While the recline looks a bit modest here, the seat’s thickness looks like it’ll provide more support than some of those ultra-thin, rigid seats airlines are sneaking in these days.

    The six-way adjustable headrests should also mean less head-wobbling when catching some shut-eye.

    The curved design of the seat backs should hopefully mean noticeably more knee space.

    It has been revealed that aer Lingus is also upping its food and beverage ante for economy passengers. In addition to a snack bar, a latest mid-flight snack will be offered.

    In a recent development, A retrofit program like this was essential for Aer Lingus to remain competitive in the transatlantic market. The introduction of premium economy was a great move, especially since the cabin is known to be highly profitable.

    Aer Lingus has also done a great job of matching the Irish color scheme and sleek design across all cabins, which is more than can be said for some airlines these days. 😉.

    Breaking: JetBlue Doubles Down In Fort Lauderdale With Fresh Flights To Grand Cayman & Honduras In 2027

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (766 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • JetBlue has confirmed two new daily international services from Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL), connecting South Florida with Grand Cayman and Tegucigalpa in Honduras from February 2027.
    • Recent findings suggest that these latest additions follow Spirit Airlines' collapse in May, which created substantial opportunities at its former Fort Lauderdale stronghold.
    • The first upcoming service will launch on February 23, connecting Fort Lauderdale with Owen Roberts International Airport (GCM) in Grand Cayman.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    JetBlue has confirmed two new daily international services from Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL), connecting South Florida with Grand Cayman and Tegucigalpa in Honduras from February 2027. Today's announcement notes that this latest move will expand JetBlue's international network at the airport to 20 destinations, strengthening its position as a gateway to Latin America and the Caribbean.

    Recent findings suggest that these latest additions follow Spirit Airlines' collapse in May, which created substantial opportunities at its former Fort Lauderdale stronghold. JetBlue has moved aggressively to capture displaced demand, with an analysis of Department of Transportation data revealing that the airline's international passenger traffic is growing even faster than its added capacity.

    The first upcoming service will launch on February 23, connecting Fort Lauderdale with Owen Roberts International Airport (GCM) in Grand Cayman. Two days later, JetBlue will begin flying to Palmerola International Airport (XPL) in Comayagua, serving the Honduran capital, Tegucigalpa. Both routes will operate daily using Airbus A220 and A320 family aircraft, with introductory one-way fares starting at $99 and $183, respectively.

    The Honduras route will be JetBlue's first service to the Tegucigalpa area, complementing its existing San Pedro Sula operation. Daniel Shurz, JetBlue's senior vice president of network planning, emphasized the airline's commitment to expanding international connectivity and providing more options for travelers visiting friends and relatives.

    According to recent reports, "We're grateful for the way customers across South Florida continue to embrace JetBlue, and we're committed to delivering even more of the destinations and travel options they're looking for. With latest international service to Honduras and Grand Cayman, we're strengthening Fort Lauderdale's role as a key gateway to Latin America and the Caribbean.".

    According to recent reports, grand Cayman represents a return following JetBlue's short-lived service introduced in December 2025. The airline will also offer temporary daily flights to Port of Spain between January 29 and February 15 for Trinidad and Tobago's Carnival. Following the recent launch of newly introduced routes to Barranquilla and Cali, Colombia, JetBlue expects to exceed 150 daily departures at FLL during winter peaks, its largest schedule ever.

    In a recent development, jetBlue's international expansion at Fort Lauderdale has been substantial. An analysis of DOT T-100 International Segment data (available up until August) shows that the airline offered almost 1.7 million international seats in the first eight months of this year, up 33.4% year-on-year. The growth reflects an increasingly diverse network, with upcoming and restored routes complementing established Caribbean and Latin American services.

    In a recent development, much of the additional capacity stems from six international routes launched or restored in December 2025, including Aruba, Cartagena, Grand Cayman, Liberia, San Pedro Sula, and Sint Maarten. Meanwhile, the likes of Guayaquil, Guatemala City, and Santiago have also experienced significant growth, illustrating how JetBlue has strengthened previously limited operations.

    Sources indicate that however, growth has not been uniform. Montego Bay experienced a 33.9% capacity reduction, while Kingston, Cancún, and Punta Cana also recorded declines. The expansion has also coincided with international route reductions elsewhere in its network. The net result is that JetBlue is clearly not only growing its FLL international network, but also diversifying it, and concentrating capacity where opportunities are strongest.

    Although JetBlue's international expansion at FLL was already underway before Spirit's demise on May 2, the vacuum left by its former competitor has given it the space to accelerate that growth. To assess performance following Spirit's exit, Simple Flying zoomed in on the DOT T-100 data for just May–August 2026, compared to the same period in 2025.

    The findings are striking. JetBlue has increased its international seat capacity by 33.0%, yet passenger traffic surged by 45.8%, lifting average load factors from 79.4% to 87.0%, an improvement of 7.6 percentage points. To put that in context, Delta Air Lines averages approximately 85% load factors on its international routes, and at 87%, Fort Lauderdale is the top-performing base in JetBlue's network.

    Sources indicate that this clearly demonstrates that JetBlue has not yet touched the limits of demand at Fort Lauderdale, because even as it adds more and more capacity, it is attracting even greater numbers of passengers, and thereby filling a greater proportion of those seats. And there is the knock-on effect: Growing international passenger volumes also increase ancillary revenues, with JetBlue reporting 20% year-on-year loyalty revenue growth in Q3 2026, alongside a 55% increase in co-branded credit card acquisitions in South Florida.

    Recent findings suggest that A larger international network will certainly reinforce those trends. However, the airline's longer-term success will depend on translating this rapid passenger growth into stronger yields and sustainable commercial returns.

There’s actually no huge catch, and the changes I learned about last night on an intimate call with the Hyatt team are genuinely member-focused.

    According to recent reports, starting January 1, 2027, World of Hyatt members will start enjoying Milestone Rewards after 10 nights stayed or 20,000 base points. That’s great news for relatively infrequent Hyatt guests (like myself), who will no longer have to stay 20 nights or earn 35,000 base points to earn their first Milestone Reward.

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In January 2026, Lufthansa formally confirmed aims to retrofit its Airbus A380s with new business class seats.
    • There’s now a positive patch, as it looks like Lufthansa is running way ahead on that schedule, and all A380s should be retrofitted within the coming weeks….
    • It has been revealed that lufthansa is introducing a new business class product on its entire fleet of eight Airbus A380s.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In January 2026, Lufthansa formally confirmed aims to retrofit its Airbus A380s with new business class seats. The first plane with new cabins entered service in April 2026, and Lufthansa had committed to retrofitting all the planes by the middle of 2027.

    There’s now a positive patch, as it looks like Lufthansa is running way ahead on that schedule, and all A380s should be retrofitted within the coming weeks….

    It has been revealed that lufthansa is introducing a new business class product on its entire fleet of eight Airbus A380s. Rather interestingly, it’s only business class that’s getting new seats, while first class, premium economy, and economy, remain the same, aside from some minor upgrades (like improved inflight entertainment).

    The first A380 with new interiors entered service in April 2026, and AeroRoutes flags how as of December 18, 2026, Lufthansa is exclusively showing the new business class configuration on all routes. So starting in the coming weeks, you can expect the entire A380 network to feature the new cabins.

    Lufthansa A380s are based in Munich (MUC), and presently fly to Bangkok (BKK), Delhi (DEL), Los Angeles (LAX), Mumbai (BOM), San Francisco (SFO), and Washington (IAD). As you’d expect, there’s seasonal variation in the routes, though.

    What’s interesting is that Lufthansa isn’t introducing its fresh Allegris business class on these planes, but instead, is introducing another “off the shelf” product. Specifically, the airline has opted for the Thompson Aero Vantage XL product, which is in a staggered configuration.

    Each seat has direct aisle access, seat width of 58cm, and a bed length of at least two meters. Seats feature bluetooth connectivity and flexible partitions. Lufthansa is calling this “Premium XXL,” which… I’m not sure if that’s supposed to describe the seat, or if Lufthansa is taking some liberties on a new Grindr profile, somehow turning Vantage XL into Premium XXL.

    Recent findings suggest that as A380s are reconfigured, the business class cabin is shrinking in size by 10 seats, going from 78 seats to 68 seats. First class continues to have eight seats, premium economy continues to have 52 seats, and economy continues to have 371 seats.

    Recent findings suggest that it’s pretty cool to note how Lufthansa has reversed course on the A380. At the beginning of the pandemic, Lufthansa grounded its fleet of Airbus A380s, and the intent was that these planes would be retired, and would only reenter service “in the event of an unexpectedly rapid market recovery.”.

    With the strong recovery we’ve seen in transatlantic leisure demand, the airline made the decision to start bringing back Airbus A380s as of the summer of 2023, and eight of the initial 14 are now back in service (six of them were sold). At first, the return of the A380s was mostly described as a temporary measure, in light of delayed Boeing 777-9 deliveries. The airline didn’t commit to keeping these planes around in the long run, though that changed over time.

    According to recent reports, in recent years it has become clear that the A380 will have a long term place in Lufthansa’s fleet. Clearly this investment in the business class product reflects that.

    Industry observers note that lufthansa of course has its new Allegris cabins, including the new Allegris business class and new Allegris first class. These cabins debuted on newly delivered Airbus A350-900s, and we’re also seeing them on newly delivered Boeing 787-9s (though without first class).

    So why is Lufthansa not installing its new Allegris seats on the A380s? Well, I’d assume it comes down to a couple of factors. The biggest reason is quite straightforward — Lufthansa has had a really tough time getting its new Allegris seats certified, and these seats need to be certified on each individual aircraft. The idea is that by picking an “off the shelf” product, these seats are already certified, and therefore the airline could actually rely on getting them into service immediately.

    Second of all, I imagine that given the narrower fuselage of the A380 upper deck, it might’ve required even more complicated customization to fit the fresh Allegris seats up there.

    Recent findings suggest that for once, I’d say Lufthansa made a wise decision by just picking a generic product for its A380s. I think the big mystery is why Lufthansa just didn’t do this for its other planes, to avoid this entire mess. Separately, Lufthansa is reconfiguring its Boeing 747-8s, in a complicated two-part process. Initially, we’ll see the newly introduced Allegris business class seats on the lower deck, while the same business class seats will remain on the upper deck.

    Lufthansa is wrapping up the process of introducing a latest business class product on its Airbus A380s. The first plane with new cabins entered service in April 2026. While the initial plan was for all planes to be reconfigured as of the middle of 2027, it looks like that project will instead wrap up by December 2026, which is amazing.

    Recent findings suggest that rather than installing the new Allegris business class seats, the airline is instead installing a more generic product, the Thompson Aero Vantage XL seat, which is a significant improvement over the product you’ll otherwise find on these jets. As planes are reconfigured, business class capacity is being reduced by 10 seats, from 78 to 68.

    In a recent development, lufthansa sure is all over the place when it comes to modernizing its cabins. Either way, this change is good to see.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday.
    • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move quickly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.
    • Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move quickly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.

    Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.

    Industry observers note that “One of the things that we need to do is to move the Dream and Promise Act for DACA recipients and TPS recipients,” Jeffries said, referring to a Democratic bill introduced last year. “We should actually move that bill immediately.”.

    The proposal aims to create a path to citizenship for certain Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipients and Temporary Protected Status holders. Similar legislation has been a top priority for Democrats in both chambers for more than a decade, with Democrats unable to advance this bill in the House while Republicans have held the majority.

    Jeffries also reiterated his calls to rein in Immigration and Customs Enforcement and redirect funding allocated to the agency through Republicans' budget law known as the One Significant Beautiful Bill Act, while expressing a desire for bipartisan cooperation on immigration more broadly.

    In a recent development, “We think the border should be safe and strong and secure, and we think our immigration system overall is broken,” Jeffries noted. “We need to fix it in a comprehensive way, and certainly, it's our hope that a handful of Republicans will be willing to join us, so we can fix it in a bipartisan way.”.

    On healthcare, however, Jeffries offered fewer specifics, suggesting Democrats still have decisions to make before taking control of the chamber. Democrats broadly agree on the need to restore subsidies for intends purchased through health insurance markets that expired at the end of 2025. But the question of what additional steps the party should pursue with the goal of expanding coverage and lowering prices is likely to be a major test of Democratic leadership’s ability to find consensus among its robust new majority.

    When asked how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that's all part of an ongoing conversation.”.

    The Latest York Democrat outlined several broader healthcare priorities, including reversing Medicaid cuts enacted under President Donald Trump, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, all of which Democrats have vowed to do over the last year.

    “Out of the gate, what we clearly have to do is fix our broken healthcare system in terms of the damage that's been done by Donald Trump and MAGA extremists over the last two years, and that clearly involves reversing the Medicaid cuts and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits, and beginning to engage in supporting medical research, particularly things like research for pediatric cancer,” Jeffries added.

    Sources indicate that democrats established a healthcare working group earlier this Congress, led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. and Terri Sewell, D-Ala., to gather perspectives and develop policy proposals as the party works toward a broader agenda.

    Without an announced challenger, Jeffries has expressed confidence that he’ll secure the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who have said they remain “undecided” ahead of Wednesday’s elections. Jeffries, who was introduced as “Speaker Jeffries” on election night, said last week he was “very confident we’ll get there” and confirmed that the caucus will hold a recorded vote in the contest.

    In a recent development, rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to go forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives, many aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America, had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

    Jeffries stated Tuesday the approach mirrors the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who is best positioned to lead based on “track record, experience and vision.”.

    In a recent development, this report was corrected to reflect Rep. Nancy Pelosi’s status as a current member.

    #53881. Tech Report: What Air Force One Pilots Do Before Flights That Most Other Pilots Never Do

    Tech Report: What Air Force One Pilots Do Before Flights That Most Other Pilots Never Do

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1420 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Standard actions for a commercial airline crew before a flight include reviewing the flight with each other, followed by a pre-flight walkaround.
    • In a recent development, the pilots of Air Force One also do these actions, but their pre-flight duties are much more thorough because of their job: transporting the President of the United States.
    • The two VC-25As are typically flown by two pilots, a flight engineer, and a navigator, while the VC-25B Bridge does not require a flight engineer (because it's based on the newer 747-8).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Standard actions for a commercial airline crew before a flight include reviewing the flight with each other, followed by a pre-flight walkaround. Later, the crew sets up the flight deck, inputs their flight plan into the aircraft's computer, and verifies the aircraft's weight and balance figures before pushback. It's a thorough procedure to ensure the aircraft is fully ready to operate safely, and these procedures apply to essentially every commercial flight.

    In a recent development, the pilots of Air Force One also do these actions, but their pre-flight duties are much more thorough because of their job: transporting the President of the United States. Air Force One is a callsign used to denote any US Air Force (USAF) aircraft flying the President, but it is most commonly associated with two Boeing VC-25As and the VC-25B Bridge, which are based on the Boeing 747. Crucially, the flight crew is concerned not just with safety, but also with security.

    The two VC-25As are typically flown by two pilots, a flight engineer, and a navigator, while the VC-25B Bridge does not require a flight engineer (because it's based on the newer 747-8). Before each flight, they coordinate with ground crews to verify that the apron and runway are clear of potential debris. The flight plan itself may look significantly different from what airliners operate, and the crew also needs to ensure that the aircraft's onboard security and defense systems are operational.

    According to recent reports, in addition to these actions, the flight crew of Air Force One needs to help maintain security. This means not just coordinating with security teams on the apron, but also with air traffic control to ensure that the airport and surrounding airspace is clear of any potential conflicts. The crew also verifies that the aircraft will receive priority handling from air traffic control, and they also must review aerial refueling procedures for the VC-25A, although this capability has never been used with the president onboard.

    The pilots typically must arrive three to four hours before the scheduled flight, coordinating with the US Secret Service to maintain security on the aircraft and at the airport. The aircraft is inspected, and its systems are tested to check for any potential technical faults. In addition, the crew has to review emergency procedures while also performing the more typical actions that you'd expect during the pre-flight flow. While this is usually a multi-hour process, flight crews are trained to perform departures with as little as an hour's notice.

    Industry observers note that every long-distance trip undertaken by the US president begins and ends at the White House South Lawn. Here, the president boards a US Marine Corps helicopter operating under the callsign 'Marine One', the callsign used for any USMC aircraft carrying the US president. The helicopter, which may be joined by several others during the trip, flies to Andrews Air Force Base, home to the Presidential Airlift Group. The flight typically takes about six to ten minutes, and when the president lands, Air Force One is already waiting.

    The VC-25s not only carry the president, but they also transport the president's Secret Service detail, senior staff, medical personnel, and advisors. In addition, the aircraft will typically carry the White House press pool, a rotating group of reporters and journalists covering the president. The president is always the last person to board the aircraft, and once he/she is onboard, the doors close before the engines are started. From there, the aircraft taxis to the runway and takes off.

    Upon arrival, the airport receiving Air Force One typically suspends operations. From there, the president may either take a motorcade or another US Marine Corps helicopter to their final destination. The vehicles required for the motorcade and the USMC helicopters are typically flown in ahead of time via a Lockheed C-5 Galaxy to ensure that they're ready for the president's arrival. When it's time to return to Washington, this process repeats itself.

    Sources indicate that the pilots commanding the VC-25s must be experienced airmen serving with the US Air Force. Generally, these crew members have prior experience operating complex multi-engine transport aircraft and must have logged a significant number of flight hours (generally at least 2,500 hours). From there, pilots usually transfer to the 89th Airlift Wing at Andrews Air Force Base and build experience transporting other executives on aircraft like the Boeing C-32 or C-40 Clipper.

    Pilots must maintain an exemplary flying record while serving in the USAF and keep a spotless permanent record. In addition, they must earn high-level qualifications to stand out further. Senior leadership evaluates the pilot roster at the 89th Airlift Wing, then handpicks the top aviators to enter the selection process for the Presidential Airlift Group. From there, the selection process includes interviews, psychological screenings, and simulator tests.

    The final piece for those selected to pilot the VC-25 is to obtain 'Yankee White' clearance. This is a special, top-level security clearance reserved for personnel supporting the US president and vice president, and getting it requires an extremely thorough background check. Investigators may interview family members and peers, as well as former neighbors or teachers to verify stability, loyalty, and dependability, in a process that can take as long as a year. Candidates must also have a spotless criminal and financial history.

    Recent findings suggest that the VC-25As that commonly serve as Air Force One are designed to serve as invulnerable command centers in the sky. They feature advanced defense and communications systems, while also being equipped with aerial refueling systems so that they may remain airborne until food and water run out. However, the 747-based VC-25As are also massive aircraft. Not every airport can easily accommodate the VC-25As, and they draw a huge amount of attention, which isn't always ideal.

    While the VC-25As are the most common aircraft that serve as Air Force One, the US president also occasionally travels on the Boeing C-32A, based on the 757-200. These planes are generally used when the president is traveling to airfields that cannot accommodate the VC-25A, and they can also be used as a backup aircraft when the president travels, as well as if a VC-25A is unavailable. Furthermore, the C-32s are useful when the president is traveling on sensitive missions, such as to active war zones.

    In February 2023, former president Joe Biden secretly traveled to Ukraine, marking the first time in modern history that a US president had visited an active war zone not under the control of the US. To get there, he took a C-32A rather than the VC-25A, stopping at Ramstein Air Base in Germany for refueling before proceeding to Poland, where he boarded a train to Ukraine. The C-32 was preferable because of the sensitivity of the mission, and the flight didn't even use the standard Air Force One callsign in this case; rather, the callsign used was 'SAM060'.

    The two VC-25As were delivered in the early 1990s and are based on the 747-200B, an aircraft that first entered service in the early 1970s. They're old and increasingly unreliable, and maintaining these aircraft is becoming difficult and expensive. As such, the USAF selected the 747-8 to serve as the platform for the replacement VC-25B in 2015, with first delivery scheduled for 2024. However, this has been pushed back multiple times, with first delivery now targeted for 2028.

    In 2025, the US government accepted a 747-8 configured as a business jet from the Qatari government as a gift. This aircraft, now titled the VC25B Bridge, is intended to serve as an interim supplement for the existing VC-25A fleet until the two VC-25Bs are ready. The focus with the VC-25B Bridge was to get the aircraft ready as soon as possible, and it entered service in July 2026, less than a year after it was accepted. The catch is that it lacks many of the safety and defense features that are typically needed for the missions.

    Three (747-200B), four (VC-25A).

    It has been revealed that the VC-25B Bridge is only intended to be in service until the VC-25Bs arrive, and the aircraft is set to be retired before the end of President Donald Trump's second term. The VC-25Bs that will succeed it are conversions of whitetail aircraft, but they are being retrofitted with a full assortment of security, communications, and defensive technologies. Not only will they replace the VC-25B Bridge, but they will also replace the VC-25As, and they will be among the world's most advanced and secure aircraft in service.

The National Executive benefit, Uber credits and the niche coupon book incentives make it make sense. CSR meanwhile makes no f-ing sense at all anymore. Used the StubHub benefit and the tix ended up getting canceled 15 min after transaction via the site. "The Edit" is just hotels assigned higher rack rates. $300 travel striked off the balance no matter what in early months is ok, I guess. What else? Nada. Getting this one immediately closed and I'm opening a CSP.

    Not listed on the negative side of the cost of these credits is the mental energy and time to track all of these coupons and remember to use them. If you don't value your time then I guess you can value the credits at closer to face value but spending hours of the month thinking about how to maximize $10 coupons is like throwing dollars away to get pennies.

    In a recent development, lucky--ever consider combining each month the $10 credit for Grubhub with the $10 promo code from Bilt (using Bilt cash). That's an easy $20 per month and if you pick up instead of deliver you avoid a lot of the pesky fees. Similarly, the $10 credit for Uber Eats can be combined with the $15 credit for Uber Eats on AMEX Platinum, which can further be combined with the $25 credit on AMEX Bonvoy, all for the same meal.

    Standing Athwart Pumpkin Tyranny

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (350 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that A pumpkin spice latte is on the menu at every coffee shop.
    • Through October and November, pumpkin is in everything everywhere all the time.
    • Abigail Anthony is a staff writer at National Review.

    It has been revealed that A pumpkin spice latte is on the menu at every coffee shop. Sometimes, the drink is served in a pumpkin-shaped mug. To lure in customers for brunch, quaint cafes serving pumpkin pancakes put a chalkboard sign on the sidewalk saying, “COME IN FOR GOURD VIBRATIONS!” Each bakery has pumpkin scones, pumpkin pie, pumpkin banana bread, and pumpkin coffee cake. An attempt to order an old fashioned will be met with an invitation from the demoralized bartender, “Do you want to try our pumpkin spice old fashioned?” The pen at the bank is topped with a rubber pumpkin; this way, customers know that all the money is kept safe. Little plastic pumpkins are in the windows displays at clothing shops, or beside the cashiers (who work in front of pumpkin-flavored nicotine patches). Squashes are piled high in cardboard bins by the entrance of every grocery store. I reach for what I think is my favorite chai tea blend on the shelves — but alas! It is now pumpkin chai with an orange label.

    Through October and November, pumpkin is in everything everywhere all the time. Anything edible is infused, swirled, drizzled, and dusted with pumpkin. You cannot escape the flavor: pumpkin cereal, pumpkin protein powder, pumpkin bagels with pumpkin cream cheese. The Asian aisle has frozen Kung Pao-mpkin Dumplings. Dog treats are flavored like a pumpkin spice latte because everyone must participate, no exceptions. Longstanding favorites are replaced, so French fries are now pumpkin fries. That peculiar squash always sneaks its way into a dish, and so the stuffed raviolis have a little bit of pumpkin. Despite its omnipresence, the pumpkin surprises you: The waiter arrives at the table with a salad that is topped — just for this week — with toasted pumpkin seeds. (Of course, the utensils are wrapped in a flimsy brown napkin dotted with little orange pumpkins.) Even things we thought were reliably mint, like gum and the dentist’s fluoride, are pumpkin spice.

    Abigail Anthony is a staff writer at National Review.

    On “ Standing Athwart Pumpkin Tyranny”.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that I’d like to think that I’m pretty understanding of airlines, and how they can fall short.
    • At the same time, sometimes there are situations where airlines act in a way that feels to me a little like theft.
    • Several weeks ago, I booked a ticket on Tunisair in business class from Tunis (TUN) to Marseille (MRS).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that I’d like to think that I’m pretty understanding of airlines, and how they can fall short. The airline industry is incredibly complex and low margin, and sometimes consumers have unrealistically high expectations, while not acknowledging the real cost and challenges of running an airline. Buying a ticket on a flight is more like buying a ticket on Amtrak than buying a night at a Four Seasons, and you should adjust expectations accordingly.

    At the same time, sometimes there are situations where airlines act in a way that feels to me a little like theft. Readers often share these stories with me, and I write about them when I can. Now I’d like to share my own story….

    Several weeks ago, I booked a ticket on Tunisair in business class from Tunis (TUN) to Marseille (MRS). A few days before the flight I received an email from Tunisair informing me that I had been downgraded. As it turns out, it was because my flight was swapped to a wet leased plane, in an all-economy layout.

    The email informed me of this change without actually acknowledging it was a downgrade. Instead, the email was in French, and it translated to “we are writing to inform you that your flight reservation has undergone changes.” And the only reference to the downgrade was that the fare class only highlighted as being “Y,” which obviously isn’t business class.

    Recent findings suggest that there was zero other proactive communication from the airline about the incident, and I flew the flight in economy. The airline of course acted as if nothing happened, and there was no mention of how to request downgrade compensation, or anything like that.

    After the flight, I submitted a request with customer service, asking for a refund for the fare difference. Making that request was a challenge in and of itself, because the customer service form is in French, and is not at all intuitive.

    Sources indicate that but anyway, it has been weeks, and I haven’t heard back. I’m a bit conflicted here. I try not to abuse credit card disputes, but you typically only have 60 days to file a dispute. So am I at the point where I should just file a dispute, or how would one handle that?

    It has been revealed that as I noted above, I try to be pretty understanding of airlines, and recognize how many different scenarios there are. Just in terms of doing business ethically, I do feel like there should be a proactive refund offer if the airline is informing you in advance that you won’t be getting the product that you paid for. I mean, if you can inform me that I’ve been downgraded, you can also process some sort of a refund.

    We’ve become desensitized to this kind of service level with airlines, but I’m trying to come up with a comparison. I guess it would be like buying premium tickets to a sporting event, being informed in advance that you’ll be given worse seats, and then customer service just not responding to you for weeks on end.

    If you managed to take my money, surely you can also manage to give it back if you can’t give me the thing I paid for, no?

    Tunisair informed me days before a flight that I had been downgraded (as it turns out, due to an aircraft swap), though there was no offer a refund for a fare difference, or anything. Weeks ago I sent an email to customer service asking for a refund for the fare difference, but I haven’t heard back.

    It just strikes me as really unethical to take someone’s money for an experience you’re not going to offer, and then not have a way to get a refund in a reasonable timeframe. I know airlines hate when people file credit card disputes, but when you’re approaching the 60-day mark with no response, what is one supposed to do?

    Am I the only one who thinks it’s ridiculous to proactively downgrade a customer, but then make getting a refund such a runaround?

    Senators still see NDAA as chance for online safety legislation

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (667 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday.
    • Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.
    • Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

    Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.

    Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.

    The Senate Judiciary Committee’s panel on Crime and Counterterrorism held the hearing after its Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., introduced a bill Monday that would ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements from affecting cases where a minor was harmed online, including by sexual exploitation.

    Hawley and Durbin also worked together on a separate bill to expand eligibility for victims of abuse to bring civil suits against online platforms that intentionally, knowingly or recklessly promoted or facilitated the abuse. It would also include penalties for certain platforms that fail to report child pornography violations on their sites.

    That bill is included in a manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill. Durbin encouraged Congress to pass the NDAA “in the closing days” of the session because “protecting children is an important part of it.”.

    “I have a few weeks left in my service in the United States Senate,” said Durbin, who is retiring at the end of his term in January. “I’m thinking each day it’s coming to an end, but I want it to come [to an] end the right way.”.

    The subcommittee has spent much of the 119th Congress focused on harms to children online, including from artificial intelligence chatbots.

    Tuesday’s hearing included testimony from survivors and experts on child exploitation on Roblox.

    Hawley said that victims are bound by pre-dispute agreements with Roblox to settle claims through private arbitration, rather than in court.

    In a recent development, “They slam the courthouse door shut in their faces,” Hawley stated. “We’re talking about children now, child victims of sexual exploitation online are denied their day in court by the very company that has exposed them to the content to begin with.”.

    A spokesperson for Roblox stated in a statement that “safety has been central” to the platform since its launch.

    “We require age checks for chat, place customers under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” the spokesperson said. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a firm’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”.

    Industry observers note that myriam Gilles, a professor of law at Northwestern University, told the panel that a 2022 law that ended forced arbitration agreements for victims of sexual assault has gaps. She mentioned Roblox has argued it does not apply to online actions, just “completed physical assault” and does not apply to platforms.

    She also stated that Hawley’s new arbitration bill would enhance the effects of his measure regarding civil suits by making sure those suits can be heard publicly if families so choose.

    “Congress can pass laws, but if [suits] just get shunted into private arbitration, they’re doing no good in the world,” Gilles said. “A right to sue that ends in secret arbitration is a right in name only.”.

    The hearing came the same day that advocates, including reality TV personality and activist Paris Hilton, held a press conference to urge House action on a bill (S 1837) that would allow individuals to bring civil suits over nonconsensual intimate depictions generated by artificial intelligence or for possession or production of deepfake porn if there was also intent to disclose the images.

    That bill passed the Senate in January but has not been taken up in the House.
