    • That was the greeting, complete with a lengthy handshake, President Donald Trump gave Vladimir Putin before two high-level meetings Thursday, including the first “trilateral” session with sitting U.S., Russian and Chinese heads of state.
    • “It’s nice to see you,” Trump told Putin before a private one-on-one meeting in China’s Shenzhen economic zone, before pulling the Russian strongman close and saying something into his ear too low for journalists’ microphones to pick up.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump arrive for a trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday. (Win McNamee/AFP via Getty Images).

    That was the greeting, complete with a lengthy handshake, President Donald Trump gave Vladimir Putin before two high-level meetings Thursday, including the first “trilateral” session with sitting U.S., Russian and Chinese heads of state.

    “It’s nice to see you,” Trump told Putin before a private one-on-one meeting in China’s Shenzhen economic zone, before pulling the Russian strongman close and saying something into his ear too low for journalists’ microphones to pick up.

    Trump and Putin then posed for the cameras with wide grins, again underscoring the U.S. president’s closeness with a world leader who has been partially shunned by the West since he launched a war with Ukraine in February 2022. Trump on Thursday also appeared several times alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping, who like Putin has been scorned by Republican and Democratic lawmakers for years.

    “We’ve had a great relationship for many years. We've known each other for a long time. And I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this — or, at least, start,” Trump told reporters as Putin beamed from a few feet away.

    They later were joined by Xi for a group photo before sitting down at a round wooden table with a large arrangement of pink flowers in the center.

    His interactions with and comments about Putin and Xi reflect Trump’s belief that his personal relationships can bend them toward U.S. interests. But that gambit clashed Thursday with his second term’s expiration date — the White House did not disclose any agreements reached during his various meetings with the two leaders, nor did Trump hold a press conference following the three-way session.

    It has been revealed that both Putin and Xi are adept at playing the geopolitical long game. The 26 months left in Trump’s term is a relatively short amount of time compared to the duo that has been in power for a combined 56 years and will remain in place for the foreseeable future.

    Indeed, even Trump acknowledged the first-ever meeting might not immediately yield much progress on its ostensible goal: paring each powers’ nuclear weapons arsenals.

    It has been revealed that “I must say, it's, quite frankly, a very hard thing to do, because once you have the nuclear weapons, it's very hard to not have them. It's very hard to give them up as the leader of a country,” Trump stated as Putin and Xi looked on. “Something that's very difficult to say, because … it's the way life works.

    “You know, you have thousands of weapons and you're supposed to give them up, and yet you have countries in addition to us, in much smaller numbers, but they have nuclear weapons, also,” he added. “So it's not an easy thing to do and give them up.”.

    Trump, who was convicted by a Newly introduced York jury in a business records case and who saw a federal election interference case against him dismissed only because of his reelection, also appeared to join Putin’s resistance to international criminal justice entities that have alleged Putin has committed war crimes in Ukraine.

    “In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nations’ sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction,” Trump said, a statement that would be almost unthinkable to hear from any other sitting U.S. president.

    It has been revealed that other world leaders, including democratically elected ones, at two Pacific region economic summits in which Trump participated this week did not receive the kind of cordial and personal treatment from the U.S. side that Putin and Xi enjoyed.

    And other world leaders and congressional Democrats this week expressed concern with Trump's closeness to the Russian and Chinese strongmen.

    Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., on Thursday called the unprecedented summit a “historic embarrassment.” He criticized Trump for leaving the meeting without any apparent concrete commitments from Moscow or Beijing on a number of issues, including curbing Chinese espionage inside U.S. companies and ending the Ukraine conflict.

    “This summit was nothing but a glorified photo op and a gift to Putin and Xi,” Schumer mentioned.

    Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote this Thursday on X, shortly after Trump’s warm greeting for the former KGB officer: “God, protect us from such friends.”.

    According to recent reports, nicolas Burns, a former senior U.S. diplomatic official under GOP and Democratic presidents, was critical of Trump’s meetings with Xi. He said it was “crucial” for U.S. and Chinese leaders to hold talks, but added: “We need stability in the relationship with China — but there’s a but.”.

    Sources indicate that “The president seems to be following a detente policy with China, with very little substance. There’s a lot of pomp and circumstance, red carpets, a lot of nice words,” the former ambassador to China, NATO and Greece told “Morning Joe” on MS NOW. “Too friendly with Xi Jinping, who’s not going to be swayed by rosy words from President Trump.”.

    Even before Trump met with the Russian and Chinese leaders behind closed doors, Republican and Democratic lawmakers said they doubted very much would come from it.

    “I want nuclear weapons to be reduced. As you know, China has been unwilling to even have a conversation with the United States about nuclear arms reduction until they reach a certain plateau in the number of weapons that they have,” House Armed Services Committee Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., told reporters Tuesday.

    Recent findings suggest that “I'm glad that they're willing to have the conversation. We do need a limit, as you know,” added Wittman, who lost his reelection bid earlier this month. “Right now, neither Russia nor China has a nuclear arms reduction treaty with the United States. It would be nice for us to actually have one.”.

    Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., an Armed Services Committee member, wanted Trump to press Putin over Ukraine.

    Sources indicate that “Ukraine is defending itself from Putin's aggression, which this president should be opposing as well,” Blumenthal remarked Tuesday. “We are spending no money on Ukraine. Let's be very clear: Arms to Ukraine are purchased by Ukraine with financial support from Europe, not America. … Let's support Ukraine.”.

    On spending, Trump and administration officials have been pressing Senate Republicans to swiftly pass another budget reconciliation measure with $350 billion more for the Defense Department. However, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and other GOP senators have signaled in the last 24 hours that they had shelved the notion of another fast-track spending measure.

    Industry observers note that “You have to have a path forward. You've got to get on it, and you have to protect it, and that takes 50 in the Senate,” Thune told reporters Thursday. “And then you've got to get it through the House. As you probably saw yesterday, a lot of folks in the House were lobbing grenades at the Senate reconciliation bill and complaints about it not being offset, et cetera. So, you know, in my view at least, you want to have a path forward to success.”.

    In a recent development, john M. Donnelly and Jackie Wang contributed to this report.

    Fascism mixed into cringey online content is easy to mock – but no less dangerous

    📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1110 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This article was originally published on The Conversation.
    • According to recent reports, against the backdrop of an unpopular war in Iran, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth declared on July 15, 2026, that the Pentagon would begin testing male service members 30 and older for low testosterone.
    • The combination of aggressive masculinity and militarism with the implications of testing for something like “spontaneous morning erections” as necessary for war fighting is emblematic of the administration’s tendency to combine fascist ideas and symbols with outright embarrassing messaging, or what I call “cringe fascism.”.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This article was originally published on The Conversation.

    According to recent reports, against the backdrop of an unpopular war in Iran, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth declared on July 15, 2026, that the Pentagon would begin testing male service members 30 and older for low testosterone. That, the department later said, would include assessing symptoms of low testosterone such as “reduced libido, loss of spontaneous morning erections, erectile dysfunction, diminished energy and physical performance, impaired concentration, reduced muscle mass, and depressed mood.”.

    The combination of aggressive masculinity and militarism with the implications of testing for something like “spontaneous morning erections” as necessary for war fighting is emblematic of the administration’s tendency to combine fascist ideas and symbols with outright embarrassing messaging, or what I call “cringe fascism.”.

    For some time there’s been a contentious debate among writers, historians and public intellectuals over whether Donald Trump’s presidency could be considered “fascist.” Some have argued that such claims are hyperbolic or inaccurate, while others say it is a useful and accurate ideological label.

    Either way, it would be difficult to deny that the Trump administration frequently draws from the well of fascist imagery and symbolism in its official messaging.

    Sources indicate that and that’s where the concept of cringe fascism fits in. In online parlance,“cringe” is a kind of embarrassment by proxy when someone posts something that should be embarrassing but which doesn’t seem to be to them.

    For their part, members of the Trump administration have relied on language and symbolism that borrows from the fascist or authoritarian playbook while doing so in a way that commenters often mock as patently ridiculous or embarrassing – or cringe.

    Industry observers note that but the purported silliness of these ideas, as with Hegseth’s testosterone policy, hides a much more serious – and to some critics, fascist – reality. That, moreover, is why the deployment of cringe can be effective: It can generate enthusiasm among conservative voters by trolling the left while reducing deadly serious policy debates to the level of online memes.

    Sources indicate that as Americans prepare for the midterms and a surely contentious presidential election in 2028, such considerations of Trump’s authoritarian tendencies are being put to the test. That’s especially true as he consistently threatens the integrity of elections, deploys immigration and other federal law enforcement officers on American streets in a highly contested manner, and attempts to target the press and restrict its access.

    As a scholar of conspiracy theories, I have been amazed at some of the more blatant efforts to repurpose fascist imagery by members of Trump’s inner circle.

    Industry observers note that consider, for example, the use of ethnonationalist and fascist imagery of “blood and soil” in sloganeering by the Department of Homeland Security, or encouraging U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement recruits to “Defend the Homeland.”.

    Sources indicate that and then there are the attacks on the press as the “enemy of the people,” echoing past totalitarian leaders, followed by Trump’s banning of mainstream media from the White House and the launch of Trump TV as the state channel. Critics view such moves to attack and restrict the press as hallmarks of fascist methods.

    Borrowing more obviously from fascist tropes was Trump posting on social media a mock-up of a potential new Space Force uniform. The post claimed to draw inspiration from Paul Verhoeven’s “Starship Troopers,” in which the soldiers are deliberately modeled on the fascist aesthetic and ideology of the Nazis.

    Alongside the authoritarian and fascist tropes, the Trump administration cannot seem to avoid “cringe.”.

    In a recent development, recent examples include the White House tweeting images of Trump as a videogame character on a select screen with sleeveless blue suit and bulging muscles, or sharing an AI parody of the new Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time game with an awkward video of a pixelated Trump running around the White House lawn. Or consider the post depicting Trump as Green Lantern, using his magic ring to raise a spectral border wall, launch a military attack and fix American industry.

    Industry observers note that on the one hand, the Trump administration seems determined to keep his party in power and enact a transformative MAGA policy agenda. On the other hand, Trump seems incapable of avoiding cringey riffs such as his digressions on men’s bodies in ways that seem strikingly at odds with his tough-guy persona. To see the commander in chief waxing poetic about Ohio Sen. Jon Husted’s rear feels deeply surreal.

    Sources indicate that trump’s seemingly incongruous comments occur at the same time that the secretary of defense is advocating hypermasculinity in the military through testosterone testing, reflecting a heady mix of masculinity and military supremacy that has long been a hallmark of fascism. Such a policy is also at odds with how the professional military has presented itself under previous administrations.

    The mixture of fascist aesthetics with cringe posting underscores the internal contradictions of the Trump administration.

    Industry observers note that it is difficult to see critics’ view of Trump’s second term as “fascist” when observers get such awkward online displays of silliness. And when official communications from the White House and federal agencies are equal parts tough talk, trolling and cringe, the underlying policies can get lost in the shuffle.

    Is is hard to know whether this flood of cringe is always intentional, but it is certainly confusing and hilarious to both Trump’s supporters and his opponents. But that belies what many critics have decried as authoritarian actions by this administration, and these comparisons with fascism continue to animate public discourse.

    Masked ICE agents continue to operate with some legal protections from the White House in their sometimes-deadly efforts to pursue and round up people it broadly accuses of being in the country illegally.

    Likewise, the DHS confirmed that ICE agents could be deployed to polling locations, while the agency has reportedly attempted to get access to voter information to investigate alleged voter fraud through increased surveillance.

    Sources indicate that the deployment of cringe might seems like a ridiculous, even unconscious, exercise by an administration that – as with the five-day tenure of former press secretary Katie Zacharia highlights – regularly exposes itself to derision and satire. Yet that’s why the use of such a concept can be so strategically effective: It turns potentially deadly serious policy consequences and ideological choices into a game of memes and online gamesmanship.

    It has been revealed that matthew N. Hannah, Associate Professor of Rhetoric, Politics and Culture, University of Wisconsin-Madison.

    • While divorce may sometimes be inevitable, it should be the exception, not the norm.
    • Hadley Heath Manning is a senior fellow at Independent Women’s Forum (www.iwf.org).

    Amanda Seyfried and her husband Thomas Sadoski — who is also the father of her children — described their recent separation this way: “We’ve got each other forever . . . and it’s GOOD.” On Instagram, Seyfried shared a quote by divorce influencer Olivia Howell, who goes even further, arguing that divorce should be “boring,” “normal,” and reframed as “just another life transition.”.

    No. Divorce isn’t “GOOD.” It’s tragic. While divorce may sometimes be inevitable, it should be the exception, not the norm.

    Hadley Heath Manning is a senior fellow at Independent Women’s Forum (www.iwf.org).

    On “Amanda Seyfried’s Divorce Decadence”.
